choice: A bar verdict on one element names the argument that brought it, by its index in the caller's list; one on a whole list, a merge's union or an element held before names the field
reason: The bar judges the decision an op leaves, whose tags and anchors are sorted sets, so the index of an element there is not the index the caller wrote, and a revise's add_tags element is no element of tags in the caller's batch. Each op hands the bar the arguments that bring elements into its lists (check::Sources: the record's lists, a revise's whole list and its add_* list), and a refusal or a warning on an element names the first argument that holds it and its position there, as ops[3].add_tags[0]. A fault no single argument holds, a count of the whole list, an element the decision held before the op, or a merge's union, names the decision's field without an index.
alternatives: Name the element by its index in the decision: rejected because a sorted set renumbers what the caller wrote
Quote the element instead of an index: rejected because an element can be long, and the argument path is what a caller fixes
origin: review findings of the stateless-server landing

choice: A batch holds at most MAX_BATCH_OPS (50) ops, so with names of at most 128 bytes its result names every op within the 24 KiB tool result budget
reason: The result of apply is one entry per op, naming its node and what it changed, never echoing texts. Its longest entry names two nodes; fifty such entries with 128-byte names fit the budget, which a unit test asserts over the longest entry each op kind can make, so a result is never cut. A larger change is several batches. Each list of an op holds at most MAX_LIST_ITEMS (100), and every text its store limit.
alternatives: 100 ops a batch: rejected because the result could then exceed the budget and be cut
Counts only in the result: rejected because the caller needs to see which op did what, a status change most of all

choice: Each op is checked against the graph the earlier ops left, and a refused batch names its first op at fault: its index, kind and target, the argument and the rule
reason: Later ops may build on earlier ones: a component added and then a decision recorded in it, a rename and then a revise of the new name. A fault in op 3 leaves the graph op 4 was written for unreached, so a fault reported for op 4 would describe a graph the batch never makes; the first fault is the one the caller fixes. Each op names the argument at fault within it (add_depends_on[1], component). A rule of the quality bar on one element names the argument that brought it (add_tags[0]), and one on what no argument holds alone names the decision's field (alternatives). Each refusal carries a typed Rule with a stable name (name_taken, not_found, depends_on_cycle, has_dependents, no_change, both_forms, not_held, reason_words_max and the rest, store/apply/refusal.rs); Refusal::path joins them as the MCP field ops[3].add_depends_on[1]. A fault of the batch itself names its argument alone: ops, origin. An issue the final validation finds is attributed to the op that last changed a node it concerns. Each op is held to the bar, its [quality] patterns included, as it runs, so a pattern's refusal, pattern_work and pattern_gave_up name the op they stop, before the fault of any later op.
alternatives: Report every failing op: rejected because an op after the first fault is judged against a graph that op never meant
Check every op against the loaded graph, ignoring earlier ops: rejected because a batch could not add a component and then decide in it
Refuse with a message only: rejected because a caller branches on the rule and the op, not on prose

choice: A batch writes only the files whose value differs from the one the batch began with and removes those it took away; a node renamed away and back is neither
reason: Writing an untouched file would rewrite a hand edit out of form and add a file to the history commit that no op changed. The undo record names every node an op touched with its starting value; a file is written when its value differs from that value, removed when it is gone, and left alone when the ops returned it to where it began. The files written or removed leave the writer's list of non-canonical files.
alternatives: Write every file an op touched: rejected because a rename and its undo in one batch would rewrite both files and every dependent for nothing

choice: A C or C++ definition is public unless static, an anonymous namespace or an access label says otherwise; class members are private and struct members public until a label
reason: A count of what a file exposes needs each definition's visibility as its source states it. In C and C++ that is linkage and access: a function or variable at a namespace's top has external linkage unless static or in an anonymous namespace says internal, and a member is as accessible as the access label before it states, a class's default private and a struct's or union's public. A C type, field and enumerator take the same rule, public, so a struct reads alike in a .h file, read by the C++ grammar, and in a .c file. A label wins over static on a member, since static there names storage, not access. A macro is no name of the language's scopes and states none. Whether a header exports a function is a build fact, which no syntax states, so a plain function is public.
alternatives: C linkage alone, functions and variables only: rejected because a struct in a .h and the same one in a .c would then differ
Public only for what a header declares: rejected because which header is included is a build fact

choice: A C or C++ file's index is keyed by its content and the part of the tree's blank set it writes; its lexical pass is a cache entry of its own, keyed by its content
reason: A key that holds the tree's whole set makes the tree one unit: an empty #define added anywhere indexes every C and C++ file anew. A file's blank depends only on the blankable names it writes outside directives, comments and literals, so its key holds those alone, and a #define a header adds indexes anew only that header and the files that write its name. Which names a file writes, and its #defines, come from one lexical pass, cached by the file's content as an index is, so an unchanged file is never lexed again; the call's own misses are read before the store, so a header lexed for the tree's set is not lexed again for its key. The headers are read first, for the set, and a header's digest from that read keys its entries, so a header whose index the cache holds is read once, as every source file is. A lexical entry is bounded by its file as an index is: a read charges each value its weight against the room of the file it is read for and refuses an entry past it.
alternatives: The tree's set in every C and C++ key: rejected because one #define added anywhere indexes the whole tree anew
The lexical pass run afresh each call: rejected because it reads and lexes every C and C++ file a second time, the largest cost of a warm check
The lexical pass inside the index's entry: rejected because two trees of one content and different sets would then overwrite each other's entry
origin: c and c++ review: macro scope, shapes and visibility

choice: A 0.4.1 code ref becomes an anchor in the 0.5 spelling where its syntax alone settles a name path; any other symbol is kept as written and reported
reason: The 0.5 grammar writes a symbol as a ::-separated path of names from the outermost container. 0.4.1 wrote a TOML or JSON key path with a dot, a Python member as Class.member, and a call or a macro with its (..) or !, and no name of those languages holds those characters, so each maps to one name path: workspace.lints becomes workspace::lints, Checker.run Checker::run, lock() lock. 0.5 has a () of its own, which narrows a Rust or Python symbol to a function or method, but 0.4.1 matched a name whatever its parentheses held, so its (..) never narrowed and the step drops it rather than keep a narrowing the ref never had. A path with an empty or . segment loses it. A spelling whose meaning the syntax does not settle is kept as it was and listed with the reason: a quoted key, whose dot may be part of a name; a key path with an empty segment; a Rust generic or impl, which 0.5 writes as Type::<Trait>::name; a dot in a Rust symbol; and every Markdown symbol, which named a word of a heading where 0.5 names the heading path. The step reads no code: whether a respelled path resolves is a question for anchor resolution, and the report prints every rewrite as old -> new. A ref whose path breaks the anchor rules is dropped with its symbol, and a symbol 0.5 refuses or a key the anchor does not hold, such as line, is dropped from it; each is a reported loss.
alternatives: Resolve each symbol in the code during the migration: rejected because the migration would need the code index and its answer would depend on the tree it ran in
Drop a symbol whose spelling is not settled: rejected because the anchor would lose the place it names, where the kept spelling may still resolve or be repaired
Keep every symbol as written: rejected because a key path would no longer name its key under the 0.5 grammar

choice: A commit stages and flushes its files in parallel on rayon's pool, and the journal keeps the order of the writes
reason: Each staged file is flushed before the journal may name it, and a flush waits on the disk, so a commit that stages many files, such as a migration, which stages one per node, spent its time in one flush after another. stage_commit stages the writes with rayon's par_iter and collects them in their order, so the journal, the renames and the report are the same as a serial commit's. When one write fails, every file the others staged is removed and the first error by order is returned, so nothing stays staged. Temp names come from a process-wide atomic counter, so the threads never share one. On WSL2, where one flush takes about 5 ms, migrating the seeded corpus of 2000 decisions written as 0.4.1 took 23 to 27 s with serial staging and 1.4 s in parallel.
alternatives: Stage one file after another: rejected because the flushes add up serially, to seconds for a store-wide commit
Flush once with syncfs at the end: rejected because std has no syncfs, and it flushes the whole file system

choice: A component rename rewrites each decision's component and each connects_to that names it; a remove is refused while a decision belongs to it or a component connects to it
reason: A component is named by its decisions and by other components' connects_to, so its rename is one op that rewrites all of them, counted as rewrote. Removing it would leave decisions without a component and connections to nothing; the store refuses, naming both lists, and the caller moves the decisions (revise component) and drops the connections first, in the same batch if it likes. A connection of a component to itself is a self-edge, refused like a decision's.
alternatives: Remove the component's decisions with it: rejected because a remove of one node would delete many decisions
Move its decisions to project on remove: rejected because a component's rules would silently become project-wide

choice: A decision's status is proposed or accepted; accepted_via only on an accepted one, accepted_text only on a proposed one, and a file that breaks this is refused at load
reason: status replaces attribution: proposed marks a choice an agent made alone, accepted one the owner accepted. accepted_via says how (elicitation or cli), and a decision migrated as accepted has none; accepted_text holds the text the owner accepted, and its accepted_via, while a revision of it is proposed, so undoing or rejecting the revision returns the decision to accepted as it was accepted. DecisionFields reads the three flat keys, and TryFrom builds Status::Proposed { accepted_text } or Status::Accepted { via }, refusing accepted_via on a proposed decision and accepted_text on an accepted one with a StatusFault, so code past the load matches on one value and never meets a combination the format forbids. The canonical form writes the same flat keys back.
alternatives: Keep attribution user or agent: rejected because it records who wrote a decision, not whether the owner accepted it, and a revision would lose the accepted text
Three independent optional fields with a validation issue for contradictions: rejected because every consumer would have to handle states the format forbids
A nested status table in the file: rejected because the format is flat keys, which read and diff more simply

choice: A decision with anchors that all name a file and no symbol is a lint finding of its own kind, file_anchors_only: none of its anchors says what part of its file it constrains
reason: An anchor that names a file or a directory alone does not say which part of it the decision constrains. A reader cannot find the code the decision governs, and a change anywhere in the file may or may not touch it. Such a decision loads and meets the bar, since one anchor of any kind satisfies anchor_required, so only a report shows it; status lists it under lint as its own kind, by name, counted in counts.lint. One symbol anchor among file anchors takes the decision off the list, which the integration fixture holds with a file anchor beside a symbol one. A decision with no anchor at all breaks the bar instead and shows as the quality finding anchor_required, so the two kinds never name one decision for one cause.
alternatives: A quality rule refusing file-only anchors: rejected because a directory or a file is the right anchor for some decisions, and the bar would refuse them
Leave it to the review: rejected because a review sees only the decisions a diff touches

choice: A definition carries its kind: a Rust item by its node and container, a fn of an impl or trait a method; a query's definition as its pattern names it; a key, target or heading for a lexical file
reason: A diff review names an uncovered definition by what it is, and a count of definitions separates functions from fields, so each definition states its kind, never a guess. A kind is a different thing in the source: a union is no struct, a static no constant, a pub use leaf a re-export of what another module defines, a trait impl the definition Type::<Trait>, a trait's type and the type an impl gives it an associated type, a type outside them a type alias. A fn in an impl or a trait is a method whether or not it takes self; one in a module, a body or an extern block is a function. Each node that defines a name is one case of an exhaustive match. A macro_rules! macro is a macro, and what an invocation produces has no kind, as it is no definition (a-macro-invocation-defines-nothing). The kinds are small Copy values on the definition itself, a byte each in the cache.
alternatives: Fold union into struct and static into constant: rejected because a report would then name a thing the source does not hold
Call an associated function without self a function: rejected because it lives in its type's namespace, which is what method names for a reader

choice: A definition's name is the text of its name nodes' leaves, comments and skipped kinds left out, a space only between two words, split at its separator and each ::, quotes dropped
reason: A name node may be more than one token: namespace A.B is a nested identifier, a test's name a string, an operator operator == with a space or none. Its text is its leaves' texts, a space where bytes lie between a leaf a word character ends and one a word character starts, so a comment inside moves nothing, operator == and operator== are one name, and operator bool keeps its space. A pattern may capture @name on several nodes, whose segments follow in the file's order, so TEST(Suite, Name) is Suite::Name. Its name.skip leaves out the subtrees of node kinds, so a template's arguments (Box<T>::get is Box::get) and a conversion's parameters are no part of a name. A pattern's name.separator splits at each leaf of that text, so A.B is two segments. A part written as a string literal is named by the text between its quotes. A :: in a part splits it as it splits a symbol, so a symbol can name any segment a reader sees. A part of no text defines nothing.
alternatives: A name node's text verbatim: rejected because a comment inside a dotted name would become part of a segment
A property per pattern to drop quotes: rejected because a quoted name is the same thing in every language, and no identifier opens with a quote
Split a name at its structure's fields: rejected because a leaf of the separator's text states the split in every grammar alike

choice: A Rust definition's visibility is its modifier, its enum's or trait's for a variant, variant field or trait member, and none for a trait impl and its members
reason: A count of definitions with and without private ones needs each definition's visibility as the source states it: private (no modifier, or pub(self)), pub(crate) and the old crate, pub(super), pub(in path), and pub, read from the modifier's tokens so a comment inside it changes nothing. A variant, a struct variant's field and a trait's member take no modifier and are exactly as visible as their enum or trait, which the file states; an item inside a variant's discriminant has its own. A trait impl and its members are as visible as the trait, which is usually defined elsewhere, so they have none rather than a guess. A macro_rules! macro is private to its module and those below unless an attribute exports it. A lexical definition (a key, a target, a heading) has no visibility, and none is invented. pub(in path) keeps no path, so the value stays a byte on the definition.
alternatives: Public for a trait impl and its members: rejected because a private trait's impl is no public API
Keep the path of pub(in path): rejected because no reader asks which path, and it would add an owned string per definition

choice: Dropping a StoreLock or SharedLock unlocks the lock file explicitly before its descriptor closes
reason: A flock or LockFileEx lock belongs to the open file, not to one descriptor, and the open file lives until its last descriptor closes. A child that another thread of the process forks inherits a copy of every descriptor and holds it until it execs; std opens files close-on-exec, so the copy goes away at exec but not before. A holder that only closed its file would leave the lock held for that window, and a waiter or a try of the lock in the same or another process would see a lock no one holds: a side write skipped, a write delayed. An unlock through any copy of the descriptor releases the lock at once, so Held unlocks in its Drop and the close only frees the descriptor. A failed unlock is ignored: the close that follows still releases the lock once every copy is gone. Every lock type of the store wraps Held, so no holder can skip the unlock.
alternatives: Close the file and rely on close-on-exec: rejected, a child between fork and exec still holds the open file and with it the lock

Process-owned fcntl record locks, which a forked child does not inherit: rejected, two descriptors of one process would not contend, so a read's shared lock would not keep out a write of the same process
Retry a try of the lock until the child execs: rejected, it turns a release that should be immediate into a wait without a bound
origin: store lock released on drop while a forked child holds its descriptor

choice: The shell indexes on workers it starts per call, a file past 32 KiB on a thread of its own with a 32 MiB stack, the files indexed at once holding at most 2 MiB between them
reason: tree-sitter releases the stack of an ambiguous parse recursively, as deep as the ambiguity runs: a chain of a?(b):c=> keeps an arrow's and a conditional's readings alive and takes about 11 bytes of stack per byte, so a file of about 200 KB overflowed a 2 MiB thread and aborted the process, which no catch_unwind answers. Stack is stated at 32 bytes per byte, about three times that. A parse also holds memory in proportion to its file, about 900 bytes a byte on error-dense input, and a thread's allocator keeps what the thread freed until it ends: on a pool, eight such files of 1 MiB held about 6 GB after their parses. So Indexer::map runs a call's reads on workers it starts and ends, one a core, of WORKER_STACK_BYTES. A worker indexes a file up to MAX_BYTES_INDEXED_BY_A_WORKER itself, keeping about 30 MB at most, and starts a thread of PARSE_STACK_BYTES, which a parse at the cap fits in, for a larger one, whose memory goes back as it ends. Each index first waits until the room of MAX_BYTES_INDEXED_AT_ONCE holds its bytes, so the parses under way hold about 2 GB at most; a file past the room is indexed alone. Worker::index is the shell's one call of code::index, and only Indexer::map hands out a Worker, so no read parses on a stack no bound states. A system that starts no thread gives ReadFault::NoThread. The bounds are in BOUNDS: code states them and the shell starts the threads, so code stays pure.
alternatives: One pool of threads with a 32 MiB stack: rejected because each keeps the memory its largest parse freed until the pool ends
A thread of its own for every file: rejected because starting a thread costs more than parsing most files, and a cold index of many small files ran markedly slower
A lower size cap: rejected because the overflow starts near 200 KB, below many generated and bundled files
Fewer threads for less memory: rejected because a tree of small files would lose the parallelism large ones cost

choice: An anchor resolves against the code root; a file-only anchor resolves when its path exists, a file or a directory, and carries no span and no hash
reason: An anchor's path is relative to the tree the call comes from, so a linked worktree or a clone judges it by its own files, and its file may name a directory that a decision governs as a whole. A file-only anchor states that the file or directory matters, not which definition, so it resolves by existence: a file the index cannot read, of a kind no resolver reads, or over the size cap still exists, and a directory resolves to the directory. It has no span and no hash, so a diff review that compares two revisions sees it touched only as the file it names, which it reports as nearby rather than open. A symbol on a directory, which defines nothing, is an outcome of its own.
alternatives: Resolve against the graph's directory: rejected because a linked worktree would judge its anchors by another branch's files
Hash the whole file for a file-only anchor: rejected because every edit to the file would then touch the decision
Refuse an anchor on a directory: rejected because a decision can govern a module or a crate as a whole

choice: A node file, project.toml, the journal, a staged file a replay reads and the lock are refused unopened unless regular; a node file's name that is not UTF-8 is refused, none skipped
reason: Every reader holds the shared lock while it loads, so a FIFO named like a node file would block every read and, behind it, every write. Each file the store reads by a name anyone can replace is checked before it is opened, one metadata call each, its symlinks followed, made by the parallel read of a node file so a load of many files does not wait on them one by one; the lock file, opened without blocking, is checked by its handle. The listing takes every entry named *.toml, as the history's pathspecs commit them, so nothing a commit holds is skipped by the load: a name that is not UTF-8 fails the load naming it, and a stem that is no node name is a validation issue. The batch file of trurlic apply may be a pipe, as stdin is, since no lock is held while it is read.
alternatives: Open with a non-blocking flag: rejected because std has no portable flag, and a constant per platform is a dependency on libc in all but name
Skip what is not a regular file: rejected because the history would commit what the load never read
origin: review findings of the stateless-server landing

choice: A graph commit's objects reach the disk through git's batch fsync: a write's blobs in one update-index on a scratch index, a hand edit or first commit in one update-index of its files
reason: Under core.fsync=committed alone each loose object is fsynced on its own, about 8 ms each on the seeded corpus's disk: a 50-op batch spent 250 to 330 ms in git. With core.fsyncMethod=batch (git 2.37, bulk-checkin.c) a command inside an object transaction writes each object with a writeout-only flush into a temporary object directory, then fsyncs one dummy file to flush the device cache before it renames the objects into place, so no object gets its name before its data is on the device. update-index opens one transaction for all its paths, so a write's blobs are written by one update-index on a scratch index whose work tree is .state/tmp/, before the commit point, and a hand edit commit or the first commit of a repository stages its files with one update-index; git commit opens one for its trees. hash-object opens none: measured, 581 ms for fifty blobs against 24 ms for the scratch index, so it writes only a symlinked node file. A git before 2.37 warns and fsyncs each object, slower and as durable.
alternatives: Keep a full fsync per object: rejected because a design batch or a first commit then costs seconds in fsyncs for the same journal ordering
hash-object -w --stdin-paths for a write's blobs: rejected because it opens no object transaction and flushes each blob on its own
fsync the objects from trurlic after a hash-object that fsyncs none: rejected because an object would have its name before its data is durable, and git keeps a torn one

choice: The tree's blank set is the fixpoint over its headers' #defines; a file blanks the names of it that it writes, and its own #defines are judged with the headers' of the same names
reason: A header's #define reaches every file that includes it, and which files do is a build fact, so a header's macros are the tree's; a source file's (.c, .cc, .cpp, .cxx) reaches no other file, so a flag one defines (curl's #define DONE) never erases an enumerator of that name elsewhere. With clang as the oracle on seven projects this scope lost no definition the tree-wide one found. The fixpoint is a least one over a worklist, so a cycle blanks nothing and its work is linear in the #defines, each body read up to MAX_MACRO_BODY_TOKENS tokens and a blanked call's arguments up to MAX_BLANK_ARGUMENT_BYTES. A name a file defines itself is judged by its own #defines and the headers' of that name together, so a file that redefines a header's attribute as a value blanks it nowhere in itself. A file of another worktree or of git's history is read against the calling tree's set, the only one known without walking that tree or that history, its own #defines judged with it; a set that changed since makes a symbol unparsable there, a missed repair, never a wrong one.
alternatives: Every file's #defines tree-wide: rejected because a flag one source file defines erases that name in every other

Never blank a name the tree also defines as an enumerator, variable, function, member or type: rejected because it lost hundreds of definitions on the seven projects, where a macro and a member often share a name
Another tree's own set for its files: rejected because it needs a walk of that tree for a few anchored files
origin: c and c++ review: macro scope, shapes and visibility

choice: A shared write's staged files become blobs before its commit point, named in the journal; its history commit's index is set from those ids, so it holds the write's bytes whatever the files hold
reason: The commit used to stage the write's files as they were on disk after the renames and judge by content whether it was made. A hand edit of one of those files between a stopped write and the opener that finished it was then committed under the write's Origin, and while a read keeps a history commit that waits, that window is open-ended. Store::write_blobs runs one update-index on a scratch index in .state/tmp/, with that directory as the work tree, so the staged bytes become blobs in one object transaction flushed once, and ls-files --stage reads the ids back; the repository's index and work tree are not touched. The journal's HistoryStep carries the message, the parent (the branch's commit after any hand edit commit) and each blob id, and commit_history sets the index from them with update-index --index-info, a removal at the null name, then commits. An opener that finishes a stopped write looks for its commit first: the first commit after the parent on the first-parent line whose tree holds the blobs and none of the removed files is the write's, reworded, amended, packed or followed by a hand commit since, and none is made again. A blob git lost since, to a gc --prune=now or a repository made again, is staged from the file on disk with a warning. Measured on this disk: the scratch index costs 11.5 ms for one blob and 23.9 ms for fifty, against 10.5 and 23.6 ms for the update-index it replaces after the commit point.
alternatives: Stage the files as on disk after the renames and judge the commit by content: rejected because a hand edit made before the opener runs is committed as the write's
hash-object -w --stdin-paths: rejected because it opens no object transaction, so every blob is flushed on its own, 581 ms for fifty blobs
fast-import with marks: rejected because it writes a pack and loosens it in a child unpack-objects, about twice the scratch index's time for one blob
A write id in a trailer looked up at HEAD: rejected because a reword drops it and a hand commit after the write hides it

choice: A history commit's subject names the tool, its trailers carry Origin: and Session:, and the journal carries both, so a write the next opener finishes keeps them
reason: A review reads a shared graph's history by Origin, so the trailer must reach the commit on every path, an interrupted write's included. CommitMessage holds the Tool (init, fmt, migrate, apply) and the optional origin and session, each checked when the message is made as one line of at most MAX_TRAILER_BYTES (200) with no control, invisible or reordering character (store::text, TextField::Origin and TextField::Session): a line break would end the trailer and forge another. render writes the subject, then the trailers the write has as a paragraph of their own. The journal holds the message as its [history] table and checks it again when it reads it back, so the opener that finishes the write commits with the caller's trailers. A command with no origin passes CommitMessage::of(tool); the commit of hand edits is "hand edit" with no trailer.
alternatives: Rebuild the message at recovery from the placement: rejected because the origin and the session exist only in the call that made the write
Put the origin in the subject: rejected because git interpret-trailers and %(trailers) read the last paragraph, and the subject names the tool
Take any origin text: rejected because a line break in it would end the trailer and start a forged one

choice: A key of an old file the step does not map is a reported loss, never a refusal; a mapped key whose value the 0.5 type cannot hold fails the migration naming the file
reason: 0.4.1 read its files without refusing unknown keys, so a hand edit or another tool could leave any key in them, and 0.4.1 ignored it. The step to 0.5 builds each table from the keys it knows and reports every other one with its file, dotted field and value: in project.toml, its [project] table, a component, a decision, a code ref, a pattern, graph.toml and its node entries. A refusal would block a whole migration over a value 0.4.1 itself never read, and the backup keeps the old file. A key the step does map but whose value is not of its type (a choice that is a number) was unreadable to 0.4.1 too; it reaches the strict typed read, which fails naming the file, and nothing is written.
alternatives: Refuse a migration that meets an unknown key: rejected because a key 0.4.1 ignored would stop the migration of the whole store
Drop unknown keys silently, as the old migrate did: rejected because a value would vanish without a word

choice: A language beyond Rust is read by the general resolver from a grammar compiled into the binary and a query file; its only code is a check or a same-length rewrite before the parse
reason: A language added as a Rust module of its own repeats the walk, the scopes, the budgets and the hash for its grammar, and each copy drifts from the others. One engine reads any grammar's tree by a query file kept beside the code, so a language is a grammar crate, a query file, a row of language.rs and of FileKind, and a fixture corpus. A grammar is compiled into the binary: one loaded at run time is a dynamic library, which needs unsafe, a WebAssembly runtime, which is a heavy dependency for every user, or a helper process, too slow for a hook; and each would make what a call returns depend on what is installed. Rust keeps its own module, because its attributes, impls, re-exports and module files need code. Since no query runs before the parse, the only code a language may add runs there: a check of its bytes its grammar's scanner forces, such as Python's bound on indentation widths, or a rewrite of the bytes that keeps every offset, such as C's and C++'s blanking of the macros their tree defines as attributes (language/c_family.rs).
alternatives: A Rust module per language: rejected because each repeats the walk, the scopes and the hash, and drifts from the others
Grammars loaded at run time: rejected because loading one needs unsafe, a WebAssembly runtime or a helper process, and the index would depend on what is installed
The grammars' own tags.scm queries: rejected because they state no kind, visibility, test role or span growth the index carries

choice: A leftover index.lock in the graph's repository fails check and refuses a write before its commit point, with nothing written; uncommitted files and a missing repository are warnings
reason: Under trurlic's exclusive lock no other trurlic process runs git in the graph's repository, so an index lock there is a person's git command, which a retry outlives, or the leftover of one that stopped, which no wait clears; git would fail every staging while it stays. prepare_history looks for it before anything is staged and refuses with Error::GraphIndexLocked naming the file and the repair, so the write leaves nothing pending. A lock that appears after the commit point fails the history commit, which the next writer makes (WritePending). check fails on it, as every write would; uncommitted files and a missing repository are mended by the next write, so they warn.
alternatives: Wait for the lock, as for the store's own: rejected because a stopped git's leftover never goes, and every write would pay the timeout
Remove a lock that looks stale: rejected because trurlic cannot tell a stopped git from a running one
Let git find it at the commit: rejected because that fails after the commit point, leaving a write pending

choice: A revise gives a list whole or by add_ and remove_, never both; removals run first and each must be held, then additions, an element already held staying once
reason: Most revises change one list by one element (an anchor added, a tag dropped), and a whole list from a stale read would undo another writer's element, so add_/remove_ is the common form and the whole list the explicit reset. Both forms for one list in one op have no single meaning, so it is refused (both_forms) rather than ordered by a rule the caller must remember. A removal of an element the list does not hold means the caller's view of the decision is wrong, a typo'd anchor most of all, and is refused (not_held); an addition of one it holds leaves the list as the caller wants it. An added edge is checked as a new one (dependency_missing, connection_missing, self_edge); one already held is not, so a dangling edge a hand edit left blocks no other change. Alternatives keep their order; sets stay sorted.
alternatives: Apply the whole list, then the additions and removals: rejected because the caller must then know an order the batch does not show
Accept a removal of an element the list lacks: rejected because a typo in an anchor to remove would pass silently and leave the stale one
Whole lists only: rejected because a one-anchor change would carry, and race, every other anchor

choice: A load fails only when a file is not its type; names, edges and text rules are validation issues, so status, the reads and check still work on a hand-broken graph
reason: With hand edits the only write, a broken graph is an ordinary state, and the tools must be able to say what is wrong with it. A load fails, naming the file, only when a file cannot be read as its type: it cannot be read, it is over the node cap, it is not TOML, or its type refuses it (an unknown key, a wrong type, a status its fields contradict, an anchor path outside its rules). Everything a set of well-typed files can hold but should not (a component or an edge that names no node, a name two kinds share, a cycle, a broken text rule) is an Issue that ProjectState::validate reports with its file: check lists them all and fails, status counts them, open_store warns, and get_context and get_decisions_for_file still answer. What the types refuse is what no code past the load could hold; what validation reports is a relation between files that a fix in one of them resolves.
alternatives: Fail the load on every issue: rejected because one dangling edge would stop status, check and every read, and check could not report what it cannot load
Skip a malformed file and load the rest: rejected because a decision would drop out of every brief without a word
Read every file untyped and report type faults as issues too: rejected because every consumer would then handle values the format does not allow

choice: In Rust a macro_rules! macro is a definition of kind macro, and no macro invocation defines anything, whatever the macro's body or the invocation's own tokens spell
reason: A wrong definition is worse than a missing one, and only rustc knows what an invocation produces: its matcher parses fragments with rustc's parser and edition, matches nested repetitions, scopes a macro by textual order, #[macro_use] and $crate, and transcription can rename, wrap, paste or cfg what it emits. So a definition is an item tree-sitter parsed outside every token tree, and nothing wrong is defined by construction. An invocation where an item stands keeps the distinct identifiers among its top-level tokens (RustFacts::invoked), charged to its file's room, which define nothing: when an anchor's last name is one of them and its file defines nothing it names, the resolution is SymbolInInvocation, whose message names what to anchor instead: the macro, an item of the type written outside the invocation, such as a method of its impl, or the file. A stale anchor of that resolution is not searched for elsewhere, as its code is still in its file.
alternatives: Emulate macro_rules! by matching each invocation against the rules its crate's macros hold: rejected because each review of the matcher found new phantom definitions, its model of fragments, scope and transcription not being rustc's, and its uncached work took seconds a call
Define the items an invocation's own tokens spell: rejected because a macro may emit another item than it is handed, as a renaming or wrapping macro does and thread_local! makes a static a const
Define a spelled item only where the invocation stands as an item and the macro emits its input: rejected because no rule that reads only the invocation knows what its macro emits
Re-parse an invocation's token tree as items: rejected because almost no item-position tree parses alone, and one that does is still the macro's to rewrite
Expand with rustc: rejected because it needs a compiler, the crate's dependencies and its cfg, far past what an anchor needs

choice: Markdown defines its ATX headings outside fenced code, each named by its path through the headings above and spanning its section; a Makefile defines each target of a rule over its recipe
reason: A heading names a section, so Install::From source is the From source section under Install, spanning from its line to the next heading of its level or a higher one, trailing blank lines left out: a symbol names a section, not a word in one. A fence of three or more backticks or tildes hides what looks like a heading, as does an indent of four spaces; the closing #s and runs of whitespace are dropped from a title. A Makefile rule defines each target before its first colon outside a $(...), unless an equals sign comes first or the colon opens an assignment (:=, ::=); its span runs through the tab-led recipe lines after it, blank and comment lines inside it neither ending it nor joining it, a backslash continuing a line and a define block holding no rule. The targets of one rule share its span, so its text is hashed once for all of them. Setext headings and make's recipe prefix variable are not read: this repository's documents and Makefile use neither.
alternatives: Any heading holding the word: rejected because a word names no section to hash, and many headings hold it
A Makefile variable as a definition: rejected because an anchor on configuration names a rule or a key, and a variable is neither

choice: A merge keeps the survivor's text, status, origin and created, unions in the absorbed decision's anchors, tags and depends_on, repoints every edge to it, and drops its text
reason: Two decisions that state one rule become one; the survivor is the one whose text stands, and history keeps the absorbed text. Taking any of the absorbed text (an alternative, a reason) would change the survivor's text and with it the status of an accepted survivor, so the text a caller wants kept is a revise of the survivor in the same batch, under the revise rule. Anchors, tags and edges are where and how the rule applies, which both decisions held, so they are unioned; an edge between the two, or to the survivor from itself, is dropped. A merge that closes a depends_on cycle through the survivor is refused naming its members.
alternatives: Union the alternatives too: rejected because it changes the survivor's text, which an accepted decision may not change outside a revise
Keep the newer decision's text: rejected because the caller names the survivor and must get the one it named

choice: A migration rewrites the graph as TOML tables, reads the result strictly as the current types, and commits the changed files and the removal of dropped ones at once
reason:
A step must see shapes the current types cannot parse (a supersedes edge, a 0.1.0 connects_to list, graph.toml, a pattern file), so the Tree holds every graph file as a toml::Table. After the walk each table is read as Project, Component or Decision, which refuse any key they do not know, so a value no step mapped or dropped fails the migration naming the file instead of vanishing; a file the current format has no place for, such as graph.toml or a pattern, is Error::Unmigrated unless a step removed it. The step to 0.5 removes both from the tree.
Each kept file is prepared in canonical form and written only when its bytes change, and every file the tree no longer holds is removed, all in one commit_batch: a crash after the journal finishes the migration and never leaves a store between formats. project.toml sorts first among the writes and the removals come after every rename, so until the first rename the store is old-format with a journal, refused by every command but migrate, which recovers it under its lock; after it the store is current and any command finishes the commit, removals included. Store::commit_migration then removes the patterns/ directory it emptied, and leaves one that holds anything else.
alternatives: Typed structs for every historical format: rejected because a copy of each schema would be kept for one step
Read leniently and compare each table key by key with what the type keeps: rejected because deny_unknown_fields already refuses an unknown key, and a step must drop or report it explicitly
Write each file on its own with write_atomic: rejected because a crash leaves files of two formats
Leave graph.toml and patterns/ for the user to delete: rejected because they would hold edges and rules nobody reads, with no word that they are dead

choice: A missing git is Error::GitMissing at init of a shared graph, which then leaves no .trurlic/ behind, and at every write to a shared graph, before its commit point
reason: A shared graph's history is git, so git missing is never a silent skip. Store::create makes the repository before any graph file and removes the directory it made when anything fails, so a refused init leaves nothing that a second init would refuse as existing. The history step runs git status before a write stages anything, so a missing git refuses the write with the graph as it was. status and check of a shared graph ask git for their findings and fail the same way; a tracked graph's reads and writes need no git.
alternatives: Skip the history when git is missing: rejected because the history would have a hole nothing reports
Leave a half-made .trurlic/ after a failed init: rejected because the second init would refuse it as existing

choice: A shared graph whose repository is gone gets a new one from its next write, with a warning; a repository's first commit holds every graph file, and one git cannot read is refused
reason: One rule for a deleted .trurlic/.git. The history it held is lost already, and a refusal could not bring it back: it would stall every agent's write until a person ran the repair, which is what the write does. prepare_history (and the opener that finishes a stopped write) makes the repository again and prints a warning that its history starts with this write; status and check report it as Missing until then. A repository with no commit yet stages every graph file git lists with the write's, so its first commit holds the whole graph, whichever made it: init, a migration to shared, or a write after a loss. A repository git cannot read fails git status in prepare_history with git's error, before the commit point.
alternatives: Refuse the write and name a repair: rejected because the history is lost already and the repair is what the write does, while every write until a person acts would fail
Make it again silently: rejected because the owner must learn that the history restarted
A first commit of hand edits, then the write: rejected because no edit came before a history that did not exist

choice: A node file or project.toml over MAX_NODE_FILE_BYTES (1 MiB) is refused unparsed: the read stops at the cap and the error names the file
reason: A node holds a decision, not a document, and every call loads every node, so one oversized file, by accident or on purpose, would cost every load its memory and parse time. read_node_bytes reads through take(cap + 1), so a file that grows while it is read, or one that never ends, costs at most the cap, and a read that passes it fails with Error::NodeTooLarge naming the file before the TOML parser sees a byte. The migration reads every file through the same function, so a store of an old format is held to the same bound.
alternatives: Check the length in the file's metadata, then read it whole: rejected because the length can change between the check and the read, and a special file reports none
Parse first, then measure: rejected because the parse cost is what the cap exists to avoid
No cap: rejected because one file could make every call slow or exhaust memory

choice: A node's name is its file stem, kebab-case, at most 128 bytes and unique across components and decisions; no file holds a name, and project is reserved
reason: A name field beside the stem was a second source for one name that could disagree with it, and a rename had to edit both. The stem is the name, so no node type has a name key and deny_unknown_fields refuses one. A name is unique across kinds so that one name means one node wherever it appears: a tool argument, a brief, a report, an edge. project is the component of the project-wide decisions and has no file, so a node of that name would be ambiguous. A name is at most MAX_NAME_BYTES (128): a file system takes 255 bytes for a file name, .toml included, and a write must never stage a file it cannot rename into place, which would leave a journal no opener can finish. store::state::name_fault holds the three rules for validation and for apply alike. A stem that is not kebab-case or is too long, is project, or is shared by a component and a decision is an issue naming the files (NameInvalid, NameReserved, NameShared), so a hand edit that breaks a name stays readable to check.
alternatives: A name field in each file: rejected because stem and field can disagree, and a rename edits both
Names unique per kind only: rejected because a name in a brief or a report would not say which node it is

choice: A panic while a request is handled is caught in Server::answer, answered -32603, and the server serves the next request
reason:
Release builds unwind, so one catch_unwind per request turns a bug in a handler into an error the client can report instead of a dead session. The boundary is sound because nothing a request leaves half-done outlives it: the server holds no graph between calls; a Writer's file lock is released as unwinding drops it, and a commit it began is finished from the journal by the next opener, as after a crash; the client record changes only by whole steps (an id taken, a request queued or dequeued); and every line sent to the client is serialized into a buffer before it is written, so the stream never holds part of one. AssertUnwindSafe is justified at that site. The answer is written after the boundary.
The graph.loaded failpoint panics right after a load, before its caller uses the graph, in both load paths: Store::load_state under the shared lock and Store::begin_write under the exclusive one, so one site places a panic under either lock. tests/integration/server_failpoints.rs panics a get_context under the shared lock, then runs trurlic fmt, which takes the exclusive lock and commits, and the next call is answered.
alternatives: panic = "abort": rejected because one bug ends the session and every call after it
catch_unwind around tools/call only: rejected because initialize and tools/list build values too; one boundary per request covers every handler
A thread per request: rejected because stdio is one ordered stream, and a thread adds a join and a channel for what catch_unwind does in place
A panic site under the exclusive lock only, as before: rejected because every listed tool is now a read, so a server test could not reach it

choice: A file's index holds its paths as a tree of scopes, each its own segments and its parent; the tree charges all an index holds to its file's room, and every path counts toward 64 segments
reason: A path copied into every definition makes an index grow with its file times its nesting. A scope stores only the segments its own name adds and the id of its parent, created before it, so a path is walked from its last segment up and the walk ends. A container that is no definition, an inherent impl's type, is a scope too. A rule that copies text per entry can still outgrow its file, as a pub use list of twenty thousand selfs under a long module name once did. So every resolver enters its scopes and adds its definitions, module files and invoked names through the one tree, which index() hands it for its file's kind and size. The tree charges each what its cache entry costs (an-entry-s-room-is-its-file-times-what-its-kind-s-densest-definitions-cost) and refuses the file past its room as TooComplex. A path of more than MAX_NESTING segments is TooDeep.
alternatives: Keep an owned path per definition and cap the definitions: rejected because a cap that happens to hold today is no bound, and the waste stays
Intern the path segments in a table: rejected because the copies of a path, not of its segments, are what grew
Bound the entry by a test over the densest inputs found: rejected because the next rule's input is not among them

choice: A path the store derived that breaks its own layout is Error::StorePath with a typed StorePathFault, never a formatted string
reason: Six places reported a path outside the store, a path with a parent-directory component, or a store root with no parent as Error::Validation(String), the variant meant for messages the validator formats, each with its own wording and nothing a caller could match. Every one of them guards a programming error: each path is derived from the root, so none fires in correct code. Error::StorePath { path, fault } names the path and one of Traversal, Outside or NoParent, so verify_path, the journal's relative paths, write_atomic and Store::parent_and_name, which placement and migrate use for the directory that holds the graph, refuse alike, and Error::Validation is gone.
alternatives: One variant per fault: rejected because the three are one concept, a derived path that breaks the layout, and only the fault differs
Keep Validation(String) for them: rejected because its message is free text no caller or test can match and it duplicates the validator's variant
origin: review findings of the stateless-server landing

choice: A Python definition whose name is a dunder name such as __init__, or has no leading underscore, is public
reason: The owner's rule makes a name with a leading underscore private and says nothing of the rest. A dunder name such as __init__ or __all__ starts with an underscore but is a protocol the language reads from outside the class or module, so it is public; so is every name without the underscore, which is the language's default. The rule is the query's: the visibility.private mark is on each identifier that matches ^_ and not ^__.*__$, and each definition pattern sets visibility public, which a mark overrides, so it holds alike for a def, a class and a name a module or a class binds.
alternatives: A dunder name private too: rejected because __init__ and __all__ are read from outside the class or module
No visibility for a name without the underscore: rejected because a count of public definitions would then lose every plain name

choice: A Python file whose lines start at more than 256 distinct indentation widths is refused before the parse as TooManyIndentations
reason: tree-sitter-python's scanner keeps the widths of the open blocks on a stack and writes them, two bytes each, after the open string delimiters into tree-sitter's buffer of 1,024 bytes; its loop stops at the buffer's size only on an even count, so some 380 open blocks under an odd number of open strings write one byte past it, and tree-sitter's assertion aborts the process, which no unwind catches. The stack holds strictly increasing widths, each measured from a line break, so it is no deeper than the distinct widths the file's lines start at, counted as the scanner counts them: a space 1, a tab 8, in 16 bits that wrap, every line counted, one inside a string or brackets too. A backslash before a line break continues a width only while the width is open; after any other byte, a comment's last among them, the line break starts a width, since the scanner ends the comment there and pushes what follows. At 256 every entry and delimiter fits with room. The check runs before the parse, since the abort happens during it.
alternatives: A bound on the tree's nesting: rejected because the abort happens during the parse, before any tree
A patched copy of the grammar's scanner: rejected because a vendored fork of a C grammar must be kept in step with every release
Parse in a child process: rejected because it spawns a process per file and a call would no longer be one process

choice: A Python file with a run of more than 256 line continuations holding no other line break is refused before the parse as TooManyContinuations
reason: tree-sitter-python's error recovery summarizes the stack of line_continuation extras of the logical line it is in, at a cost no budget of the parse counts: a run of continuations inside a parse error costs the square of its length, so one run of a megabyte would take about an hour. The bound is the run's length, each backslash right before a line feed counted, one ending a comment or standing in a string too, and the run ends at any other line feed. Valid code holds runs of many dozens, CPython's own test suite among it, so the bound lies past every run found in real code; a run past it is generated. The bound caps this one shape of the cost alone: error recovery has others with no continuation in them, which it does not cap. The check runs before the parse beside the indentation bound, both rows of Python's language data, and its value enters the cache key with every other bound.
alternatives: A bound of 64: rejected because valid code, a statement of CPython's test suite among it, continues more lines and was refused
A smaller cap on a Python file's size: rejected because valid files of a megabyte parse in milliseconds and the cost is the run's, not the file's
Count only continuations outside comments and strings: rejected because it needs a lexer of Python before the parse, and a run that long is never written by hand

choice: A Python definition whose name starts with an underscore is private
reason: A count of definitions with and without the private ones needs each definition's visibility, and Python has no modifier: a leading underscore is the language's own convention for a name a module or a class keeps to itself, which PEP 8 states and import * and name mangling honour. The rule is the query's, a visibility.private mark on each identifier whose name starts with an underscore, so it holds alike for a def, a class and a name a module or a class binds. Which underscored names are public all the same is a decision of its own (a-python-dunder-name-and-every-name-without-an-underscore-is-public).
alternatives: No visibility for Python: rejected because the underscore is how Python states privacy, and a count could not leave private helpers out

choice: A query file is refused for any capture, property, predicate, node kind, definition kind or container the resolver does not read, by a test per language; it compiles once per process
reason: Query::new refuses an unknown node kind or field, a syntax error and an impossible shape, but takes any capture name, any #set! key and any predicate it does not evaluate itself, so a misspelt key or a predicate outside its pattern's parentheses would define nothing without a sign. Rules::compile reads each pattern as a definition pattern, which captures @definition once and @name once or on several nodes and sets its kind, or a mark pattern, which sets no property, and refuses anything else, naming the pattern, a supertype named as a node kind among them, since no node of a tree is of one; every pattern has one root, since the resolver starts each pattern at one node. The check runs in each language's unit test: a build script would compile every grammar again for nothing a test misses. A query is a file of tree-sitter's query language, language/<name>.scm, compiled into the binary by include_str!, the one read at build time the index's purity admits. It compiles once per process, on the first file of its language the cache does not hold, a cost the query_compile benchmark holds, and its text enters the cache key with its grammar's identity, since its patterns are rules of the index.
alternatives: The query as a Rust string constant: rejected because the owner's decision names a query file, and a string in Rust is no file the query language's tools read
A build script that compiles the queries: rejected because it builds every grammar twice and checks nothing a unit test does not
Refuse a broken query per file at run time: rejected because a query is fixed when the binary is built, so its fault is the build's and no input causes it
Raise INDEX_FORMAT by hand on each query edit: rejected because an edit the fixtures do not show would keep a stale cache entry

choice: A definition the general resolver finds is under the innermost definition or unnamed scope whose captured node holds its own @definition node, two of one node being siblings
reason: A query pattern names a fixed nesting and cannot say the enclosing class however deep, so containment comes from the nodes the patterns capture: sorted by start, the widest first, each definition is under the innermost open definition whose @definition node holds its own, and one whose pattern sets container false opens none. The captured node places, not the span grown from it, so each declarator of one statement holds what its own node holds. Two definitions of one node are siblings. A node an @scope.unnamed capture marks is a container of its own that within never admits, so a callback's locals define nothing; what it defines takes its path from the definition around it, and what no definition holds defines nothing (an Express route handler). A node an @scope.none capture marks is no scope: what it holds stands where it stands. TypeScript marks so a class a name binds, whose members are the name's, and a wrapper of the whole file, which is the module: an unnamed function a statement of the file's top calls (an IIFE, also as !f() or (f).call(this)), a factory such a call passes (UMD), and the factory of a top-level define (AMD). A callback deeper, or a jest.mock factory, stays unnamed. within keeps a definition only at the file's top or in containers of the kinds it names, and kind.in gives it another kind in a container of a kind. A span grows through definition.via ancestors to a definition.to one, over definition.wrap ancestors and definition.preceding siblings. A visibility mark applies to a definition whose span holds it, a @visibility.within mark to each whose name it holds that no such mark gives one, and a @visibility.after label to each whose name lies in a later sibling, over both. A name with no text defines nothing.
alternatives: Containment by the grown span: rejected because the declarators of one statement share it, and whatever one held landed under the last
An unnamed function's locals at the file's top: rejected because a callback's or a CommonJS export's locals read as module variables, two callbacks' locals as one path
A segment of its own for each unnamed scope: rejected because every unnamed scope of a file would share it, merging unrelated functions under one path
Every top-level callback as the module: rejected because an Express route handler's or a jest.mock factory's locals would read as module variables

choice: Read commands load under the shared lock; a command that writes holds the exclusive lock from its load to its last commit
reason: query loads through open_store, which warns when the graph has issues; check and the status twin load through Store::load_state; each takes the shared lock for its load alone. fmt and the apply twin write through the Writer of Store::begin_write, which holds the exclusive lock from its load to its commit, and migrate takes Store::lock and plans under it, since it reads files the current types cannot. A write command therefore always validates against the graph loaded under its lock, a read waits only while a writer holds the lock, and no command can write without holding it: every commit takes a StoreLock.
alternatives: One open function that always takes the exclusive lock: rejected because status and check would wait on each other and on every MCP read
Lock on demand inside each command: rejected because scattered locking is how a write forgets its lock, and the proof type makes the lock a parameter

choice: A refused tool call is an isError result whose text is {error: {kind, field?, op?, rule?, message}}; a JSON-RPC error answers only a malformed message, an unknown method or tool, or a panic
reason: The MCP tools specification sends input validation and business errors as tool results with isError, which a client hands to the model so it can correct the call, and protocol errors for requests that fail the CallToolRequest schema and unknown tools. result::ToolError carries one ErrorKind (invalid_argument with the field's path, no_project, unsupported_format, store_error, refused, batch_refused) and the message; a batch the store refused also names the argument at fault as field (ops[3].add_tags[0]), the op as {index, op, name} and the rule, from the store's typed Refusal, so a caller branches on kind and an agent reads the message; every refusal goes through tool_error and fit_payload, so it is JSON within the result budget. The tools that predate specs refuse with kind refused. A missing store or one in another format is a refusal too, since the call itself is valid.
alternatives: The bare message as text: rejected, a caller cannot tell an argument fault from a missing store without parsing prose
JSON-RPC -32602 for an invalid argument: rejected, the specification sends input validation as a tool result so the model sees it
structuredContent on a refusal: rejected, a tool's outputSchema describes its result, and a refusal does not conform to it

choice: A remove is refused while decisions depend on it, naming them, unless repoint_to names the decision their edges point at instead; an heir's own edge to it is dropped
reason: Removing a decision others depend on would leave dangling edges, which validation reports; the store refuses it instead, listing the dependents (ten named, the rest counted). With repoint_to each dependent's edge moves to the heir in the same op, and the heir, which depended on the removed decision, does not come to depend on itself: its edge is dropped. A repoint that closes a depends_on cycle through the heir is refused naming the members.
alternatives: Drop the dependents' edges with the decision: rejected because the dependents would silently lose a constraint
Remove the dependents too: rejected because a cascade of deletes is not what one remove names

choice: A gone path's rename is a git mv not committed, else what the last commit changing it renamed it to, while the next commit changing the new path neither deleted, copied nor renamed it
reason: git pairs files by similarity alone, between the two sides of a diff, so the question is asked of the diff that removed the path, and only for check and the repair_anchors op, for the files of stale anchors with nothing at their path: status asks the project's git nothing. What is not committed comes first: git diff HEAD with -M -C, so a git mv is seen; a file moved without git and not added is a deletion and an untracked file, which no diff pairs. Else one git log --name-status --no-renames walk over HEAD's history, limited to the asked paths as literal pathspecs, lists the commits that changed each, newest first; the newest for a path gone from HEAD deleted it, and git diff of that commit against its first parent says what it became, at git's default similarity: one rename is the answer, with its similarity and its commit; several records (a split shows as a copy beside the rename), a copy or a plain deletion are none. The new path is then judged by the next commit that changed it: an edit ends the chain there, and so does no commit while the path exists; a rename is followed the same way, at most MAX_RENAME_HOPS, one walk per hop; a deletion, a copy or several records, or no commit and nothing at the path, and the file left it, which another may fill now: no answer. Every history read pins the settings that change what git prints (git::renames::PINNED). Any git failure leaves the anchor stale without a repair. A merge's deletion is not seen.
alternatives: One walk per gone path: rejected because each walk costs a whole history even with changed-path filters, so many gone paths cost many times one walk
git log --follow per path: rejected because it takes one path per process and follows a path forward from its history, not to where a gone file went
Any similarity threshold of our own: rejected because git's default is what git status and git log show the user
Trust the newest commit that added the new path: rejected because a commit that renames the file away and writes a new one at the path leaves the path modified, never added, to git log --no-renames

choice: A revise, a component revise or a rename to the same name that leaves every file's canonical bytes as they are is refused as no_change
reason: A write that changes nothing is a mistaken call: a stale read, a revise of the wrong decision, a field set to the value it holds. No-op is defined on the value: the revised decision or component equals the one the graph holds, which is exactly that its canonical text is unchanged, since every write's text reads back as its value. A file that is not in canonical form is not rewritten by a revise that changes nothing: putting it in form is trurlic fmt's write. A field given with the value it holds is no change of that field, and its text is not checked again.
alternatives: Accept a no-op as a success that writes nothing: rejected because the caller learns nothing of the stale view that made it
Compare the bytes on disk: rejected because a hand edit out of canonical form would make every revise of it a change

choice: A revise of an accepted decision's choice, reason or alternatives proposes it and keeps the accepted text with its accepted_via; a later revise keeps it, and one back to it accepts again
reason: No op writes accepted, accepted_via or accepted_text: acceptance is the owner's. A record is proposed. When an agent changes the text the owner accepted, the decision is proposed until the owner answers, and accepted_text keeps what the owner accepted and how (accepted_via inside [accepted_text], an optional key), so a later revise keeps the first accepted text, not an intermediate one, and a revise back to exactly that text returns the decision to accepted as it was accepted, which a reject in accept will do too. A change of the component, anchors, tags or edges, a rename and a merge into the decision leave the status alone. Each revise reports a status it changed.
alternatives: Drop accepted_via while a revision is proposed: rejected because undoing the revision would then restore an acceptance with no record of how it was given
Stay proposed after a revise back to the accepted text: rejected because the decision would wait for the owner to re-accept text the owner accepted

choice: Under shared the graph directory is a git repository of its own, made by init and migrate, and each write ends with one commit there; under tracked trurlic never commits
reason: A graph kept out of the project's git had no history: a revision of an accepted decision could be neither seen nor undone, and node files carry no history of their own. Under tracked the project's git holds every revision of every node file, so trurlic commits nothing there and never interleaves its commits with the owner's. Under shared nothing else versions the graph, so .trurlic/ is the repository: Store::create makes it and commits project.toml as init, commit_migration makes it when a migration lands on shared, and commit_batch, given History::Graph, ends each write with one commit after its files are in place. History::of(placement, message) is the one place the placement decides it, and a writer reaches it through Writer::commit.
alternatives: Commit to the project's repository under both placements: rejected because a shared graph stays out of the project's git by its definition, and under tracked trurlic's commits would land among the owner's
A history file in .state/ or beside each node: rejected because node files carry no history, and git already gives log, diff, blame and revert
A bare repository beside the graph that a write copies into: rejected because every write would copy the graph, and the owner could not run git in .trurlic/

choice: init keeps a shared graph out of git with /.trurlic/ in the common dir's info/exclude, and a tracked graph's .state/ with the .gitignore beside it
reason: A shared graph stays out of the project's git, which check holds it to, but an untracked directory shows in every git status and git add --all commits it. info/exclude of the common dir is read by every worktree of the repository and is no tracked file, so the project's history never names a graph it does not version and every clone decides for itself. The entry is anchored, /.trurlic/, so it matches the top of each work tree only. A tracked graph keeps its .state/, the lock and the journal, out of git with .trurlic/.state/ in the .gitignore of the directory that holds it, as before; outside any work tree nothing is written. Each entry is appended once.
alternatives: A /.trurlic/ line in .gitignore: rejected because a tracked file of the project would name a graph the project does not version, in every clone
Write nothing under shared: rejected because git add --all would commit the graph, which check then refuses

choice: A shared graph's write first commits, as hand edit, every graph file its last commit does not hold as it is on disk, so the write's own commit holds the write alone
reason: A hand edit is a legal write, so the graph's work tree can hold changes no tool made when a write starts; folded into the write's commit they would carry its Origin. Store::prepare_history runs before the commit point under the exclusive lock: git status over the graph files, and when the branch has a commit and any of them differs, they are staged as they are on disk and committed as "hand edit". A failure there leaves the graph as it was. In a repository with no commit yet there is nothing to edit: the write's commit is the first and holds every graph file.
alternatives: Fold hand edits into the write's commit: rejected because the commit would claim the write's Origin for edits it did not make
Refuse a write while hand edits are uncommitted: rejected because a hand edit is a legal write, and the owner would have to commit by hand before every tool call

choice: A source file is refused past its kind's size cap, unreadable or not UTF-8, past a budget of work per byte, or with a path past 64 segments
reason: The index reads whatever a tree holds, a hostile file among them, and nothing may panic, abort, hang or recurse unbounded. The shell reads a file's metadata first, so a FIFO is refused before it is opened and a symlink loop is a read fault. It reads at most the largest kind's cap and one byte more, and takes a file that vanishes between the walk and the read as absent; each kind's cap is a decision of its own, as are a parse's stack and memory. No count bounds the parser's error recovery: on random bytes at the 1 MiB cap the typescript grammar takes about 29 seconds and the tsx one 11, linear in the size, once per content since the index is then cached. The budgets are work.rs's, each per byte of the file and refused as TooComplex past it, so a file is refused on every machine or on none. The parse counts the bytes its lexer is served, not its steps, which tree-sitter keeps in proportion to the tokens: 64 a byte, served 64 at a time, as it rescans the chunk it holds uncounted. The nodes the general resolver enters and the text a query's predicates read may take 16 a byte, and a lexical resolver hash 2 times MAX_NESTING bytes. A tree-sitter span hash needs no budget: each unit is hashed once by construction. A language may add bounds checked before its parse, each a cost of its grammar no budget counts during it, as Python's indentation widths and line continuations are. Every walk keeps its own stack, a path of more than MAX_NESTING segments is TooDeep, and the index's size is bounded by the scope tree's charge.
alternatives: A wall-clock timeout on the parse: rejected because code reads no clock, and a file would be refused on a slow machine and not a fast one
One budget for the parse and the work after it: rejected because a parser step, a scanned token and a hashed byte cost too differently to share a unit
Recursive walks: rejected because a nesting as deep as a file allows would overflow the stack
Chunks of 1,024 bytes to the lexer: rejected because a run of Python line continuations rescans within one chunk, uncounted, for seconds

choice: A span hash is t1: and the BLAKE3 of a span's units, each token after its length, each group mark a length no token has, a nested definition its hash; a lexical span hashes its normalized text
reason: A diff review compares a definition's hash between two revisions to tell whether a change touched it. So the hash must move with what the code does and stay put under what it does not: whitespace, a comment, a doc comment, a token of no meaning. Which reformats move no hash is each language's decision, by rules that never give two programs of different meaning one hash; a reformat no rule covers moves the hash. The tokens of the parse tree cover every byte but comments and whitespace (a-tree-sitter-span-s-tokens-are-the-language-s-whatever-the-grammar-lexes). Each token goes in after its length, so a b and ab differ. A query's unit is a node's text, the comments inside left out, cut where a child the query also marks is taken by its own mark. A grammar whose layout is syntax no byte holds, as Python's is, has its query mark groups, each opened and closed by a mark no length takes. A definition nested in the span goes in as its own hash, after a mark no length takes, so each unit is hashed once however deep the definitions nest. A query's definition hashes the units from the start of its span's first node to the end of its last, so a group's mark belongs to the node holding it and a definition's hash never depends on what follows it. A Rust item's span takes in its attributes and doc comments, and the hash drops the comments. A TOML key, a JSON key, a Makefile rule and a Markdown section are hashed by their text, each run of whitespace made one space. The scheme prefix names the rules and is fixed from its first release: no t1 hash was released before these rules, and a later change is t2.
alternatives: Hash the span's raw bytes: rejected because every reformat and comment edit would read as a change to the code
Hash the tokens without lengths: rejected because two token runs that join to the same bytes would hash alike
Hash every definition over all its own tokens: rejected because a token n definitions deep is hashed n times, which a file of nested items makes quadratic
Hash the leaves alone: rejected because a repetition's separator and an error's bytes are in no leaf, so changing them moved no hash
No scheme prefix: rejected because a stored hash would silently compare against one computed by other rules

choice: A stale anchor follows its gone file's rename only when the rename carried its code: the same span hash before the rename and in the file the rename made
reason: A wrong repair hides the staleness it mends, and repair_anchors writes every repair unattended, while git pairs files by similarity alone. So a symbol anchor follows a rename only when its definitions at the old path before the rename have the span hash they have in the blob the rename's commit wrote at the new path, read in the one git cat-file batch (for a rename not committed, the work tree's file), and its symbol resolves at the new path now to definitions of the kinds it named in that blob.
