The rename is judged where it happened, so a later edit of the file keeps the repair, and an edit since that moved the item out and left a declaration of its name does not land the anchor on the declaration. A file anchor follows an exact rename into a file that defines an item, or a rename one of its symbol anchors followed, and for an inexact rename only while no symbol anchor that resolved in the old file is missing from the blob the rename made: one boilerplate main carried unchanged does not carry a file whose own functions stayed behind. A symbol the rename carried that is no longer at the new path is searched for from that file.
alternatives: Trust an exact rename without comparing code: rejected because a later edit may have moved the item out of the new path and left a declaration of its name
Compare the symbol before the rename with the new path at HEAD: rejected because any later edit of the symbol in the renamed file would then lose the repair
Follow every rename git reports: rejected because a shared license header or boilerplate pairs unrelated files, and every binary resolves main

choice: A stale Rust symbol is repaired to the one file of its target that writes it when the commit its file last lost it in gave that file the same span hash
reason: Names alone do not show where code went: a function deleted for good in the commit that writes an unrelated function of its name elsewhere is no move. So the search, CodeFacts::namesakes, finds the one other walked Rust file of the same target by place (roles::target_of) that writes the symbol as a whole path, no re-export or module declaration, an item a macro invocation produces being no definition; never when the searched file still defines its last segment or an invocation there spells it (Resolution::SymbolInInvocation). The searched file is the anchor's, or the one a rename carried the symbol into. Its loss is the newest of its commits, read in rounds of the newest one, four and sixteen, whose parent wrote the item, or the work tree when HEAD wrote it; the repair is given when, across that loss, the candidate went from writing no such item to definitions of the span hash the searched file's had, and no later commit added or deleted the candidate. The hash compares tokens, comments and whitespace aside, and tolerates nothing else, not a changed visibility or attribute, not a rename of the item: an edited move is left stale rather than guessed. The reads are one walk for the searched files and their candidates and at most four blob batches, whatever the history's length.
alternatives: Follow the code through later commits and carrier files: rejected because a namesake written in the commit a carrier lost its own item was taken for the code, and one pickaxe walk per search cost minutes on a long history
Accept an edited move above a text similarity: rejected because no threshold separates an edited move from a rewrite by name without an owner's call
Judge the anchor's file at the parent of its last change: rejected because any later edit of the file then turns its repairs off

choice: status fits its sections to the budget by the level search, keeping each one's leading items; a section that leaves items out gives omitted and more, naming where the rest is, or for lint how it ranks
reason: A broken graph can hold thousands of issues, and a large one hundreds of components, so a section's items can exceed the result budget alone. Each section's item sizes go to budget::level, so short sections stay whole and long ones keep a prefix; the section then carries total, the items kept, omitted and more, which names where the rest is: trurlic check lists every issue, and the component and decision files hold every row. section returns one section with the whole budget. Only the lint section takes a cursor, from: no other surface judges a stored decision's patterns, so its result names in next the first decision whose quality findings the page did not list whole. No status result is cut by the generic truncation, which a test over a graph of 400 issues and 300 components asserts.
alternatives: A cursor argument to page every section: rejected because trurlic check lists every issue and the files hold every row; the pattern findings, which no other surface judges, are the one place that takes from
Fixed item counts per section: rejected because item sizes vary, so a count either wastes the budget or exceeds it

choice: A Store holds the graph directory and the code root, the tree the call comes from; anchors resolve against the code root, and .state/ lives in the graph directory
reason: A linked worktree and a symlinked clone read a graph that is not theirs, and their code differs from the main worktree's: a branch adds files and moves symbols. Anchors resolve against the tree the call comes from, so Store carries the code root beside the graph directory (Store::reached_from), the load hands it to ProjectState::code_root, and get_context counts an anchor orphaned only when the calling tree lacks its file; span hashes will use the same root. The graph directory is held by its real path, so .state/, the lock and the commit journal, is one directory for every tree that reaches the graph: writers started in the main worktree, a linked worktree and a symlinked clone exclude each other, and a commit one of them left unfinished is finished by a command in another. The backup migrate makes sits beside the real graph too. status prints both roots when they differ, and messages name the graph by its path then, since the tree holds no .trurlic/ of its own.
alternatives: Resolve anchors against the graph's parent: rejected because a linked worktree or a clone would judge its anchors by the main worktree's files, another branch
Keep .state/ per tree: rejected because two trees writing one graph would not exclude each other, and a journal left in one tree would never be finished from another
Hold the graph by the path through the symlink: rejected because migrate's backup and its git listing would land in the clone, which is another repository

choice: A Rust or Python symbol's last () names a function or method alone and (x) is refused; in TypeScript a last () names those or a segment written with it, other parentheses text
reason: A struct field and its getter share a path (Store::code_root), and a decision may mean one of them, so the grammar needs a spelling that tells them apart without a second path syntax. A trailing () is how a reader writes a call: Store::code_root() names the function or method of that path and nothing else, while Store::code_root names every definition of the path, the field and the getter together as one set. The narrowing comes first: among a path's definitions () keeps the functions and methods, so a set of functions and other kinds is narrowed to its functions, and it is the one narrowing by kind. A function is a fn item, in a module or a body, and a method a fn of an impl or a trait; a tuple struct's constructor, a const of a fn type, a macro and a pub use leaf are not functions here. The parentheses hold nothing: a call's arguments are no part of a name, so (x) is refused, and so is a ) that closes no (. Whitespace before them is allowed as within a name, so open () is open(). A trait segment is no function, so <Display>() is refused. The suffix is a rule of the languages, by the syntax each language's row names: in a TOML or JSON key, a Makefile target or a Markdown heading parentheses are text. TypeScript names a test by a string that may hold anything, which a segment must spell as the file reads: there parentheses are text, and a last () names the functions of the path without it or any definition whose last segment is written with it.
alternatives: A kind prefix such as fn:Store::code_root: rejected because it is a second syntax to teach, and () is how a call is written
Let () hold an argument list to pick an overload: rejected because Rust has no overloads, and a list is no part of a name
Read () in every kind of file: rejected because a heading or a key may end in parentheses, which would then name nothing
Keep the migration's parentheses as a call: rejected because 0.4.1 parentheses never narrowed what a ref named

choice: A symbol is a ::-separated path of names from the outermost container, a Rust trait impl a <Trait> segment; it names each definition whose path ends with it, those of one path together
reason: One grammar serves every kind of file, so an agent spells an anchor the same way in Rust, TOML, JSON, Makefiles and Markdown: Store::open, Config::<Display>::fmt, profile::release::panic, Install::From source, ci. A definition's canonical path runs from the outermost container, and a symbol names every definition whose path ends with its segments, so a bare name resolves where the file defines it under one path and the qualified path where it does not. Definitions of one full path, cfg twins or a field and its getter, are one thing the symbol resolves to with every span (a-symbol-names-every-definition-of-its-one-path); definitions of several paths, one variant name in two enums or a function and a test of its name, are Ambiguous with the number of paths rather than resolved to the first, so a span hash never covers the wrong one, unless the symbol is the whole path of one of them (a-symbol-that-is-a-definition-s-whole-path-names-it). In Rust, angle brackets group a trait's arguments, so :: splits only outside them; other kinds split on :: alone, and a heading, a key or a test's string that holds :: is split the same way, so a symbol can name it as the user reads it in the file; a name with a :: at an end or two in a row has an empty segment no symbol spells.
alternatives: Accept any definition of the name in the file: rejected because two definitions of one name give no single span to hash
Resolve an ambiguous symbol to its first definition: rejected because the order of a file is no statement of which one the decision meant
A dotted path for TOML and JSON keys: rejected because a key may hold a dot, and one grammar for every kind is simpler to teach

choice: The definitions a symbol names that share one full path are one thing it resolves to, every span and one hash; only definitions of several paths are Ambiguous(n), n the paths
reason: Ambiguity is a property of names, not of how many definitions a name has. cfg twins of a function, a field and its getter, a key each element of an array holds, a heading or a Makefile target defined twice: each is one thing no spelling can split. A symbol matches as before: the definitions whose path ends with it, those whose whole path it is winning, a trailing () first narrowing to functions and methods. The matches are grouped by full path; one group resolves to all its definitions, several are Ambiguous with the number of paths. Kind takes no part in what is one thing, and () is the one narrowing. Definitions holds a first span and the rest in file order, so it is never empty, their count, and whether their kinds differ, for the anchor findings to warn of. Its one hash is a single definition's own, or the hash of the members' hashes in the order of the hashes, so twins that swap places move nothing. Its text is the count, the first span and the hash. A lossy path merges silently. Known approximations: a heading or a key holding :: beside the nested one, and an impl for &T beside one for &mut T.
alternatives: Keep Ambiguous for every symbol of several definitions: rejected because cfg twins and a field with its getter could then be anchored by no symbol at all
Let kind split a path's definitions into things: rejected because a type and its value, or a property and its setter, are one name a reader means together, and () already narrows to functions
Hash the members in span order: rejected because two unchanged twins that swap places would move the hash, as moving one definition does not
Print every span of a set: rejected because a key held by thousands of array elements printed a text far past a tool result's budget

choice: A symbol on a file the C++ grammar reads, a header among them, is text, so operator() and ~Box are spelled as written; on a .c file it is a name
reason: C++ names an operator, a conversion and a destructor with punctuation (operator(), operator<, ~Box), which the grammar of names refuses, so a symbol on a file the C++ grammar reads is text, matched against the names as the index spells them. C names nothing so, and a symbol on a .c file is a name, which refuses a malformed one at once. A .h file is read by the C++ grammar, so a symbol on a C header is text too: there f(x) names nothing, where on a .c file it is refused as malformed.
alternatives: Names on every C and C++ file: rejected because operator() and ~Box could then not be named
Text on every C and C++ file: rejected because a malformed symbol on a .c file would then name nothing instead of being refused
origin: c and c++ review: macro scope, shapes and visibility

choice: Among the definitions a symbol names, those whose whole path it is, no segment left out, are what it resolves to; only when none are does every suffix match count
reason: A symbol names every definition whose path ends with it, so a module-level function open and a method Store::open are both named by open, and without a further rule no spelling names the function alone: its whole path is open, which is also a suffix of the method's. The same holds for a function and the test named after it in tests, and for a type and one of the same name in an inner module. A symbol that is a definition's whole path states exactly that path, so among the matches those of the whole path win, and a shorter suffix of a deeper path stays the shorthand it was. The definitions left are then grouped by path: those of one path resolve together, as cfg twins or a field and its getter do, and the symbol is Ambiguous only when they hold several paths, as two trait impls' methods named without their trait segment do. This refines the grammar the owner set, under which every such symbol was ambiguous.
alternatives: Every symbol that names several definitions is Ambiguous: rejected because a module-level item that shares its name with any member could then be named by no symbol at all
A leading :: for a path from the file's root: rejected because the whole path already is from the outermost container, and a second spelling of one path is what anchors avoid

choice: A symbol that names one path's definitions of several kinds, a field and its getter, is no anchor finding
reason: The code index unites the definitions of one path under one set and one hash on purpose, so a field and its getter, or the cfg twins of an item, are one place an anchor names, whose every span a change may touch. A warning on such a set could be cleared only toward the method, by spelling it with its parentheses: no spelling names the field alone, so a decision about the data would carry the warning for good. lint::anchors therefore classes every resolved anchor alike, whatever the kinds its set holds, and status has no count for such sets.
alternatives: Warn of every set of mixed kinds: rejected because no spelling clears it for a field, so a decision about the data warns for good
Warn only of a set that is not a field and a function: rejected because it needs a list of kind pairs that are fine, for sets no tree has shown

choice: A call of describe, it, test or their kin is a test named by its first string; so is a call of a chain of one or two members from such a name, but context, when a function follows the string
reason: A JavaScript test is a call, not a named function, and a proof names the test it ran by the strings of the calls that hold it. A call of describe, context, suite, it, test, specify, bench or their jasmine forms whose first argument is a string or template literal is a definition of kind test, named by that text without its quotes, interpolations and .each placeholders kept. So is a call of a chain of one or two members from such a name, called directly or through a call (it.only, test.describe.serial, it.concurrent.only, describe.each(table), describe.runIf(x), test.extend({})), when a function literal follows the string, right after it or after one argument between (Playwright's details, Vitest's options). The shape tells a runner's call from a call on a variable of a runner's name: test.set("Content-Type", "text") passes no function. context roots no chain, since it is the usual name of a Playwright browser context or a canvas context, whose route("x", handler) has the shape. No list of modifiers is kept, which each runner release would outgrow. Over react-hook-form, webpack, react, vite, excalidraw, eslint, express, mocha, jest and Playwright's own tests the rule takes no call that is not a test or a Playwright step, and misses calls whose function is computed (it.concurrent("x", testFn("x"))) or absent (it.todo("x")). A test nested in another's callback is under it. A name that is no string literal defines nothing, nor does an empty one. A test and everything its callback defines are test code; the call has no visibility.
alternatives: Test calls as no definitions: rejected because a proof could then name no test of a JavaScript project
A list of the runners' modifiers: rejected because Vitest and Playwright add group forms each release (runIf, for, serial), and a list that lacks one drops every test under it
Any member call whose first argument is a string: rejected because Playwright's context.waitForEvent("page") and express's test.set("a", "b") would become tests
The template literal with its interpolations evaluated: rejected because the index reads no value a program computes

choice: A tool call reaches the client through Peer::request: the wait answers ping, queues other requests (16 at most), ends on cancellation or EOF, and has no timeout
reason: accept asks the owner through an elicitation form during its tool call, so the server must send a request of its own and read the answer from the same stdin it reads every request from. Peer::request refuses before sending when the client's initialize did not declare the capability the method needs (form elicitation: elicitation with form, or empty), takes the next id of the server's own, writes the request and reads lines until the response with that id: a ping is answered at once, as the specification requires; any other request is queued and served after the call is answered, since a client may send parallel tool calls while one waits on a form; past 16 queued a request is answered -32000; a stray response is ignored; notifications/cancelled for the call ends the wait and the call gets no response, and for a queued request drops it. The wait has no timeout, because the answer can be a person reading a form; the client's cancellation and the end of stdin end it, the latter with a clean exit.
alternatives: Refuse client requests during the wait: rejected, it fails valid parallel tool calls while one waits on a form
A timeout on the wait: rejected, a person answers the form; cancellation and EOF already end the wait
A reader thread with channels: rejected, reading the one line stream in place keeps its order and needs no synchronisation

choice: A tool's CLI twin finds the store, parses and runs the tool through mcp::twin and prints through commands::answer: the call's JSON with --json, every refusal included
reason: Every tool has a CLI twin on the same code. trurlic apply reads a JSON object from a file or stdin, at most one MCP message's size, and trurlic status builds its arguments from its flags; mcp::twin discovers the store from the working directory, as a call does, and runs ToolSpec::run, the parse and the access a call takes, without a client, returning the tool's result or its ToolError. commands::answer is the one path both twins print through: lines for a terminal, or the call's text with --json, a refusal's JSON on stdout included, a store that discovery cannot find or read among them, so the twins cannot differ again. A document that cannot be read or is no JSON object is invalid_argument, refused before the store is found.
alternatives: A clap flag per argument of apply: rejected because a batch is a list of tagged ops a command line cannot hold, and the parse would be a second one
Parse the batch in commands with serde: rejected because the refusals and limits would drift from the tool's
Discover the store in each command before the twin: rejected because a failed discovery then left the command's path, printing no JSON under --json

choice: tracked: a work tree whose git tracks a file of the graph and ignores none; shared: git tracks none, and in a work tree it is the graph at the top of the main worktree
reason: A file of the graph is tracked when the index holds its path, the rule the migration reads git's listing by (store::placement::partition). A tracked graph needs one tracked file, not all: a decision written and checked before git add is a change waiting for its commit, as any new source file is; a graph git tracks none of, the state between init and the first commit or one that never reached git, is refused, since linked worktrees check out nothing. A file an ignore rule matches can never be committed, so one is refused. Outside any work tree a tracked graph is refused and a shared one passes: nothing versions it, and symlinked trees reach it. A shared graph in a work tree is the main worktree's at its top, where linked worktrees look; elsewhere, or in a bare repository's worktree, it is SharedOffMain. Every other graph directory is a second graph: a linked worktree's beside a shared main graph, found from the main worktree with its branch, and this graph when the main worktree's is shared, found from the linked side whatever placement it states.
alternatives: Every file tracked: rejected because a decision written and checked before git add would fail check
Only an ignore rule contradicts tracked: rejected because a tracked graph never committed would pass while every linked worktree finds no graph
Report a second graph only from the main worktree: rejected because a check run in the linked worktree, which reads its own graph, would pass

choice: A symbol may leave out a <Trait> segment but never its own last one, may write a trait without its arguments to name every argument's impl, and names a trait by its last path segment
reason: A method of a trait impl has the path Type::<Trait>::method, and most anchors name it as Type::method: when the type has one method of that name the shorter spelling is unambiguous, and when two impls define it the symbol is Ambiguous, which says to add the segment. The last segment is never skipped, so Table names the type and not its Table::<Display> impl, which only a symbol ending in <Display> names. A trait with arguments is written with them, <From<Kind>>, whitespace removed on both sides; written without them, <From> names the impl of every argument, ambiguous when there are several. The trait is named by its last path segment, so <fmt::Display> and <Display> are one spelling, as the import a file uses decides nothing about the impl. A trait name written as a plain segment (Shape::area for the impl Shape for Circle) names nothing, since a plain segment is a type, module or item.
alternatives: Require every trait segment: rejected because Type::method is how a reader names a method, and an ambiguity is reported anyway
Let a plain segment match a trait segment: rejected because Shape::area would then name the impl of Shape for every type in the file
Keep the trait's full path: rejected because the same impl would have two spellings by how the file imports the trait

choice: A file of a tree-sitter kind is refused past 1 MiB and one of a lexical kind past 4 MiB, each as TooLarge naming its size and its kind's cap
reason: tree-sitter's error recovery costs work its progress count of steps does not show: on generated error-dense input a parse takes microseconds a byte whatever the budget of steps, so no budget stops it, and the bound on its time is a bound on the file's size. At 1 MiB the worst seen takes seconds, once, since the index is then cached; at 4 MiB it would take a minute or more. A lexical resolver's work is the index's own and counted per byte, so data and prose files keep 4 MiB. The cap is FileKind::max_bytes, checked by the pure index, and the shell reads at most the largest cap and one byte more, so every surface reports the one refusal.
alternatives: One cap of 4 MiB for every kind: rejected because an error-dense file that size takes a minute or more to parse cold
A wall-clock timeout on the parse: rejected because code reads no clock, and a file would be refused on a slow machine and not a fast one
A check of the bytes' density before the parse: rejected because no measure of the bytes predicts the parser's error recovery

choice: A span's tokens are every byte but whitespace and comments, by the lexicon each grammar declares; a Rust hash also leaves out the commas, braces, parentheses and pipes of no meaning
reason: A grammar's tree is no exact lexer of its language, and the hash must follow the language. Each leaf is a token, and each node of a lexical literal kind is one whole, so a string's prefix and delimiters are hashed and -1 and - 1 agree. A repetition's separator and what error recovery passes over lie in no node, so each run of such bytes is a token too. tree-sitter-rust lexes a comment as tokens after a repetition's separator, so a token that opens a comment by the grammar's declared syntax starts bytes no token is taken from. tree-sitter-python leaves a line continuation before a string in no node, so a grammar that declares continuations holds one in those bytes as whitespace. A metavariable $a written $ a is hashed as the two tokens Rust has. Each grammar states its literal kinds, comment delimiters, continuations and glued kinds as data in one Lexicon. Rust's hashes leave out what carries no meaning: a list's trailing comma, but the one of a one-element tuple; the braces around a closure's or a match arm's body of one expression, or of one return, break or continue, with that semicolon; the outer pair of nested parentheses around an expression; and a match arm's leading pipe. So rustfmt's edits to them move no hash. A comma or a brace inside a macro's tokens stays, as only the macro gives it a meaning, so the trailing comma rustfmt adds to a vec! it breaks moves the hash, and so does its merge of two derive attributes. Python's commas and parentheses of no meaning are its query's (what-a-python-span-hash-covers). TypeScript's hashes keep every comma, as a trailing one can carry meaning (an array's hole, TSX's <T,>).
alternatives: Hash the leaves alone: rejected because a repetition's separator and an error's bytes are in no leaf, so changing them moved no hash
Hard-code Rust's comment syntax in the token walk: rejected because each grammar the index adds has its own
Leave a trailing comma in a macro's tokens out too: rejected because a macro may give it meaning, as a repetition without $(,)? refuses one
State that a reformat moves the hash: rejected because every rustfmt run would then touch decisions in a diff review
Name the silent tokens as Lexicon data of every grammar: rejected because the rule reads each grammar's node kinds, Rust's in code and Python's in its query

choice: A .trurlic that is a file, or a symlink that dangles, loops or leads to a file, is a typed error naming it, and stops the walk
reason: A .trurlic in a tree says which graph the tree means; when it leads nowhere, a graph further up is another project's or the parent repository's, and a write would land there. graph_in reads the entry with symlink_metadata and resolves a symlink with canonicalize, which follows the whole chain under the system's bound on symlinks, so a loop fails at once instead of hanging. A dangling or looping link is Error::GraphLinkBroken with the link and the system's reason, a file or a link to a file Error::GraphNotDirectory; serve answers either as a store_error refusal.
alternatives: Skip the entry and walk on: rejected because the graph found above is not the one the tree links to
Follow a link one step at a time with a counter of trurlic's: rejected because canonicalize already bounds the chain

choice: A TypeScript declaration is public when an export holds or names it or an ambient module with no export form holds it, else private; a member is public unless private, # or protected says so
reason: A count of definitions with and without private ones needs each one's visibility as the source states it. In a module, export is the visibility: a declaration an export statement holds, one an export list names (export { a, b as c }), one export default or export = names, and in CommonJS one module.exports names, a class or a function module.exports is, is public; any other declaration of the module's or a namespace's top is private to it. In an ambient context TypeScript exports every declaration unless the body holds an export form (an export list, export *, export = or export default of a value): what declare module "x", declare namespace or declare global holds is then public at any depth, and with an export form only what an export marks is. declare module "x" itself is public, since any file imports it by its name. A re-export (export { a } from) names another file's definition. A nested function is private. A class member is public unless private, a # name or protected states otherwise; protected is a visibility of its own. An interface's, a type literal's, an object literal's and an enum's members have no modifier and are public. A test is a call, which nothing names from outside, so it has none.
alternatives: Members as visible as their container: rejected because TypeScript states a member's visibility on the member, public by default
protected as private: rejected because a subclass in another file may name it
Ignore CommonJS exports: rejected because module.exports is how a CommonJS module exports, and its functions would read as private

Every declaration of an ambient module public: rejected because TypeScript exports only the marked ones once the body holds an export form (declare module "*.svg" { const c: string; export default c })

choice: Only check runs git for other worktrees; one holds a missing anchor when its work tree differs at the file from the fork and resolves the anchor where the fork did not
reason: Pending needs the repository's other worktrees, and asking git costs a process, so sources asks only for check, only when an anchor of a decision ever accepted is missing here, and only when git::dot_git finds a .git at or above the code root: status spawns nothing for its anchors. git runs in the code root, never in a graph directory. The calling tree's own worktree is the listed top nearest at or above the code root, a submodule's main worktree, which git lists by its git directory, taking the code root's top when the calling tree is it; the code root's place in it is where each other worktree is read. A worktree may hold an anchor at the paths its work tree differs in from the merge base of the two HEADs, by git diff --name-only from that base and git ls-files --others --exclude-standard, so code written and not committed, or not yet added, counts whatever that worktree's commit. It holds the anchor only when the anchor resolves in those files there and not in them as the merge base held them, read in one git cat-file batch: a branch cut before a deletion, whose work tree still holds the code, never hides it, whatever else it changed in the file. Two lines that share no commit count every path. The worktrees are read in git's order for the anchors no earlier one holds, and none once every one is held; only the changed files, never a walk, each read against the calling tree's crates and module declarations. A git failure, a calling tree git lists as no live worktree and a path that cannot be made canonical leave worktrees unread, a check warning.
alternatives: Count any worktree whose HEAD is no ancestor of this tree's: rejected because a branch cut before a deletion, with any commit of its own, still holds the deleted code and would hide the deletion
Skip a worktree at the calling tree's commit or behind it: rejected because the same uncommitted code would then count in one worktree and not in another, by a commit unrelated to it
Count committed changes alone: rejected because a new worktree holds an agent's code uncommitted until its first commit, and check would fail on an accepted decision about it meanwhile
Walk each worktree ahead whole: rejected because each check would read every source file of every such worktree for crates and module declarations the calling tree holds already in the usual case
Ask the worktrees in status too: rejected because status is called often and asks the project's git nothing, so it names such an anchor unresolved instead

choice: Advisory file locking via std File::try_lock and try_lock_shared with 5-second polling timeout
reason: Prevents concurrent mutations from CLI and MCP server processes. Writers take the exclusive lock on .state/lock with std's File::try_lock in a polling loop (50ms interval, 5s deadline); the blocking File::lock has no timeout, so a hung holder would hang every writer. Every read loads under the shared lock (try_lock_shared, same loop), which keeps writers out without excluding other readers, so a read never sees a commit halfway through its renames. std reports contention as TryLockError::WouldBlock on every platform. The lock file is opened read and write, which never blocks, and refused unless it is a regular file before it is locked or read. StoreLock is a proof-of-lock type: every function that changes a file under .trurlic/ takes it, and a Writer owns one. The lock file stores the exclusive holder's PID for the timeout's message.
alternatives: A mutex in the process: rejected because it does not work across the separate CLI and MCP processes
No locking, last writer wins: rejected because concurrent writes that race lose data silently
A database with built-in concurrency: rejected because it adds a heavy dependency for a file-based store

choice: An access label in a #if arm holds past the arm, a function body starts public, an anonymous union's members are under the outer label, and a blanked macro that holds static is written static
reason: Every arm of #if is read as written, so a label in one arm and one in the next both stand before what follows #endif: the query marks each arm @visibility.through, so a label in it holds past it, and the last in source order holds, the one a reader meets last and the one an #ifdef ... #else takes when its macro is undefined. A label states the access of its class's members, not of what a member function's body defines, so a body's brace starts public, as a free function's is. The members of an anonymous union or struct with no member name are the outer class's own, so the label in force there holds for them; an unnamed type with a member name, a typedef or a declaration is a type of its own, public within. A macro the tree defines as static, alone or beside other specifiers, in every arm but an empty one (curl's UNITTEST, FreeRTOS's STATIC) makes what it marks private in every build but that arm's, so the blank writes static in its place when its name is at least as long as the word, and the definition stays private; a shorter name is blanked, the limit c_family.rs states.
alternatives: A label that ends at #endif: rejected because what follows then takes the class's default, which no arm says
A static macro blanked as any specifier: rejected because what curl and FreeRTOS keep private then reads as public
origin: c and c++ review: macro scope, shapes and visibility

choice: A resolved one-name symbol on a code file that is not the whole path of a definition there is weak when WEAK_FILES (10) or more walked files of its kind define the name at any depth
reason: A name alone that many files define does not show a reader where to look when it reaches its definition through a suffix, a method or a nested item named without its type or module: a fuller spelling such as Runner::run tells it apart, and the warning names it. A symbol that is already the whole path of a definition in its file, a module-level item, has no fuller spelling, since the anchor names the file, so CodeFacts::lone_name leaves it out and it is never weak whatever the count. CodeFacts::spread counts, in one pass over the definitions of the tree, the walked files of the anchor's kind that hold a definition whose own name is the name: items, fields, variants and pub use leaves. A file only an anchor brought into the facts is not counted, so the verdict is the tree's whatever decisions origin narrows to. Only a kind whose every file the walk takes can be counted, which FileKind::is_code states for the source languages, Rust, Python, TypeScript, C and C++, a .ts and a .tsx file, like a C and a C++ file, being two kinds counted apart; a data or prose file is read only when an anchor names it. With no such anchor no definition is read. A qualified symbol, a file anchor and an ambiguous anchor are never weak: one finding per anchor.
alternatives: Weak whatever the symbol resolves through: rejected because a module-level fn fmt beside thirty Display impls would warn with no spelling that clears it
Every symbol that resolves through a suffix, with no count: rejected because a trait segment the grammar lets a symbol leave out would warn too, too many to act on by hand
Count per anchor over the tree: rejected because hundreds of anchors would each scan every definition of the tree
A bound in project.toml: rejected because no project has asked to move it, and a constant is one place to change it

choice: An anchor matches a path when one names the other or a directory holding it, so a directory anchor covers its files and a directory query finds the anchors under it
reason: A decision anchored on src/auth constrains src/auth/token.rs, and a query for src/auth asks for every decision inside it: matching only the query as a prefix missed the first, exact matching missed both. Anchor::overlaps compares whole segments, so src/auth does not match src/authz. ProjectState::decisions_in and anchors_in use it for get_decisions_for_file and trurlic query file, which report the anchors that matched.
alternatives: Exact match only: rejected because a directory anchor would never match a file in it
The query as a prefix only: rejected because a directory anchor would miss every file under it
Prefix match on raw strings: rejected because src/auth would match src/authz

choice: An anchor path has one spelling: relative to the code root, separated by /, with no .., no empty or . segment, no backslash, no leading / and no drive
reason: Anchors are a set matched by string, so two spellings of one file would be two anchors that sort apart and match differently. Anchor::new refuses, at parse and through the type, a path that is empty, longer than MAX_ANCHOR_PATH_BYTES, holds a control character, a backslash, a leading / or a first segment ending in a colon, a .. segment, or an empty or . segment (which also refuses a trailing /), naming the fault. A path given to a query is first put in that spelling by normalize_path (a leading ./ and repeated or trailing / dropped) and then held to the same rules, so a query cannot name a place outside the code root. An anchor's file may name a directory.
alternatives: Normalize anchor paths at load: rejected because the file would hold a spelling the state does not, and fmt would rewrite paths behind the author's back
Resolve paths against the file system: rejected because the answer depends on the tree it runs in, follows symlinks, and fails for a file that does not exist yet
Accept a backslash as a separator: rejected because a backslash is a legal file-name character on Linux, so the path would mean two things

choice: An anchor resolves to Resolved, FileMissing, SymbolMissing, Ambiguous(n), SymbolOnDirectory, NoResolver, Unindexable(fault) or Malformed(fault), each cause named apart
reason: Each outcome asks for a different fix, so none is folded into another. FileMissing means the path is gone; SymbolMissing that the file defines nothing the symbol names; Ambiguous(n) that its matches hold n distinct paths and the symbol needs a qualifier, which always exists; SymbolOnDirectory that a symbol was put on a directory; NoResolver that the file is of a kind the index does not read, which is not the file's fault; Unindexable carries the read or index fault (no regular file, over its kind's size, not readable, not UTF-8, a TOML or JSON syntax error, work past its budget, a nesting past the bound), which a stale anchor report must not hide behind symbol missing; Malformed carries the grammar fault of a symbol (an empty segment, an angle bracket that does not pair). Resolved holds a file, a directory, or the definitions of the one path the symbol names: their spans in file order, at least one, and one hash. Each has a Display text, the cause a report prints.
alternatives: Fold every failure into one stale outcome: rejected because the fix for a missing file, a file the index cannot read and a symbol needing a qualifier differ
Report a file the index cannot read as symbol missing: rejected because the anchor may well be right, and the report would blame it

choice: The tree's crates and test files come from the files the walk takes; an anchored Rust file outside them is read against those and the manifests above it, and adds nothing to them
reason: What an anchor resolves to, and the role of what it names, must be a function of the tree and that anchor, never of which other anchors there are. So the facts build the tree's crates and test files once, from the walked files. A walked file's crate is read from the walked manifests alone. The shell reads, for each anchored Rust file the walk does not take, every Cargo.toml on its path, and such a file's crate is read from those and the walked ones. A manifest an anchor brings thus governs no file the walk took, a symlinked Cargo.toml beside walked files included. An anchored file outside the walk is a root or module of the test walk whose own declarations are not followed, so its crate and role reach no other file. The cost is linear in the tree and the outside files. Its own unwalked crate's other files are not read, so their declarations are not followed.
alternatives: Walk every unwalked directory an anchor points into: rejected because its manifests and declarations would then reach the walked files and move their roles
Let every manifest read govern every file below it: rejected because anchoring a symlinked Cargo.toml then moved a walked file into another crate

choice: A warn pattern writes the batch and warns once per op at its first match; the result lists one per op by argument and pattern index, counts the rest, and carries each message once
reason: A rule that needs judgment must not block a right write, yet the writer has to see it, and the batch is written whether or not its warnings reach the caller, so a cut warning is lost. Thirty-two warn patterns over fifty ops can draw 1,600 warnings, which no result lists beside the fifty op entries within 24 KiB. So each op and the batch's origin list MAX_WARNINGS_PER_OP, as field, rule, pattern index and byte offset, with the op's name only in the op's own entry; more_warnings and more_origin_warnings count the rest exactly, which the caller recomputes from the patterns of project.toml; patterns carries each named pattern's message once, the warn messages together bounded at config load. The arithmetic sits beside the test that holds a full batch's worst result to the budget.
alternatives: List every warning in the shape of a refusal: rejected because a full batch's result is cut, and the cut warnings of a written batch cannot be read again
A warning per match: rejected because one pattern over a long reason would fill the result
Drop the messages and name the pattern alone: rejected because the caller would read project.toml to learn what a warning says

choice: An index entry's room is its file's bytes times what its kind's densest definitions cost per byte, every heap block charged as glibc's malloc takes it
reason: No file a kind's size cap admits may be refused for the definitions it holds, and a forged entry may take no more memory than its file's room. So the scope tree charges each part of an index, and a read charges it again before it allocates: its bytes in the entry, the slot of each value in its collection by size_of, and each heap block it owns at the allocator's minimum, at least 32 bytes and the request with an 8-byte header rounded to 16, a scope's depth too. A read charges each collection's block whole, and the overhead holds what they round. The room per byte is the cost of the densest definition a kind holds, a scope of one segment and the definition with each number as long as the kind's cap makes it, over the bytes it takes: a two-byte item `A,` of a tree-sitter kind, a one-byte table of a dotted TOML key, a Makefile target sharing its rule's span, an empty Markdown heading, an empty JSON key in five bytes. A definition is charged its span as one byte when it repeats the last one admitted, as the entry writes it. The sizes and each kind's room are in BOUNDS, so another target or rule is another cache key.
alternatives: A hand table of weights per value: rejected because it lumped a 24-byte token with a 104-byte rule and drifted from the types it stood for
One room of 64 bytes a byte for every kind: rejected because a variant of two bytes costs about 260, so dense legal files were refused
Charge requested bytes and state the bound as a factor of the room: rejected because the factor is the allocator's, and a forged entry of one-byte names took 1.6 times the stated room
One size cap of 1 MiB for every kind: rejected by the owner, who keeps 4 MiB for data and prose files
origin: code index: a macro invocation defines nothing

choice: A match of a pattern that sets exclusive drops each match of a pattern without it that captured the same @definition node, whatever the patterns' order
reason: Two patterns can capture one node as a definition where a language means one: const f = () => 1 is a declarator every binding pattern takes, and only the pattern for a function bound to a name may define it. A query cannot say not this kind, so a pattern that sets exclusive claims its @definition node: a match of a pattern without it on that node is dropped. Every match that captures a node is recorded by the time the walk reaches the node, since a match's root is the node or above it, so the claim is settled there in one step and no order of the patterns carries meaning. Two exclusive matches of one node both stand, as definitions of one span.
alternatives: The earlier pattern wins a tie: rejected because the order of a query's patterns would carry a meaning no refusal shows
The widest span wins per name: rejected because a declarator's two readings have one span
A kind chosen by the value's node kind: rejected because the two readings differ in where they are kept, not in kind alone

choice: An op is held to the quality bar in each field whose value it changes; a field it leaves as it is keeps what it held, below the bar or not
reason: A migrated decision without an anchor must stay revisable: a revise that fixes its reason should not have to invent an anchor first. Every rule of the bar reads one field, so a field the op does not change cannot newly break one, and the rule is exact. A record changes every field; a revise the fields changed() lists; a merge the survivor's anchors and tags when the absorbed decision brings ones it lacks. A field the op writes meets the bar whole: adding an alternative to a list that holds an overlong one is refused, so the bar rises one field at a time and never falls.
alternatives: Hold the whole decision on every write: rejected because a migrated graph would need anchors and alternatives before any other change
Refuse only a fault the op newly adds: rejected because a revise could then rewrite a field below the bar and leave it below

choice: An unnamed default export, or an unnamed function or class module.exports is, is a definition named default, its members under default::; any other value of more than one leaf a variable
reason: export default function () {} and export default class {} have no name of their own, so without one their members would land at the module's top beside its named definitions. The module's own name for the export is default, which an import names, so the definition takes it, and its methods are default::render. CommonJS's module.exports = function () {} is the same export, which an ES import of the module names default, so it is read alike, its helpers under default::. A function expression, arrow function or generator is a function, a class expression a class; an object, a call, a string or any other value of more than one leaf of the tree is a variable, and an object's methods are its own as a top-level const's are. A default export of a single leaf defines nothing: export default x names a definition the module already holds, which the export makes public, and export default 42 a number no reader looks up.
alternatives: No definition for an unnamed default export: rejected because its members would then stand at the top beside the module's named definitions
A definition named default for export default x too: rejected because x is already defined, and its span holds its body

choice: apply is the one write: a batch of ops applied in order to the writer's graph, validated once, then one journaled commit and one history commit, or refused whole with nothing written
reason: A design, a rename with its cascade and a maintenance pass over ten decisions are each one change of the graph, and a half-applied one is a graph nobody chose. Writer::apply runs the ops on the graph loaded under the exclusive lock, in place, keeping each touched node's starting value in an undo record (store/apply/edit.rs); every op is checked against the graph the earlier ops left; then the resulting graph is validated once under no new errors; then the changed files go through one Writer::commit with CommitMessage(Tool::Apply, origin, session). A refused batch, or a commit that fails before its commit point, restores the writer's graph from the undo record. The MCP tool and trurlic apply hand it the same parsed Batch, so both surfaces refuse alike and write the same bytes. Ops: record, revise, rename, merge, remove, the component ops add, revise, rename, remove, and repair_anchors; at most MAX_BATCH_OPS (50).
alternatives: One tool per op, as 0.3 had: rejected because a design or a cascade then lands in several commits, and a failure halfway leaves a graph no op meant
Apply the ops to a copy of the whole graph: rejected because the undo record holds only the touched nodes, and a 2000-decision copy costs more than the batch
Validate the whole graph after every op: rejected because each op's own checks name its argument, and a batch of 50 would validate 50 times

choice: apply judges each op's [quality] patterns as it runs, on a bar compiled before the lock, charging bytes to MAX_WRITE_PATTERN_BYTES and cache growth to MAX_PATTERN_CACHE_TOTAL_BYTES
reason: A write judges under the exclusive lock, which another reader or writer waits for at most 5 s, so what its patterns cost there is bounded. Compiling is done before: the handler compiles the bar with no lock held (Store::prepare_bar), and the writer compiles it again only when [quality] changed in between. On the lazy DFA alone what remains is the bytes the patterns read and the states their caches build. Writer::apply makes one Scan per batch: a cache per pattern, the bytes left and the cache left. The batch's origin is judged first; then each op holds what it writes to the text rules, the limits and the patterns as it runs (Bar::judge). Each pattern charges the bytes it would read, one more per text, before it reads any; past the bound the batch is refused as pattern_work at that op. After each pattern's search its caches' growth is charged to the total, so the growth may pass it by one pattern's two caches. Building states costs at most about 0.6 us a byte for a constructed pattern, so 1.5 MiB with that overshoot and 100 MB of reading keep the worst write near 1.4 s of CPU; a 32-pattern table of word lists, phrases and scripts grows under 1.1 MB over a full batch of English prose and a reason in fifteen scripts. A full cache is refused as pattern_gave_up, the total as pattern_cache_total naming the pattern that grew most; each says whether the op's texts alone did it, and the remedy follows: shorter text or a simpler pattern for one op, a split batch otherwise.
alternatives: Charge the whole batch before any pattern runs, then judge: rejected because it needs a second pass and a copy of each decision an op wrote, kept from the ops that follow
Retry an op over fresh caches after a give-up: rejected because each retry pays another fill under the lock
Charge a pattern's work as bytes times its weighed NFA states: rejected because on the lazy DFA alone the cost per byte belongs to the engine, and the weights overstate an ordinary table
One bound for the report and the write: rejected because a write holds the exclusive lock while it judges, and a bound that suits a report outlasts the lock timeout of every other caller
Bound the building of states by each cache's cap alone, small enough for 32 of them: rejected because the cap would starve a word list over a full batch while bounding nothing a smaller table needs
origin: apply: a batch's pattern work is bounded

choice: apply refuses a decision that breaks a quality rule, naming the field, the rule, the measured value and the limit in the rule's unit, on every surface
reason: A bar kept in a skill holds no agent at the write, and a graph kept to it by cleanups drifts between them. Writer::apply holds every decision a record, revise or merge writes to the bar, so the MCP tool and trurlic apply refuse alike. Built in: the store::text rules, a one-line choice of at most 200 bytes among them, at least one alternative, at least one anchor. From [quality]: reason_words min and max, alternatives_max, alternative_words_max, anchors_max, require_origin and patterns. A refusal is a typed Rule::Quality(QualityFault): a Limit carries the measured value and the bound, so the MCP rule name (reason_words_max) and the message (6 words, over the maximum of 5) come from one value. A refusal that states no measure leaves the caller guessing how much to cut.
alternatives: Keep the bar in a skill and clean the graph by script: rejected because nothing holds an agent to a skill at the write
Refuse with a message only: rejected because a caller branches on the rule name and cuts by the measured value

choice: apply's handler, not the store, warns of likely duplicates in the graph the write left: each decision whose text the batch wrote, its three nearest, listed while the result has room
reason: store imports no module above it, so Writer::apply cannot call lint, and a likely duplicate is not a rule of the write. The batch is written first; the handler then releases the exclusive lock and looks for duplicates in the graph the write left, within MAX_DUPLICATE_WORK, since a lookup over a large graph would hold every other reader and writer past LOCK_TIMEOUT. Past the bound duplicates_unsought gives its work instead. The CLI twin runs that handler too, so both surfaces warn alike. The decisions are those a record wrote or a revise changed the choice or reason of, followed through the batch's renames and dropped by a remove or a merge that absorbs them; an anchors-only revise warns of nothing. Each gets its three nearest at the threshold or above, best first. Fifty such warnings at 128-byte names exceed the 24 KiB result beside the longest ops, so the warnings fill the room the rest leaves, the repairs and stale anchors a repair_anchors op lists before them, in op order, and more_duplicates counts the others, whose pairs status ranks under lint.
alternatives: The check in Writer::apply: rejected because store would import lint, and a warning is no rule of the write
A fixed count of warnings per batch: rejected because the longest batch leaves room for none while a usual one has room for all
Only the best neighbour per decision: rejected because a decision can restate two others, and the caller then sees one

choice: Atomic file writes: canonical text read back in memory, staged and flushed in .state/tmp/, renamed into place, the directory flushed
reason: Prevents partial writes from corrupting on-disk state. prepare_write renders a value's canonical text and parses it back as its type, refusing with Error::CanonicalUnreadable when the text is no TOML of the type and Error::CanonicalDrift when it reads back as another value, before anything touches disk. Store::stage writes the bytes to a fresh temp file in .state/tmp/ (create_new, named after the process id and a counter, so no write reuses a leftover) and flushes them with sync_data; the file is then renamed into place and its directory flushed with sync_dir, because a rename is atomic but not durable: after a power loss the new name can survive without its data. A commit of several files is atomic as a whole through the commit journal. write_atomic is the single-file form, used by init before a graph exists; fmt and migrate commit through the journal. Temp files are removed only under the exclusive lock.
alternatives: Direct write to the final path: rejected because a crash mid-write leaves a truncated TOML file that fails every later load
Read the staged file back before the rename: rejected because it reads the page cache, not the disk, so it proves nothing the flush does not

choice: Benches and property tests draw from a seeded corpus written as canonical files in one journaled commit
reason: store::corpus writes a store shaped like a large real graph, plus a Rust source tree its anchors resolve in, with the share of anchored files a parameter. Reasons run from 600 to 1200 bytes, with up to 20 anchors; one decision in ten is proposed, and a quarter of those carry accepted_text. One decision in sixteen is project-wide, about one in two depends on an earlier one, and a component per 40 decisions connects to the next two. Words are drawn by rank band from a long-tailed vocabulary of 8,191, so a few words are in most texts and the rest in few. One decision in 25 opens its reason with half of an earlier one's, so the duplicates pass finds a few pairs as in a real graph; a uniform draw from a short list made nearly every pair one. Every node goes through prepare_write and one commit_batch, the path every write takes, and its tests hold the graph valid, every file canonical, and every node's bytes a fixpoint of read and write. Draws come from SplitMix64 in store::seeded and timestamps are a fixed epoch plus offsets, so the same Corpus value writes the same bytes on any machine, rand release or day: benches compare commits only while the corpus is byte-identical. The same generator is the one seeded source of the crate's unit property tests, such as the timestamps of store::time and the random payloads of mcp::truncate, so no test carries a second PRNG or a rand dependency. The corpus is crate-private and reaches benches as trurlic::bench::Corpus; both compile under cfg(test) and the bench feature only, so release builds carry neither the corpus nor the generator, and the store's public surface is the same with the feature.
alternatives: rand's StdRng: rejected because its algorithm is not guaranteed stable across releases, which would move every bench baseline on a dependency bump
One commit per decision: rejected because thousands of journaled commits take minutes and stamp wall-clock times
Commit a fixture corpus to the repo: rejected because it puts megabytes of generated TOML in git and fixes size and anchored share

choice: Benches drive the MCP server in process through Server::serve_one, reachable only with the bench feature
reason: Server holds the directory it finds the store from and its record of the client, and serve_one runs one read-dispatch-write turn over any BufRead and Write: run_server loops it over stdin and stdout, and benches/corpus.rs over a byte slice, so a bench times the exact request path minus the transport, the load every call makes included, with no second process or pipe in any sample. The benches run locally with plain criterion through `make bench`, and no CI job runs them: the project has one user and no public performance dashboard to maintain, so a hosted bench job would spend CI minutes and a third-party service on numbers nobody reads. Criterion compares each run with the previous one on the same machine, which is how a change is judged. The library's public surface stays cli and store: trurlic::bench re-exports Server only under the bench feature, the bench target requires it, and release builds never enable it. cargo-deny's wildcard ban rules out the alternative of a self dev-dependency that enables the feature for plain `cargo bench`, so `make bench` passes it.
alternatives: Spawn `trurlic serve` per bench: every sample would add pipe round trips and a second process's scheduling to the request path it means to time
Run the benches in a CI job on a hosted benchmarking service: CI minutes and a third-party account for numbers one user does not read
Make mcp a public module: widens the library surface the owner fixed at cli and store
Self dev-dependency enabling the feature: refused by cargo-deny's wildcard ban

choice: C files (.c) are read by tree-sitter-c and every other C or C++ file (.h, .cc, .cpp, .cxx, .hpp, .hh) by tree-sitter-cpp, through c.scm and cpp.scm, with no bound of their own before the parse
reason: A header cannot say whether C or C++ includes it, and the C++ grammar reads C headers about as well as the C grammar does (on curl and redis, within a percent of the definitions), so every .h is read as C++ and the two grammars meet the two languages once each. Both crates are at their newest releases whose ABIs tree-sitter 0.27 reads, and they add about 4.3 MB to the binary, which is the price of both languages. No bound of their own runs before the parse: tree-sitter-c has no scanner, tree-sitter-cpp caps its raw string delimiter itself, and thirty hostile shapes at the 1 MiB cap, nested parentheses, casts, unclosed templates, a most vexing parse, deep #if nesting and continued macros among them, each finish in linear time on a 128 KiB stack. The time, stack and memory a parse may take are the bounds every grammar shares, which a-file-is-indexed-on-a-stack-a-parse-at-the-cap-fits-in-within-a-bound-of-memory states.
alternatives: Read .h by the C grammar: rejected because a C++ header then misreads its classes and templates, while the C++ grammar reads a C header within a percent of the C grammar
Decide a header's grammar by a sibling .cpp file: rejected because the index of a file would then depend on another file's name
A bound before the parse like Python's: rejected because no hostile shape measured needs one

choice: store::canonical is the one serializer of graph files: node types derive Deserialize and no Serialize, and each write reads its text back as the value written
reason: The form is defined by Trurlic, not by the TOML library's printer: the printer decides array layout, quoting and key order itself and may change them in a release, so a dependency update would rewrite files nobody edited. With no Serialize on Project, Component, Decision or Anchor, no other code can write one, and each type's canonical text is spelled out key by key in canonical.rs. prepare_write parses the text back and refuses it with Error::CanonicalUnreadable or Error::CanonicalDrift unless it reads as the value it came from. A load tells whether a file is canonical with is_canonical, which drives the same emitter into a sink that matches each piece against the file's bytes and stops at the first difference; a timestamp or a format version is written straight through its Display and a word range bound by bound, so the check allocates nothing and costs no more than the bytes it matches.
alternatives: Derive Serialize and print with the TOML library: rejected because the layout would follow the library, not the format, and could change on a dependency update
Format with a layout-preserving TOML editor: rejected because it is a new dependency that keeps a document's layout where the format needs one fixed layout
Render the canonical text and compare strings at load: rejected because it allocates a file-sized string per node on every load for a yes or no

choice: The limits every node file and value is held to live in store::limits and are applied where every file passes: the read, the types and validation
reason: A limit kept per surface drifted: one surface accepted what another refused. store::limits holds MAX_NODE_FILE_BYTES (1 MiB, the cap of every node read), MAX_CHOICE_BYTES (200), MIN_REASON_BYTES (10) and MAX_TEXT_FIELD_BYTES (50,000) for a decision's text, and MAX_ANCHOR_PATH_BYTES (500) and MAX_ANCHOR_SYMBOL_BYTES (200) for an anchor. read_node_bytes caps each read, Anchor::new refuses at parse and store::text runs in validation, so a hand edit, a migration and any later write tool meet the same bound with the same message, and a change of a constant reaches all of them through the compiler. A tool's argument limits on the wire are declared with its spec and bound what it accepts; a value it hands the store then meets these. This absorbs the rule of the deleted pattern on limits at trust boundaries.
alternatives: Per-surface limit constants: rejected because they drifted, one surface accepting what another refused
No explicit limits, relying on the TOML parser: rejected because the parser accepts any size, and explicit bounds keep one file from costing every load and force concise decisions

choice: check and status report a shared graph's uncommitted tree, a leftover index.lock and a missing repository, each a typed HistoryFinding with a stable form
reason: The owner learns from them what the history lacks before a review reads it. Store::history_findings returns nothing under tracked, where the project's git holds the history. Under shared it returns Missing when .trurlic/.git is gone, IndexLocked when .git/index.lock is there, and Uncommitted with the graph files git status lists, sorted, asked under the shared lock so no write is halfway. status is a read and writes nothing to the repository: git status runs with --no-optional-locks, so no refreshed index is saved and a leftover lock does not stop it. Each finding's Display is its one form, printed by check as an error or a warning, and returned by the status tool as a history item of its kind and that message, which trurlic status prints as a history: line.
alternatives: Run git status plainly: rejected because it saves a refreshed index when it can lock it, so a read would write to the repository
Make them validation issues: rejected because validate runs on every read and every write without git, and the history is not the graph

choice: check prints every issue and finding by severity, errors, then warnings, then notes; it fails counting the errors, a stale or ambiguous anchor among them, and is consistent only when silent
reason: check is the gate before a commit, so what fails it must come first and be counted: the graph's and its placement's issues, a quality pattern that does not compile, a history finding that refuses writes, and a stale, malformed or ambiguous anchor are errors; a file not in canonical form, a history the next write mends, an unverified or weak anchor, and another worktree git could not say enough of, where a stale anchor may be pending, are warnings; a pending or a planned anchor is a note, which needs no action now. check exits 1 on an error and 0 otherwise. Each anchor kind's severity is stated once, by lint for check's own finding type, and Error::CheckFailed counts the errors. A graph is called consistent only when nothing was printed, so a note is never hidden behind that line.
alternatives: Fail on a planned or pending anchor too: rejected because a proposed decision may anchor code not written yet, and a branch may hold code a merge brings
An ambiguous anchor as a warning: rejected because an anchor that names several definitions has no span to verify, so it guards nothing until it is spelled to name one
Print the findings in the order found: rejected because an error would hide among the warnings of a large graph

choice: check refuses a placement git contradicts and a second graph directory beside a shared one, each a typed issue naming the paths
reason: The placement decides how the graph is found and versioned, so a placement git contradicts breaks one of the two without a word: a tracked graph git does not version is missing from every linked worktree, a shared graph git tracks is committed with the code and checked out as a second copy, and a linked worktree that carries its own .trurlic/ hides the shared graph from itself, since the walk finds its own first. check names each as an issue of its own kind (TrackedUnversioned, TrackedIgnored, SharedVersioned, SharedOffMain, SecondGraph) whose subject is the graph directory at fault and whose message names the files or the worktree and its branch, sorted as validation issues are, and fails. Only check asks git; status and the reads do not, so they cost no process.
alternatives: Warn and pass: rejected because the owner's design has check refuse it
Check the placement on every command: rejected because every read would spawn git

choice: check fails on an error, never on a non-canonical file, which it warns about; trurlic fmt rewrites exactly those files in one journaled commit
reason: A hand edit is a legal write and its layout is a matter of form, not of the graph: failing check on it would fail every hand edit until fmt ran. The load lists each file whose bytes differ from its canonical form (ProjectState::non_canonical); check prints each as a warning naming trurlic fmt and exits 1 only on an error, and status counts them. Writer::format prepares the canonical text of each listed file and commits them in one commit_batch, so a crash lands all or none; a file already canonical is not touched, so its mtime and its diff stay, and a second run writes nothing. fmt runs over a graph with issues too: the text it writes reads back as the value loaded, so it adds none.
alternatives: Fail check on a non-canonical file: rejected because a hand edit, now the only write, would fail check until fmt ran
Rewrite every file on fmt: rejected because rewriting canonical files churns mtimes and open editor buffers for no change
Format on every load or write: rejected because a read would write, and a write would touch files it is not about

choice: Claude Code install delegates to the claude CLI subprocess instead of writing Claude Code's config
reason: trurlic install --ide claude-code runs 'claude mcp remove trurlic -s user' (best effort, stdin, stdout and stderr closed so a prompting subprocess cannot hang it), then 'claude mcp add trurlic -s user -- <binary> serve', and fails with the add's trimmed stderr when it exits unsuccessfully. Claude Code reads and writes its own config, so trurlic never parses, merges or rewrites a file whose format and validation rules Claude Code does not publish as a contract, and the owner's other keys and servers stay Claude Code's to keep. The binary is resolved to its canonical path and passed as an argv element, never through a shell. The claude CLI is looked up on PATH, then at /usr/local/bin/claude and ~/.claude/bin/claude. --dry-run prints the add command without looking for the claude CLI, so a user without it can still run the command by hand. The cost is a runtime dependency on the claude binary for a real install.
alternatives: Write Claude Code's config file directly (read, merge the trurlic entry by key, write atomically): rejected, the file's format and validation rules are not a stable public contract, so trurlic would duplicate format knowledge that breaks on a Claude Code update

Print the configuration and leave registration to the user: rejected, Claude Code is the primary MCP client and one command is the setup step the quick start relies on; --dry-run already gives the manual path

choice: CLAUDE.md and .trurlic/ are tracked; .claude/ and TASKS.md are local files, never committed
reason: CLAUDE.md is the entry point every coding agent in this repo reads, and .trurlic/ (minus .trurlic/.state/) is the project's own decision graph, so both are versioned and reviewed with the code. The owner keeps .claude/ (skills, settings, worktrees) and TASKS.md as local working files: .gitignore ignores .claude, TASKS.md is excluded locally, and if either ever lands in the repo it is removed from tracking.
alternatives: Track .claude/skills/ next to CLAUDE.md so skill changes are reviewed: rejected by the owner, the skills are local working files
Keep .trurlic/ ignored: rejected, the graph agents read would be unreviewed, unversioned and invisible to anyone cloning the repo

choice: code takes a file's kind and bytes, or the gathered facts of a tree, and returns values; sources walks, reads and caches, and is the one way a command reaches the index
reason: The index is pure so its rules are tested on bytes alone, and the same function serves a file on disk now and a blob at a git revision when a diff review compares two revisions. A file's index is a function of its kind and bytes, which is what lets a cache key it by content. What depends on other files, the files that are test code whole, is a second pure step over the indexes of the tree. The shell gathers those facts once per call: it walks the code root, reads each file within a bound, reads and fills the cache through the Store, and hands code a map of entries. Its entry point is sources::resolve_anchors, which code never imports. A test holds code to an allow list closed by construction, reading every token of its non-test code, a raw identifier as its name. It skips test code by an exact rule of its own: an item #[test] or #[cfg(test)] marks or whose body opens with #![cfg(test)], a file only such a mod declares. A path may reach only the pure modules of std, core and alloc and its Arc and once cells, the crate's code and the store's Anchor, and the crates tree_sitter, its grammars, blake3 and toml. Refused: the hashed collections' names anywhere, a glob or alias of a root or of any std path, extern crate, macro_rules, an attribute naming a path, a mod a macro's tokens declare, and the prelude macros that read files or the environment or print. include_str! of a relative path inside src/code is admitted. Still unseen: a macro the crate root defines before mod code (none), what an allowed crate does with a handle code cannot name, what a caller hands in, and the runtime's own messages to stderr.
alternatives: Let code read files as it resolves: rejected because the rules could then be tested only on a tree on disk, and a git blob would need a second path
Put the shell in commands: rejected because the status tool in mcp needs it too, and mcp does not import commands
A clippy configuration that denies std's I/O items: rejected because a deny list of std is never complete, and thirteen items and a #[path] module passed it
Compile code as a no_std crate in a test: rejected because every file would need alloc paths and code uses tree-sitter's std API

choice: Context assembly lives in mcp::context; tools.rs only parses arguments and dispatches
reason: get_context assembles a component's context: its decisions, the project-wide rules, the decisions of connected components and of what its decisions depend on, decision health (how many decisions, how many proposed, how many anchor only files that are gone) and an authoritative brief that marks each proposed decision; get_decisions_for_file is built beside it. Keeping the assembly in mcp::context leaves tools.rs a thin layer of tool definitions, argument parsing and dispatch, so a tool's schema and its result builder change independently and the builders are tested against a ProjectState without JSON-RPC. The graph walks they use (decisions_of, related_decisions, dependencies, decisions_in) live in store::query, so the builders hold no traversal of their own.
alternatives: Inline context assembly in the tool dispatch functions: rejected because graph walks, brief generation and health reporting are enough to warrant their own module
Move context assembly into store: rejected because the brief is agent-facing prose and JSON, and store stays free of MCP concerns

choice: Forbid unsafe code project-wide via Cargo lint
reason: The crate has no need for unsafe: every dependency it calls is safe Rust. Cargo.toml sets [lints.rust] unsafe_code = "forbid", which makes any unsafe block a compile error in every target, and unlike "deny" no #[allow] or #[expect] can lift it at a site (E0453). tests/lints.rs seeds both an unsafe block and an #[expect(unsafe_code)] and requires each to be refused.
alternatives: Allow unsafe with clippy::allow annotations case by case: rejected because no use case requires it and the blanket deny is simpler to audit
Use #![forbid(unsafe_code)] in lib.rs: rejected because Cargo.toml [lints] is the canonical location and applies to the entire crate uniformly

choice: Deny unwrap, expect, panic, todo, unimplemented and dbg outside tests through Cargo lints
reason: A panic in production is a bug: a CLI command dies of it, and the MCP server answers the request -32603 instead of its result. Cargo.toml's [lints.clippy] denies unwrap_used, expect_used, panic, todo, unimplemented and dbg_macro in every target; clippy.toml's allow-unwrap-in-tests, allow-expect-in-tests and allow-panic-in-tests exempt #[test] bodies, #[cfg(test)] items and, from clippy 1.100, the integration test crates under tests/, helpers included, where a panic is the assertion. The bench is not a test crate, so it carries one crate-level #[expect] for its setup helpers. Clippy before 1.100 still flags the tests/ helpers; CI runs clippy only on the pinned toolchain, and the MSRV job runs cargo check, which does not run clippy lints. An exception elsewhere is #[expect(lint, reason)] at its site: allow_attributes and allow_attributes_without_reason are denied, so no #[allow] lands and an expectation fails once it stops applying. tests/lints.rs proves each lint refuses a seeded violation.
alternatives: Allow unwrap and expect everywhere and rely on code review: rejected because review is unreliable for this class of bug
Forbid unwrap and expect even in tests: rejected because a test panic is idiomatic Rust and unwrap in a test is clearer than propagating errors

choice: depends_on cycles are found as strongly connected components by an iterative Tarjan search and reported once each, by their sorted members
reason: A cycle is a set of decisions, so its identity is its members: the report is the same whatever node a search starts from, and the no-new-issues write rule (validate::introduced) can match it across validations. Tarjan finds every component in one pass over the decisions' depends_on sets.
