The search keeps its own stack of frames on the heap, so a dependency chain of any length runs in constant call-stack depth. A node that only depends into a cycle is not a member and is not reported. A one-node loop is a self-edge, which the self-edge check reports, so the search reports components of two or more members only. Visit state is a BTreeMap keyed by name, as the lint on hash collections requires, so roots are visited in name order; the cycles are sorted on return. The search, store::cycles::cycles, runs over any graph of names a successor function gives: ProjectState::depends_on_cycles runs it on the decisions, apply from the one decision an op gave new edges (Edit::new_cycle), against the cycles the batch began with read under the names the batch's renames and merges carried their members to (validate::carry_members), and the step to format 0.5 on the depends_on edges graph.toml held, with and without the constrains edges turned around.
alternatives: Recursive depth-first search with an on-stack set: rejected because an early return left the path marked and reported a false cycle, the report named a hash-ordered root, and a 50,000-link chain overflowed a 64 KiB stack
Kosaraju's algorithm: rejected because it makes two passes over the graph where Tarjan needs one, for the same components
One issue per decision on a cycle: rejected because a cycle of n decisions becomes n errors, and the members are not listed together

choice: Discovery runs git only at the top of a linked worktree or submodule where the walk found no graph, one git worktree list; a tree that holds its graph spawns no process
reason: serve finds the graph on every tool call, so discovery is on the per-call path. The walk makes two metadata calls per directory, for .trurlic and .git, and spawns nothing where it finds the graph: a tree with its own .trurlic, a symlinked clone, a directory inside a graph. Only the top of a linked worktree, whose .git is a file, can be served by a graph the walk does not see, and there the directory is the work tree's top, so one git worktree list names the main worktree and no rev-parse is needed. A submodule or a separate-git-dir repository has a .git file too and pays that one process for no graph. Discovery never runs git inside a graph directory, where the graph's own repository would answer; git::graph alone runs git there.
alternatives: Ask git on every call: rejected because the walk already answers for every tree but a linked worktree, and a process per tool call is the cost serve should not pay
Read the .git file and the commondir file directly: rejected because that reimplements git's discovery, its gitdir files, commondir and separate git directories
Cache the answer between calls: rejected because no process holds state between calls, and a cached answer would miss a new or moved graph

choice: Discovery walks up within the cwd's work tree: a .trurlic, a symlink followed; at a linked worktree's top the main worktree's graph if shared; a .git directory ends it
reason: A graph serves the work tree it sits in. Under tracked every worktree checks out its own graph, so a linked worktree nested in the main one, on a branch without a graph, must find none instead of reading and writing the main checkout's; under shared the main worktree's graph serves each linked worktree, read for the calling tree. So the walk takes the .trurlic of each directory, a symlink followed for a clone or a copy outside the repository, and stops at the first .git. A file is the top of a linked worktree or a submodule, where git worktree list, read from the common dir, names the main worktree, whose graph serves when it states shared. A directory is the top of a main worktree or of a repository cloned inside another project's tree, and a graph above it is not that repository's, so the walk ends with none. A tree with no git is walked to the root. A graph directory is passed through to its tree, since its own .git is its history.
alternatives: Walk to the root and ask git last, as before: rejected because a nested linked worktree then reads and writes the main checkout's graph, and its code root is the main tree
Stop only at a .git file: rejected because a repository cloned inside a project would read that project's graph as its own
Ask git for the top first, then walk: rejected because every call would spawn git, and a symlinked clone or a graph outside any repository has no git answer

choice: Duplicate pairs come from an inverted index over every term, a page of probes by name at a time while their work, counted before each step, fits MAX_DUPLICATE_WORK
reason: The postings list, per term, the decisions that hold it in order, with the term's weight there. Each decision probed reads the postings of its terms, adds the products of the weights into a scratch row sized to the graph, and puts each decision it touched to the exact threshold test with that sum, their exact dot product. A pair that shares no term is never visited, and no pair allocates. A term most decisions hold, the usual case in prose, makes the pass visit and test nearly every pair, so its cost grows with the square of the decisions, and the work of every step is counted before it runs: the build by the bytes of the texts, a probe by the posting entries it reads and PAIR_WORK for each pair it may test. A call builds nothing when the texts alone pass the bound. Otherwise it probes the decisions from from on by name, the first whatever its work, while the build's work and theirs fit, and names the first it left out in next, as the patterns page. A pair is on the page of the later-named of its decisions the pass probes, so a walk lists each pair once. Under an origin either the whole pass, its pairs filtered, or the origin's decisions each against every other runs, whichever costs less. Tests hold the pairs to the exact test over every pair, a walk to every pair once, and the charge to hand-counted work.
alternatives: A dot product for every pair: rejected because it merges the term lists of pairs that share nothing, many times the work of the index on the seeded corpus

A prefix filter leaving each decision's commonest terms unindexed, with a Cauchy-Schwarz bound: it saved most of the pass on a graph sharing common terms, but was removed for its size, a second order, cursors and a bound on two comparisons; the paged charge bounds it now
Refuse the whole pass past the bound: rejected because a graph past it would list no pair at all, while pages list every pair in about its work over the bound calls
Locality-sensitive hashing: rejected because it can miss a pair, and the list must be the exact one
A cache under .state: rejected because a read would then depend on state beside the files

choice: Each historical format has a fixture graph as the trurlic of its time wrote it; a named test migrates it, runs check and pins the report and result in a golden file
reason: A migration step is only as true as the store it is tested on. The fixtures under tests/fixtures/formats for 0.1.0 to 0.4.0 were written by the binaries built from git for each format (the pre-release trurl for 0.1.0, v0.1.0, v0.2.0 and v0.3.2) through their CLI and MCP tools, so they hold connections, supersedes links, dependencies, constraints, patterns, tags, attribution, code refs and history as those versions wrote them. No release wrote 0.4.1, so its fixture is the 0.4.0 one taken through the 0.4.1 step, its hashes recomputed, and extended with what a 0.4.1 store can hold that no 0.3.x write made: a decision without attribution and with two history entries, code refs with a line, a ./ path, a path outside the root and the old symbol spellings, and tags on components. Each step has a unit test on the fixture of its from format, the step to 0.5 one per rule, editing the fixture's tables for the shapes a valid 0.4.1 graph cannot hold (a name that differs from its stem, an attribution 0.4.1 refused, an edge to no node, a cycle). format_<v>_migrates_and_passes_check migrates each fixture with the binary and the placement stated, runs check, checks the backup and the report in it, and compares the report and every migrated byte with tests/integration/golden/migrate_<v>.txt.
alternatives: Build old stores in the test by downgrading the version of a current one: rejected because the old tests did this, and such a store holds none of the shapes the steps exist for
Resurrect the 0.4 writer to produce the 0.4.1 fixture: rejected because it brings back deleted code for one file set that hand edits and the 0.4.1 step produce

choice: Each text field has one shape in store::text: a choice one line of 200 bytes, an alternative one line of 1,000, a tag one line of 128, an origin one line of 200, a description any prose
reason: One table of shapes in store::text serves validation, the bar and the apply spec, so no surface drifts. Alternatives and tags are elements of a list, each one statement or label, and a line break in one hides an element from a reader of the file; an origin becomes a commit trailer, where a line break forges another. A component's description may be blank or span lines: a migrated component has none, and a description is prose like a reason. An alternative of at most 1,000 bytes makes one record unable to pass the cap a load reads: a hundred of them, every byte escaped and kept twice in a revision's accepted text, are 400 KB, and the largest record with its accepted text is about 790 KB, which the limits test holds.
alternatives: Bound an alternative at the 50,000 bytes of a reason: rejected because a hundred of them make one record far larger than a load reads
Let a tag hold any text: rejected because an empty tag or one on two lines is written and shown as no label
origin: review findings of the stateless-server landing

choice: Each tool declares its arguments once, in Args::declare, walked for its inputSchema and for every call's parse; a key it does not read is refused
reason: A tool's schema and its parser came from two places, a hand-written JSON literal and hand parsing, and drifted: get_context's schema lists depth as an enum while its parser reads any other value as full, and no tool refused an unknown key. In mcp::spec, Args::declare reads each field through Fields::required or Fields::optional with a Kind; walked in schema mode it records each field (the value it builds from Default is dropped), walked over a call's arguments it parses them, so a field cannot be parsed without being in the schema. Every bounded kind holds its limit as a field (Text.max_bytes, List.max_items), so no declaration leaves one out; Choice is an enum, Object a nested Args, Union a tagged object with one variant per tag value, which apply's ops are. Only a required field's kind gives the Default the schema walk builds, so a union's items need none. A refusal is invalid_argument naming the field by path (ops[2].name): the first fault in declaration order, then the first undeclared key. Plain Rust, no new dependency. A table-driven test over a spec with every field kind refuses each malformed shape.
alternatives: Hand-written schema literal plus hand parsing, as the 0.3 tools have: rejected, the two drift and nothing refuses an unknown key
schemars derive with serde: rejected, a new dependency, and serde's deny_unknown_fields error names no path
Static schema data with getters by field name: rejected, a getter for a field the data does not declare compiles and fails only when called

choice: Each tool declares its result once, in Output::declare, walked for its outputSchema and for the JSON a call returns, which is structuredContent and the same JSON as text
reason: MCP clients read a result's structuredContent against the tool's outputSchema, and a schema written apart from the code that builds the result drifts as the 0.3 input schemas did. Output::declare reads each field through Shown::required or Shown::optional with a Show kind (Str, Count, Tag over a fixed list of names, Items, Nested) and an accessor; walked for the schema no accessor runs, walked over a value each accessor reads its field and the kind writes it, so a field cannot be written without being declared. ToolSpec<A, O> takes the result type, adds the truncated notice to its outputSchema, and the call returns structuredContent plus the same JSON as the text block. The tools that predate specs return text only until brief replaces them.
alternatives: serde Serialize on the result types and a hand-written schema: rejected because the two drift
schemars: rejected, a new dependency for what the spec module already walks

choice: Each edge lives in its source file: connects_to in a component, component and depends_on in a decision; A constrains B is written as B depends_on A
reason: With no index, an edge must live in a node file, and its source's file is the one place it has: a decision states which component it belongs to and what it depends on, a component what it connects to. constrains stated the dependency of depends_on from the other end, so it is folded into it: the decision held by a rule depends on that rule, and the edge sits in the file of the decision that relies on it. A new decision's edges are in its own new file, and an edge added to an existing set is one line of a sorted list, so two branches that add edges merge (tests/integration/git_merge.rs). An edge to no node is an issue check reports, not a load failure.
alternatives: Edges in an index file: rejected because every write touches it and branches conflict on it
An edge in the files of both endpoints: rejected because two copies can disagree, and adding an edge would touch a file the change is not about
Keep constrains as its own edge kind: rejected because it states depends_on from the other end, so every walk and the cycle check would handle two kinds for one relation

choice: Every write goes through a flushed journal in .state/txn.toml that names only the steps still to do, its file step and its history step, and lands once the journal is in place
reason: Renaming staged files one by one left the earlier renames on disk when a later one failed. commit_batch stages and flushes every file, under shared writes their blobs, then renames the journal (each staged file, its target and the BLAKE3 of its bytes, the files to remove, and under shared the history step: message, parent and blob ids) to .state/txn.toml and flushes .state/: the commit point. apply_journal renames, removes, flushes each touched directory, makes the history commit, deletes the journal and flushes .state/ before the writer returns and releases the lock. A journal is not replayed past what it still has to do. A history commit that fails once the files are in place narrows the journal, staged, renamed and flushed, to the history step alone, so a read that keeps the waiting commit never removes a file the owner re-created since; a journal whose deletion fails is replaced by one that names no step, which the next opener deletes and does nothing else. Replay skips a write whose staged file is gone and one whose target holds the staged bytes; a staged file with other bytes is BadJournal. After the commit point a failure is WritePending.
alternatives: Leave the deletion unflushed and make replay a no-op for a finished journal: rejected because a removal cannot tell a file never removed from one re-created since
Keep the whole journal when the history commit fails: rejected because every later read would run its removals again and delete a file re-created since
Rename in order with the last file as the only commit point, no journal: rejected because a failed rename left a graph that matched neither commit
A journal holding the new file contents: rejected because it doubles the bytes written per commit and still needs every target flushed
An undo log rolled back on recovery: rejected because a commit that failed after its journal would have to be undone by whoever opens next

choice: Every git invocation names its directory with -C and clears the variables that redirect git: repository parts, inherited -c config and pathspec magic
reason: trurlic runs inside a project's git hooks, where git exports GIT_DIR and GIT_INDEX_FILE for the repository running the hook, and a GIT_WORK_TREE or GIT_COMMON_DIR set by a caller would make git answer for another tree. The runner clears what names a repository or its parts (GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE, GIT_INDEX_FILE, GIT_COMMON_DIR, GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY, GIT_ALTERNATE_OBJECT_DIRECTORIES, GIT_QUARANTINE_PATH, GIT_NAMESPACE), the configuration a parent git -c or the environment passes down, which can set core.worktree among anything (GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS, GIT_CONFIG_COUNT), and what changes how a pathspec matches (GIT_LITERAL_PATHSPECS, GIT_GLOB_PATHSPECS, GIT_NOGLOB_PATHSPECS, GIT_ICASE_PATHSPECS). It keeps the user's and the system's configuration files and the variables that choose them, which say how the user runs git, and GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES, a user's bound on discovery that git never sets for a child; GIT_PREFIX, which git sets for an alias and reads nowhere, is left as it is. tests/integration/migrate.rs runs migrate with GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE, GIT_INDEX_FILE, GIT_COMMON_DIR and GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS pointing at another repository and finds the project's placement.
alternatives: Clear every GIT_ variable: rejected because it would drop the user's choice of configuration file and discovery bound, and tracing
Clear only GIT_DIR, GIT_INDEX_FILE and GIT_WORK_TREE: rejected because GIT_COMMON_DIR, the object directories and an inherited core.worktree redirect git as well
Run git with an empty environment: rejected because git needs PATH and HOME, and the user's configuration, such as safe.directory, would be lost

choice: Every list a tool response carries has a fixed order; std's HashMap and HashSet are refused by lint
reason: Each process seeds its hash collections afresh, so a list built by walking a HashMap or HashSet comes out in a different order in every server: two serve processes on one graph answered get_context with different bytes. Sorting at each output site was a convention a missed sort broke silently, so clippy.toml's disallowed-types refuses std::collections::HashMap and HashSet everywhere, membership sets included: every map and set is a BTreeMap or BTreeSet. ProjectState keys components and decisions by name in BTreeMaps and a decision's tags, anchors and depends_on are BTreeSets, so every query walks them in name order, and a list ordered on another key (get_decisions_for_file by component, then name) sorts stably from that order. tests/integration/determinism.rs requires every read tool, taken from tools/list, to answer with the same bytes in two serve processes, and tests/lints.rs requires the lint to refuse both types.
alternatives: Sort each response at the MCP boundary: rejected because list order in the nested payloads carries meaning (relevance, priority), so a generic sort would reorder lists ranked on purpose
Fix the hasher seed: rejected because output order would then follow hash values, which change with the hasher or the keys, and still not be an order a reader can predict

choice: repair_anchors with no repairs is filled before the write lock with every repair check shows, as a map the store applies where the op runs, leaving one the bar refuses or cannot judge
reason: The repairs check shows are what the op writes, so a reader can see them before running it. Reading them walks the code tree and runs the project's git, which under the exclusive lock would hold every other writer for as long as git takes, and would keep the index's cache from filling, since its write needs the lock free. So apply's Access::Write has a read step that runs with no lock held, loads the graph as a read does, gathers the findings with sources::checked_findings and compiles the bar; then the writer takes the lock. The tree can change in between: under the lock, sources::still_holding reads the files each repair names, with no git, and leaves each repair whose stale anchor resolves again or whose repair no longer does. What the read hands the write is keyed by anchor, since the graph can change too. The caller wrote none of these repairs, so none may refuse the batch: the store, under the lock and over the batch's caches, judges each repair on the anchor it brings and leaves one a refuse pattern matches or a pattern cannot judge, the rule its cause. An earlier op of the batch can so never turn one into a refusal. The result lists what was written and the stale anchors left with their causes, stated against the graph the write left under its lock, under the names there; as many as fit the budget, the rest counted, and trurlic check lists every one.
alternatives: Read the repairs under the writer's lock: rejected because a slow git or a large tree would hold every other writer past its lock timeout, and the index's cache would never fill
Hand the write the repairs as an explicit list: rejected because a list names what earlier ops may have renamed or removed, and is refused naming an argument the caller never wrote
Refuse the batch on a repair the bar refuses: rejected because the caller wrote no such repair, and one would keep every other repair from being written
Leave the stale anchors left out of the result: rejected because the reader then cannot tell repaired all from repaired some
Sift the repairs before the lock over a scan of their own: rejected because the write's caches, filled by the ops before, can still give up on a repair the sift passed

choice: Every read command tells of the issues of the graph it loads, status by listing them and query by a warning naming trurlic check; the store's load finishes an interrupted write
reason: status lists the issues of the graph it loads, counted and fitted to the result budget, and open_store in commands/mod.rs loads the graph for query and warns on stderr when it has issues, naming trurlic check, so the user always learns of a broken graph without being blocked: an issue is reported there, and only check fails on one. Recovery and the format check are not the commands' job: Store::load_state and Store::begin_write refuse a store in another format before reading anything else in it, and finish a commit an interrupted writer left, so a crash heals on the next command of any kind. The one exception is a migration stopped before its first rename: project.toml is still in the old format, so every command refuses the store and names trurlic migrate, which finishes the commit. serve checks nothing at start: each tool call loads through the store, so a store in another format, or one whose version does not parse, is refused per call as unsupported_format.
alternatives: Recover only on an explicit trurlic check: rejected because temp files and unfinished commits would linger after a crash until someone ran it
Fail every command on an issue: rejected because one dangling edge from a hand edit would block status and every read while the files are still readable

choice: Every tool result fits MAX_TOOL_RESULT_BYTES (24 KiB); a larger payload keeps its shape, cuts tails to one level and names each cut
reason: Claude Code warns above 10,000 tokens of tool output and moves a result above 25,000 tokens to a file the agent reads in part; on a seeded 600-decision graph 1033 of 2305 calls exceeded 24 KB, up to 1.07 MB. result::tool_result and result::tool_error wrap every result, so the cap lives there: truncate::fit_payload serializes into a buffer that stops at the budget and sends a payload that fits as it is; otherwise it cuts every array and string reachable from the root through objects to the highest common level budget::level finds, arrays by trailing items (kept or dropped whole) and strings at a character boundary, sizes counted in compact JSON bytes. A truncated array at the root names each cut by RFC 6901 pointer with omitted_items or omitted_bytes; a skeleton that alone exceeds the budget is sent as one whole-payload omission, the only case that measures the payload whole. A spec-built tool's result is structuredContent and the same JSON as text (result::structured_result): the text is cut first and parsed back, so a cut result is cut alike in both, and its outputSchema admits the truncated notice. A refusal is a payload like any other, {"error": {...}}, cut by fit_payload. Each unit, and each array item in it, is counted only until it passes the budget (no longer prefix can be kept, so one decision carrying megabytes of alternatives costs no more than the budget to measure), and a string keeps escaped-size checkpoints every 64 bytes, so a cut costs in proportion to the budget: cutting that graph's 738 KB get_context payload takes 78 us against 180 us to serialize it whole (release, measured). The level search lives in the budget module, which has no internal dependencies. A seeded property test checks fit, parse, prefix-only cuts and exact counts over 1000 payloads; tests/integration/budget.rs holds every tool to the cap through the binary.
alternatives: Cut the serialized text at the byte limit - rejected: the agent receives invalid JSON and cannot tell what is missing
Refuse an over-budget result with an error - rejected: the agent loses the answer entirely and has no argument to ask for less until the cursor contract lands
Give each list an equal share of the budget - rejected: short lists lose entries to empty shares while long ones waste none; a common level keeps short lists whole
Add max_bytes and cursor arguments now - rejected: that is the budget-and-cursor contract with deterministic ranking, a separate change; the cap is the guarantee it builds on

choice: Every write validates against the graph loaded under the exclusive lock, held with that lock in the Writer that begin_write returns
reason: A write that validated against a graph loaded before it took the file lock silently lost another process's commit in between. Store::begin_write takes the exclusive lock, checks the format, recovers, loads the graph under the lock and returns a Writer that owns both. Every graph write is a Writer method and the Writer's fields are private to the store, so no caller can pair the lock with a graph loaded before it, and a graph a read loaded can never be committed. Each commit leaves the writer's graph equal to the files. Today the one write method is Writer::format, behind trurlic fmt. A spec-built MCP tool whose Access is Write gets its Writer from SpecTool::call, one per call, so the dispatch and not the handler takes the lock. migrate takes the lock itself, since it plans on files the current types cannot read.
alternatives: Validate against a graph loaded earlier, then lock and commit: rejected because that is the lost update
Lock and reload inside each tool handler: rejected because every handler must remember to validate after the reload; one call site cannot forget
Skip the reload when file fingerprints match: rejected because the store keeps no fingerprints, and the unconditional load is correct and within budget

choice: trurlic fmt commits a shared graph's hand edits as hand edit even when no file needs a rewrite, so fmt then check leaves the history settled
reason: The way to land a hand edit is trurlic fmt, then trurlic check. Under shared, check warns about graph files the history does not hold, and without this rule a canonical hand edit would wait for the next write, which may come after a review has read the history. Writer::format runs Store::prepare_history alone when it has nothing to rewrite, so it makes the one hand edit commit a write would; with files to rewrite it is one hand edit commit and one fmt commit.
alternatives: Commit hand edits only at a write that changes files: rejected because the owner would have no command but git to settle the history
A trurlic commit command: rejected because the surface has none, and fmt is the command that settles the files

choice: A write adds no issue: the graph it commits has no issue, matched on kind and subject, that the graph it loaded lacked
reason:
Every write is validated against the whole graph before it touches disk: validate::introduced keeps the issues of the graph a write would commit, matched on (IssueKind, subject), that the graph loaded under the writer's lock does not have, and apply refuses the batch at the first of them (Edit::first_introduced), naming the op that last changed a node the issue concerns. Issues the graph already had, from a hand edit or an older release, do not block a write that leaves them as they are, so one invalid file never freezes the store. A message can change with a count while the issue stays the same, so messages are not the key. A batch is validated once, after its last op, not once per op; the graph it began with, which the batch's undo record gives back in place, is validated only when the new graph has an issue, so a write to a valid store validates once (about 4 ms at 2000 decisions).
Writer::format needs no check: it commits only canonical text that reads back as the value loaded, so the graph it commits is the one it loaded; tests/integration/invalid_graph.rs runs fmt over a graph with issues and finds them unchanged. This absorbs the rule of the deleted pattern on fail-closed validation.
alternatives: Validate only on read: rejected because a write would put an error on disk that every later reader inherits
Validate only the changed part of the graph: rejected because cycles and names shared across kinds need the whole graph, and a whole validation is cheap at these sizes
Refuse every write while the graph has any issue: rejected because one hand-edit mistake would block every write, the fix included

choice: git::graph is the one module that runs git inside a graph directory, in the graph's own repository; store::history is its one caller, and discovery never runs git there
reason: Inside a graph directory git answers for the graph's own repository, not the project's, so the boundary must be visible: git::graph::Repository is the only type whose calls name a graph directory as their repository, and it builds every such call through isolated(), so no call site can forget the isolation; git::graph::index holds what reaches its index and object store. store::history decides when (the history step, the findings) and calls it; that is the store's one arrow to git. Discovery and the placement facts ask git only of the directory that holds a graph, as before. The pure parts are unit-tested without git: status records (parse_status), object names (Oid), and the message and its trailers (CommitMessage::render).
alternatives: Put the graph repository's calls in store: rejected because spawning git and reading its output is the leaf's work, and the isolation belongs beside the runner it changes
Pass extra arguments to the project runner at each call site: rejected because any call site could then run git in the graph without the isolation

choice: TEST, TEST_F, TEST_P, TYPED_TEST and TYPED_TEST_P define a test Suite::Name; a C or C++ file under tests/ or test/, or named *_test.<ext> or *_unittest.<ext>, is test code
reason: A C++ test is a macro's call with a block, and a proof names the test it ran by its suite and its name, so googletest's five test macros define a test whose segments are their two arguments as written, and what the block holds is test code. The list is the one both C++ corpora measured use; Catch2 and doctest name their tests by strings beside a block the grammar keeps apart, which no measured project needs, and a project's own test macro (jemalloc's TEST_BEGIN) is not read as a test. A file's bytes do not say whether a test runner builds it, so the places are data in each language's row: the tests/ and test/ directories, and the *_test and *_unittest names over each extension of the language.
alternatives: Catch2's and doctest's TEST_CASE and SECTION too: rejected because no measured project uses them and their block needs an engine feature
Any macro call with a block as a test: rejected because a project's helper would become a test

choice: History commits are made with a fixed identity, --no-verify and commit.gpgsign=false, the variables that redirect git cleared, so a call from a git hook reaches only the graph's repository
reason: trurlic runs inside a project's git hooks, where git exports GIT_DIR and GIT_INDEX_FILE for the repository running the hook; a history commit made there must land in the graph's repository and in no other, with no hook of its own run, no signing prompt, and an author that names the program. Every call clears what git::CLEARED lists and names the graph's repository outright; the author and the committer are trurlic <trurlic@trurlic.invalid>, an address no mailbox can have. tests/integration/history.rs runs fmt with GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE, GIT_INDEX_FILE and GIT_COMMON_DIR set to another repository, whose history and index stay as they were.
alternatives: The user's identity: rejected because a person did not make the commit, and useConfigOnly or a missing user.email would refuse it
Run the user's hooks: rejected because a hook of the project's or the user's could refuse or rewrite a commit of trurlic's own repository

choice: init refuses tracked outside a work tree or under an ignore rule, shared in a work tree off the main worktree's top, and any graph a shared main graph serves
reason: init is where a placement is stated, so it refuses what check would refuse at once, before it writes anything. Tracked needs a git work tree (Error::NoWorkTree) whose ignore rules do not match .trurlic/project.toml (git check-ignore, Error::GraphIgnored). Shared in a work tree belongs at the top of the main worktree, where linked worktrees look (Error::SharedOffMain naming it); a bare repository's worktree has none (Error::SharedInBare). Outside any work tree shared needs no git, and is served to symlinked trees. In a linked worktree that the main worktree's shared graph already serves, a new graph of either placement would be a second graph and is refused (Error::SharedGraphServes). The next row's history repository is not made here.
alternatives: Leave every check to trurlic check: rejected because the graph would be made and refused in the next breath
Allow a shared graph in a subdirectory and map the linked worktree's path: rejected because one place to look keeps discovery to one stat

choice: Initialization gate: tools/list and tools/call require prior initialize handshake
reason: The server records the client's capabilities at initialize (peer::Client), and tools/list and tools/call answer -32600 until that record exists. initialize always answers and replaces the record; ping is allowed before it, as the MCP lifecycle has it; a notification (a message with no id) is never answered, per JSON-RPC 2.0 section 4.1. A refused initialize (no string protocolVersion) leaves the gate shut. This keeps a client from calling tools before it has negotiated the revision and the capabilities the server's own requests depend on.
alternatives: No initialization gate, tools served at once: rejected because MCP requires capability negotiation before tool use
Stateful session tracking with client identity: rejected because stdio is single-client by construction

choice: initialize answers the client's protocol revision when PROTOCOL_VERSIONS holds it (2025-11-25, 2025-06-18), else the latest
reason: The MCP lifecycle requires a server that supports the requested revision to answer with it, and otherwise to answer with another it supports, preferably its latest; the server answered 2025-11-25 to every client. PROTOCOL_VERSIONS lists, latest first, the revisions whose features the server's answers and requests use: 2025-06-18 introduced elicitation, outputSchema and structuredContent, and 2025-11-25 adds elicitation modes, where an empty elicitation capability still means form mode, so the server's messages are valid in both. An initialize without a string protocolVersion is refused with -32602.
alternatives: Answer one fixed revision: rejected, the specification requires echoing a supported requested revision
Also list 2025-03-26 and 2024-11-05: rejected, neither has elicitation or structured tool output, which accept and the 0.4.0 tools rely on

choice: install owns InstallError, which wraps Error; the error module depends on store alone
reason: Error carried InstallError through a transparent Error::Install variant, so the error module imported commands, the one arrow in the module graph that ran back up from the foundation, and every match on Error outside install needed an arm for failures only install has (a missing home directory, a binary path that is not UTF-8, a missing or failing claude CLI). install never opens a store, so none of its failures belong to the store's error. commands::install now returns Result<(), InstallError>, and InstallError::Io(#[from] Error) carries the I/O failures it shares with the crate (locating the binary, starting claude, writing to stdout), so those keep naming their file or call through Error::io and Error::system instead of a second set of path-carrying variants.
alternatives: Keep Error::Install: rejected, it makes error depend on commands and puts install-only failures into every match on the crate's error
Give InstallError its own Io and System variants instead of wrapping Error: rejected, it duplicates the path-carrying variants and their map_err adapters for three call sites
Fold the install failures into Error as plain variants: rejected, that is the same back-edge with more variants; Error describes the store and the commands that open it

choice: JSON-RPC 2.0 over newline-delimited stdio; every line gets at most one answer, and a line over 10 MiB is discarded whole
reason: MCP requires JSON-RPC 2.0, and stdio is its transport for a local server: one JSON object per line, blank lines skipped, every line written whole from a buffer. protocol::read_message sorts a line into a request, a notification or a response, or answers it: invalid JSON -32700; valid JSON that is no message (no jsonrpc 2.0, a method that is not a string, params that are not an object, a null or non-integer id, which MCP forbids, a batch array) -32600, with the line's id when it is a string or an integer and the line has a method. A line without a method would be a response, whose id is from the server's own id space, so its error carries null whatever else is wrong with it. A notification and a response are never answered. read_line holds at most MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES (10 MiB) of a line; past it the line is read to its newline and dropped, and answered once.
alternatives: HTTP transport: rejected because MCP stdio is the standard for local tool servers, and HTTP adds port management
Length-prefixed framing (a Content-Length header, as LSP has it): rejected because newline-delimited JSON is sufficient for single-line messages and is MCP's convention

choice: Leftover journals and temp files are cleared only under the exclusive lock: by every write, and by a read that finds one under the shared lock, which goes on past a history commit that waits
reason: Every command used to delete everything in .state/tmp/ on start, without the lock, so a status, check or serve started mid-commit deleted that commit's staged files and the commit failed at its first rename. Store::recover(&StoreLock) finishes a leftover journal, its history commit included, then removes every temp file, the scratch index of a write's blobs among them: under the exclusive lock no commit is in flight, so each one is a leftover. begin_write recovers under its lock, so every write starts clean and applies a journal before it loads. A read asks Store::has_leftovers under the shared lock, where no commit is in flight either, and only on a leftover takes the exclusive lock to recover, so a read of a clean store never waits for the exclusive lock and every read sees a whole commit. When the history commit of the journal cannot be made (git refuses it, as with an index lock left in the graph's repository), a read (PendingHistory::Keep) warns and loads, since the files are whole, and keeps the journal narrowed to the history step; a writer (PendingHistory::Fail) is refused with WritePending, so no write journals over one not finished. Both check the format first, so nothing in a store of another format is touched; migrate takes its lock, refuses a store it cannot migrate, then recovers.
alternatives: Clean .state/tmp/ on every command without the lock: rejected, deleted a concurrent commit's staged files (status during a commit made it fail)
Read commands wait for the lock to recover: rejected, a status would stall up to the 5 s lock timeout behind a writer, for a recovery the writer makes unnecessary
Recover only when a server starts: rejected, a crash would linger until a restart, and a write must apply a pending journal before it loads

choice: Two decisions are likely duplicates when the TF-IDF cosine of their choice and reason is at least 1/2: lowercased [a-z][a-z_]+ terms less 35 stop words, smoothed idf
reason: The rule is a plain TF-IDF cosine that a few lines of any scripting language recompute, so a reader can check every pair listed: the text is the choice, a space and the reason, lowercased; a term is each run of the regular expression [a-z][a-z_]+, ASCII letters only, that is not one of 35 stop words; a weight is the term's count times ln((1 + n) / (1 + df)) + 1 over the graph's n decisions; the cosine of two weight vectors at 1/2 or more, compared with >=, marks a pair. A test pins the scores of a fixture to the same rule in double precision. The threshold is a named constant, not a [quality] key, since no project needs another. A high score selects a pair to read and does not prove one rule twice, so it warns and never refuses.
alternatives: A threshold in [quality]: rejected because no project sets another, and a key nobody uses is surface to keep
Jaccard similarity of word sets: rejected because it weighs a word every decision holds like a rare one, so shared filler makes pairs
Refuse a write that duplicates a decision: rejected because a score above the threshold selects a pair to read; it can be two rules on one subject

choice: lint is a top-level module of findings no rule refuses, pure over ProjectState: it reads no file, no clock and no git, and a shell hands it any other fact
reason: A finding such as a likely duplicate selects something to read; it is not a rule of the write, so it does not belong in store, whose rules refuse a batch and which imports nothing above it. status and apply both report findings, likely duplicates, quality findings and anchor findings, so the findings sit in one module both surfaces call, below mcp. Pure functions over the loaded graph keep every finding a function of the files on disk and testable on a built ProjectState without a store or a server. A test holds lint to the code index's purity check with an allow list of its own: the pure modules of std, the crate's lint and code, the store's value types lint reads, and rayon's prelude of parallel iterators. It names no path type: a worktree's path reaches lint as text. The prelude's fold can see how the pool splits its work, so tests at one thread and eight hold each pass's result the same. Any other path, to a file, a clock, the environment, git or the console, fails it.
alternatives: Findings in store beside validation: rejected because a finding refuses nothing, and store would grow a second kind of check that no write obeys
Findings computed inside the status and apply handlers in mcp: rejected because both need the same pass, and mcp code is tested through a server or a spec

choice: The MCP server delegates every disk write to the store's Writer and never touches a file under .trurlic/
reason: A write tool runs on a Writer the dispatch begins for the call: SpecTool::call hands a spec-built tool whose Access is Write the Writer of Store::begin_write, which holds the exclusive lock and the graph loaded under it, validates, commits through the journal and keeps its graph equal to disk. apply is the one write tool: its handler turns the parsed arguments into a store::Batch and calls Writer::apply, which holds every rule; status, get_context and get_decisions_for_file are reads on Store::load_state. The MCP module parses arguments and builds the JSON result but never opens a file under .trurlic/, so the store stays the single authority for disk mutations and no tool bypasses its atomic write guarantees.
alternatives: The MCP module writes TOML files directly: rejected because it would bypass the atomic writes, the file lock and validation in the store
A separate write layer between MCP and the store: rejected because the Writer already is the right abstraction

choice: A type literal's members are fields and methods of the type alias it is the value of, and an object literal's methods are methods only of a top-level const or a default export
reason: A type literal is anonymous wherever it stands but as a type alias's value, where type P = { x: number } is how many projects write what an interface states, so its members are the alias's fields and methods. An object literal is a value anywhere: one a call takes or a function returns is no part of a module's names. One a const binds at a module's or a namespace's top, or a module exports as its default, is an API a reader names as api::get, so its methods and the arrow functions and function expressions its keys hold are methods of that name. The patterns root at the program, the namespace body and the export, so an object a const binds inside a function, or inside another binding's value, defines nothing, however the definitions around it nest.
alternatives: Members of every type literal: rejected because a literal in a parameter's type is no name a reader looks up
Methods of every object literal: rejected because an object a call takes defines nothing a reader names
Methods of an object any const binds: rejected because a local's object is no part of the module

choice: migrate keeps the report in the backup directory beside .trurlic/, both flushed before the commit, and a backup never lands in an earlier one
reason: The patterns and the tags a migration takes out of the graph exist nowhere else afterwards, so the report must outlive the terminal. migrate copies the store, but for .state/ and a graph repository's .git/, into a new .trurlic-backup-<UTC time> directory beside .trurlic/, writes the report it prints into migration-report.txt there with create_new, and flushes every file and directory before the commit; a power loss after the commit can then not take the only record with it. The copy flushes in parallel, since each flush waits on the disk. The directory is created with create_dir, and a taken name gets -2, -3 and on, so a second migration in the same second, after an interrupted one, never merges into or deletes an earlier backup. A failure before the commit point removes the new backup; a WritePending keeps it, since the write lands. The backup stays outside the graph's own repository under shared: that history holds only files the current format reads, which a reader of it parses, and the migration's commit there (the repository's first when the migration makes it) already shows every change; the backup is removed with rm -r, touching neither history. The dry run writes nothing.
alternatives: Print the report only: rejected because what the graph loses would live in scrollback
Write the report into .trurlic/: rejected because the store would hold a file that is no node, versioned with the graph under tracked placement

Commit the old files to the graph's repository before the migration instead of a backup: rejected because its history would hold a format no reader of it parses, and a tracked graph has no such repository
A report file beside the backup directory: rejected because the two would be moved or deleted apart

choice: migrate writes placement tracked when git tracks every file of .trurlic/, shared when none; a mix or no work tree is refused, and --placement states it
reason: 0.4.1 stores hold no placement and 0.5 requires one, and git already knows the answer: a graph the project's git tracks is tracked, one it keeps out is shared. migrate runs git ls-files in the directory that holds .trurlic/, never inside it, where a graph kept in a repository of its own would answer for that one. The store compares the listing with the files it read: all of them tracked is tracked, none is shared. A mix, such as a new decision not yet added, and a directory git cannot read as a work tree (no repository, git missing, a failed command with its stderr) are Error::PlacementUnknown, which names the files on the smaller side or git's error and says to run trurlic migrate --placement tracked or --placement shared; nothing is written. A stated placement is written as given and git is not run. The report says which placement was written and how it was told. The command gathers the git fact and the store takes it as data, PlacementSource, so the store spawns no process; a store with nothing to migrate never looks at it, so a missing git does not fail an up-to-date store.
alternatives: Default to tracked when git cannot tell: rejected because a guess would decide how the graph is versioned
Ask git which placement inside .trurlic/: rejected because a graph that is its own repository would answer for itself
Run git from the store: rejected because the store would spawn processes where the command can hand it the answer

choice: migrate walks an ordered registry of steps, one per format change from 0.1.0 on, that must chain to the current format, and reports what each step drops and decides
reason: The old migrate round-tripped every file through the current types, so a field the current format lacked vanished without a word, and a 0.1.0 component's connects_to list was lost. Each Step names its from and to versions and the change, and records what it drops as a Loss with the file, the dotted field and the TOML text of the value, and what else the owner must be able to read after the fact as a Fact: the placement and how it was told, a constrains edge written as depends_on, an anchor respelled or kept as written, a history count, a pattern with its edges and tags, a component's tags, a name field that differed from its stem. Facts are sorted per step, so each kind is one section of the report. A store migrates only along a chain: the steps from its version, each starting where the last ended, up to FORMAT_VERSION. A version no step names, or one from which no unbroken chain reaches the current format, is Error::NoMigration naming both versions, refused before anything in the store is touched, so a binary whose registry stops short never half-migrates a store. The walk stamps each step's to version after it, and the report lists the steps in order, so the output is deterministic. A new format appends one step and raises FORMAT_VERSION; one test holds the chain unbroken from 0.1.0 and another requires its last step to reach the current format.
alternatives: Round-trip through the current types, as before: rejected because it drops unknown fields and old edges silently
One hand-written function per pair of formats: rejected because it needs n squared paths where a chain of steps covers every start
Run the steps there are and stamp the last version reached: rejected because the store would state a format this binary does not read, and every command would then refuse it

choice: Module visibility: pub(crate) default, only cli and store are pub
reason: Enforced in lib.rs: pub mod cli and pub mod store are the only public modules. All others (budget, commands, console, error, git, mcp) are pub(crate). This keeps the library surface minimal and internal module boundaries enforced: external consumers can only reach the CLI entry point and the store API. One gated exception: with the `bench` feature, which only the bench target requires and no release build enables, lib.rs adds `pub mod bench` re-exporting mcp::Server, and store adds `pub mod corpus`, so benches/ can drive the server in process.
alternatives: Make all modules pub for maximum flexibility: rejected because it exposes internal implementation details and makes breaking changes harder to track
Make everything private and only expose a facade module: rejected because cli and store have legitimate external consumers (the binary and potential library users)

choice: No load cache: load_state parses every node file on each load until a bench shows the parse is the bottleneck
reason: The owner decided a load cache is built only if the benches show it is needed, and that it would be JSON unless a binary serializer is approved. No process keeps the graph between calls, so every tool call pays one load, and benches/corpus.rs measures load_state from disk, shared lock included, on the seeded corpus: about 1.9 ms at 50 decisions, 4.7 ms at 600 and 16 ms at 2000 (WSL2 ext4, warm page cache, criterion medians), against a budget of 50 ms at 2000. A cache would add a second representation to keep coherent with the node files, the opposite of node files being the only truth, and would bring back the state between calls that the server dropped. The bench runs locally with criterion (`make bench`), which compares each run with the previous one on the same machine; there is no CI bench job, so a change to the load path is benched before and after it, and that run is what shows a regression that changes this answer.
alternatives: JSON snapshot of the parsed graph keyed by node hashes: saves TOML parsing but needs invalidation against every node file and a fallback path, for a load that is already well under budget
Binary serializer cache: same coherence cost plus a dependency the owner has not approved

choice: No map: the map server, its web UI and its dependencies are deleted; the owner reads the graph through the agent, the files and status
reason: Users work with Trurlic through their coding agent over MCP, and the owner reads the graph the same way: by asking the agent (get_context, get_decisions_for_file), by reading the TOML node files under .trurlic/, and with trurlic status. The map was a third write surface beside MCP and the CLI: its REST API, WebSocket push and second watcher had to keep every store contract (lock order, reload before write, text rules) in step, and it carried an async runtime, an HTTP stack, an embedded TypeScript web UI and a Node.js toolchain through build, CI and release for a view the owner does not use. Deleting it dropped tokio, axum, tower-http, rust-embed, opener and rand and every Node.js step, left the whole binary synchronous, and made a Rust toolchain the only build requirement.
alternatives: Keep the map and maintain it: rejected, it keeps a third write surface whose store contracts must stay in step with MCP and the CLI, and an async runtime, an HTTP stack and a Node.js toolchain in every build, for a view the owner does not use
Keep a read-only map without REST writes: rejected, it still needs the HTTP server, WebSocket push, the web UI and its Node.js build, while the agent and the node files already answer every read

choice: No new errors matches an issue the graph began with under the names the batch's renames and merges gave its nodes, so a node's issues move with it and a new one is still refused
reason: An issue's subject holds the names of its nodes, so renaming or merging a decision with a dangling depends_on or a short reason changed the subject, and the issue it always had counted as new: no batch could rename or merge such a decision. Edit::carry records each node of the starting graph a rename or a merge carried to another name, twice renamed included, and validate::introduced rewrites the subjects of the starting issues through that map before it compares. The map follows the node, not the name: a removal ends a starting node's identity (Edit::end), and a node the batch makes under a name a starting node left is another node, which carries none of its issues. The target of a missing edge names no node of the edge's kind, so it is kept as written. A cycle's members are read through validate::carry_members, sorted and each once, the one reading the op's cycle rule uses too. The rule itself is unchanged: a batch that adds a real issue under cover of a rename, such as a self-edge the new name closes, is refused naming its op.
alternatives: Compare issues by kind alone for renamed nodes: rejected because a rename could then hide a new issue of an old kind
Exempt renames and merges from the comparison: rejected because the rule would no longer hold for every write
origin: review findings of the stateless-server landing

choice: No process holds graph state between calls; every read loads under the shared lock and first finishes a commit an interrupted writer left
reason: What a call returns is a function of the files on disk. The MCP server kept the graph in an Arc<RwLock<ProjectState>> that a notify watcher reloaded 100 ms after a change, so a call inside that window answered from the graph before a hand edit, a git checkout or another process's commit, and keeping it coherent took a commit counter, an overtaking rule between the watcher and the server's own writes, and a lock order between the state lock and the file lock. The server now holds only the directory it was started in and finds the store from it on every call: a read tool loads with Store::load_state and a write tool through a Writer, so the next call after any change sees it. A read takes the shared lock, so it waits for a commit in flight; a journal or a temp file seen under that lock was left by a writer that stopped, so the read takes the exclusive lock and finishes the commit before it loads. No read sees half of a commit. The load is on every call's path: about 16 ms at 2000 seeded decisions in make bench, against a budget of 50 ms.
alternatives: Keep the graph in the server and reload it from a file watcher: rejected, a call inside the reload window answers from the graph before the change, and coherence needs a counter, an overtaking rule and a second lock order
Cache the parsed graph keyed by file fingerprints: rejected, a second representation to keep coherent with the node files, for a load well under its 50 ms budget
Read without a lock: rejected, a read during a commit can see some of its renames and not the rest

choice: apply's history commit carries no Session: trailer: neither an MCP request over stdio nor a command names the agent's session; the hook phase is its first source
reason: MCP's initialize carries clientInfo, which names the client program and its version, and tools/call carries _meta, whose only defined key is progressToken; the session id of the Streamable HTTP transport does not exist over stdio. A client's own _meta key would be a protocol field no specification defines, and a session the server minted per process would match nothing a hook records. So Batch::session is None on both surfaces, and the trailer appears when the hooks supply the agent's session id.
alternatives: A session argument of apply: rejected because the surface lists none and an agent cannot know its own session id
The server process as the session: rejected because it matches no session a hook or a transcript names

choice: No workflow engine: advance, get_step_prompt, steps, modes and concern tracking are deleted; what is open for a change will come from a diff review of the graph and the code
reason: In real use the engine did not steer. Nearly every advance loop reached ready within a call or two, the next action the server named (get_step_prompt) was not followed, interactive mode was never used, and the step evidence agents passed was mostly "done" or "none". The decisions that do constrain code already reach the agent through get_context and get_decisions_for_file; the engine added a second path of seven task types, gated steps, mode-specific prompts, ten keyword-matched concern areas and a 90-day staleness clock in front of them, about ten thousand lines with its tests, two of fifteen tools and fields on four tool results (concern_coverage, coverage_impact, pattern_opportunity) that pointed agents at it. What is actually open for a change (the decisions it touches, the choices it makes that no decision covers) is a property of the diff, not of a step sequence computed from the graph alone, so a later diff-review tool will compute it from the graph and the code. Until then an agent reads the component's decisions with get_context and a file's with get_decisions_for_file, implements within them, writes a choice no decision covers as a decision file, and runs trurlic fmt and trurlic check before committing. The deletion is a surface break with no compatibility shim; nothing on disk changes.
alternatives: Keep the engine and enforce it (refuse get_context or writes until advance reports ready): rejected, a gate an agent clears with 'done' as evidence adds calls without adding review

Keep only concern coverage in get_context and the removal reports: rejected, keyword matching against ten fixed areas reports gaps nobody acted on and says nothing about what a given change leaves open
Keep advance as a thin alias that returns get_context: rejected, a second name for one tool, and the one user is owed no backward compatibility
Build the diff-review tool in the same change: rejected, it is a design of its own; deleting first means it starts from the graph and the code rather than from steps

choice: Store::prepare_write refuses canonical text over MAX_NODE_FILE_BYTES: apply names the op as file_too_large, fmt and migrate fail with CanonicalTooLarge, and nothing is written
reason: A file over the cap is refused by every load, so a write that stages one leaves a graph no command can read, and apply remove cannot repair it. Every write of a graph file passes prepare_write, so the check lives there once: lists grown op by op through add_* or a merge's union, and a hand edit whose literal strings of backslashes double when fmt escapes them, are both caught before anything touches disk. apply maps the error to the refusal file_too_large, naming the op that last changed the file, its size and the cap; fmt and migrate report the typed error naming the file. A legal file whose canonical form would pass the cap still loads, stays listed as not canonical, and fmt says why it is not rewritten.
alternatives: Bound every stored list: rejected because the cap is on bytes, and a list bound would still let text pass it
Check in apply alone: rejected because fmt and migrate write through the same function and can stage an oversize file too
origin: review findings of the stateless-server landing

choice: The graph is project.toml and the node files alone: no graph.toml index and no per-node hash, so a hand edit needs no rebuild and no re-hash
reason: graph.toml held the edges and a BLAKE3 hash per node, a second copy of what the node files say: every write rewrote it, two branches that each touched one node conflicted on it, a hand edit left it stale until a re-hash, and a lost one took with it the edges no node file held. With every edge in its source file and nothing derived on disk, a load reads the node files and nothing else, a hand edit is a legal write that the next load validates, and version control, not a stored hash, records what changed. A load ignores any other file under .trurlic/, so a leftover graph.toml is inert; the migration removes it.
alternatives: Keep graph.toml as a cache rebuilt from the node files: rejected because a second representation conflicts across branches and must be kept coherent with every hand edit
Keep per-node hashes for tamper detection: rejected because every hand edit would need a re-hash, and under tracked placement git already records every change

choice: Node files carry no history: a decision file holds its current text, and version control holds the revisions
reason: A history list in each decision grew the file with every revision, conflicted when two branches revised one decision, and duplicated what version control keeps; the store carried a cap and migration code for it. Under tracked placement the project's git holds every revision of every node file with its author and date. The one earlier state the format needs, the text the owner accepted while a revision is proposed, is accepted_text.
alternatives: Keep the history field: rejected because it grows every file and conflicts on merge, for what git keeps
A history file beside each decision: rejected because it is a second file per node to keep in step for the same record

choice: Every graph file has one canonical form: keys in a fixed order, sets sorted one per line with a trailing comma, empty ones left out, multi-line text as triple-quoted strings
reason: Two writers that lay one value out differently make diffs churn and merges conflict, so every write emits one form. A set (tags, edges, anchors) is sorted, one element per line with a trailing comma, so two branches that add elements at different places of one list touch different lines and git merges them with its own driver; an empty set or list is left out, so a file holds only what it says; a text with a line break is a triple-quoted string, so a reason reads as its lines in a diff. Hand edits are legal and need not be canonical: a load notes each file whose bytes differ, check warns about it and trurlic fmt rewrites it. tests/integration/git_merge.rs merges two branches of a tracked graph in a real repository and requires check to pass.
alternatives: Accept any layout: rejected because each writer and each hand edit would leave its own, and a one-line list conflicts on every addition
A git merge driver for node files: rejected because sorted one-per-line sets already merge with git's own, and a driver must be installed in every clone

choice: Parallel loading via rayon: the two node kinds read concurrently, each file read once, bounded, parsed and checked for canonical form
reason: Store::read_graph reads the component and the decision directories at once with rayon::join, since each kind's directory listing and its slowest file are serial steps, and read_nodes reads and parses the files of one kind on rayon's pool. Each file is read once by read_node_bytes, capped at MAX_NODE_FILE_BYTES, and the same bytes are parsed as the node's type and compared with its canonical form, so a load makes one read per file and allocates nothing for the comparison. Results come back in name order, and when several files fail the error names the first by name, whichever thread met it first, so a load fails the same way on every run. make bench times load_state at 50, 600 and 2000 seeded decisions.
alternatives: Sequential file loading: rejected because each file's open and read adds up serially, which a cold cache makes dominant
Memory-mapped files: rejected because it adds complexity for small files, and a bounded read already caps what one file costs
Incremental loading of changed files only: rejected because it needs a persistent record of file state between calls, which the store does not keep

choice: Every path a commit writes or removes passes verify_path, which refuses a parent-directory component and a path outside the store root
reason: All store paths are derived from the store root, so the check should never fire in correct code; it guards against a programming error that would write or delete a file outside .trurlic/. prepare_write checks each target and commit_batch every write and removal before anything is staged, and replay refuses a journal that names a path outside the store (Error::BadJournal). The check rejects .. components before the prefix test, since starts_with on a path that is not canonical does not stop /root/../etc. Control characters cannot corrupt a node file: the canonical form escapes every control character but tab, and a line break outside a multi-line string.
alternatives: Canonicalize paths before comparison: rejected because canonicalization follows symlinks, which could resolve to unexpected places; refusing components is predictable
No path check, trusting internal callers: rejected because one bug in path construction could delete arbitrary files, and the check is cheap

choice: Patterns are deleted as a node kind, with their member_of and applies_to edges; a rule a pattern stated is a decision
reason: A pattern grouped decisions under a named synthesis and applied it to components, but a brief already carries the decisions themselves, agents rarely recorded one, and the pattern edges were the main source of the deletion rules (a pattern kept at two members, a removal that shrank one). A rule a pattern states is a decision like any other, project-wide when it applies everywhere; the migration reports every pattern with its description and edges so the owner can record such a decision. Each of this repository's three patterns stated a rule decisions already hold: the limits in store::limits, validation before a write, and the no-panic lints with the one error enum.
alternatives: Keep patterns as a node kind: rejected because their edges carried most of the deletion rules for little a brief used
Turn each pattern into a tag: rejected because a tag states no rule

choice: ProjectState holds the node files by name and nothing derived from them; queries walk its BTreeMaps, with no adjacency index and no Arc sharing
reason: The graph lives for one call: every call loads it, answers and drops it. InMemoryGraph built forward and reverse adjacency maps of interned names on every load, and ProjectState wrapped each node in an Arc to share it with that graph; with the edges in the node files and a brief touching one component and its neighbours, a walk of the maps answers each query, so the index cost every load for lookups a scan does as well. The state holds the Project, BTreeMaps of Component and Decision by stem, and the files not in canonical form; store/query.rs walks them in name order, and make bench times the read tools with the load included.
alternatives: Keep InMemoryGraph with reverse adjacency: rejected because it is rebuilt on every load for lookups a scan of the maps answers
Arc-wrap the nodes: rejected because nothing shares them once there is no second structure

choice: project.toml names its format in format_version, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH apart from the crate version; a version that does not parse is refused by every load and by migrate
reason: The key was trurlic_version, though the number is the format's, not the release's: format 0.4.0 was written by 0.3.x. The old check compared versions leniently, a part that was not a number counting as 0, so garbage passed for an older format and migrate rewrote the store as if it were one. FormatVersion::parse accepts only the exact text Display writes, and the error names the file and the text. The version is read under format_version, trurlic_version or trurl_version, newest first, so an old store is told to run trurlic migrate instead of failing on a missing key. The check has one home, store/version.rs, used by every read, every write and migrate: a newer format is refused naming both versions, an older one the registry names is told to run trurlic migrate, and one it does not name is Error::NoMigration.
alternatives: Keep the trurlic_version key - rejected: it reads as the release version, which the format has not followed since 0.3.x
Parse leniently and treat garbage as the oldest format - rejected: the old behavior, which migrated a store whose version was a typo

choice: [quality] in project.toml is typed with every key optional, absent meaning the built-in rules alone, refused at load when no write could meet it, and written canonical
reason: The table is part of the format the store reads, so it is read as a type that refuses an unknown key, a maximum of 0 and a reason_words min past its max, with the file named: a misspelled key that set no limit would pass unseen. An absent table and an absent key mean no limit beyond the built-in rules, so a 0.5.0 store reads as it is and fmt leaves it alone, with no migration. Words are counted one way: runs of text between Unicode whitespace. A pattern names its fields from a closed set (choice, reason, alternatives, tags, anchors as file::symbol, origin, the batch's, read once per batch) and a level, refuse or warn. The canonical form writes the limits, then each pattern as a [[quality.patterns]] table whose pattern is a literal string, so its backslashes read as written.
alternatives: A free table of rules read by name: rejected because a misspelled key would silently set no limit
A format bump with a migration: rejected because an absent table means the built-in rules, so every 0.5.0 store reads as it is

choice: A [quality] pattern is a regex compiled for the lazy DFA within stated bounds, once per call: by a write before its lock, by check, and by status only for its lint section asked for alone
reason: A project rule such as a whole word, or a sentence past 25 words, needs classes and counts that a substring cannot state. Classes and case folding are Unicode's, since a decision's text is in any script. load_state parses the table and compiles nothing. A write compiles every pattern once, before it takes the lock, and reuses the bar for every op, repairs included; check compiles them to report the one that fails; status compiles them only when its section argument is lint, since on every call the table, not the graph, would set the cost of a read agents call often. A short pattern can ask for a large automaton, so compiling is bounded by construction: MAX_QUALITY_PATTERNS, MAX_PATTERN_BYTES of text, parsed once for both directions; then, before translating, the code points its case-insensitive classes fold (MAX_PATTERN_FOLDED_CODE_POINTS, counted over the parsed pattern by regex-syntax), since folding is the one part of translation whose cost no other bound holds; then MAX_PATTERN_COMPILED_BYTES of NFA each way and start states within MAX_PATTERN_CACHE_BYTES. The worst legal table of 32 compiles in about 0.1 s of CPU, which bounds the compile of any call. One that fails is Error::QualityPattern naming project.toml, its index and why, with the remedy: the engine's message, a narrower class or a scoped (?i:...), the rewrite of a Unicode word boundary. check reports it, every write is refused, and status still answers, its lint section judging the limits alone.
alternatives: Literal substrings: rejected because a whole word or a sentence length needs a class and a count
ASCII classes: rejected because a word boundary would split a word at its first letter outside ASCII
Patterns in every status call: rejected because their cost follows the table and the text of every decision, so a legal table would make the most frequent read slow
Compile under the write lock: rejected because a table near its bounds would hold every other caller for its compile
Bound compiling by a deadline: rejected because the answer would depend on the machine, and folding has a count to bound

choice: Every [quality] pattern runs on regex-automata's lazy DFA alone, each direction's cache capped at 320 KiB and giving up instead of clearing; a Unicode word boundary is refused at compile
reason: A search on the lazy DFA costs time linear in the bytes it reads once the states it walks are built, and it builds them in a cache the caller owns. Capped at MAX_PATTERN_CACHE_BYTES per direction, with minimum_cache_clear_count(Some(0)), the cache gives up when full instead of clearing, so the engine itself holds one search to one fill of each cache. The cost of a call is then the bytes its patterns read and the states their caches build, and a call bounds both: bytes, and a total of cache growth (MAX_PATTERN_CACHE_TOTAL_BYTES). The cap is 320 KiB because a 48-word case-insensitive list grows about 215 KB in one direction over a whole graph of ordinary prose, and a 96-word list less than a full batch would need; a pattern past it gives up rather than starve the others, and the total, not the cap, bounds a write. The regex crate hides which engine it runs and falls back to the PikeVM, whose time per byte follows the pattern, after a give-up or for a Unicode word boundary over text outside ASCII. That boundary is the one construct the lazy DFA runs over ASCII text alone, so Compiled::new refuses it, naming the rewrite (?:^|\W)word(?:\W|$), or (?-u:\b) over ASCII text. An automaton whose start states pass the cache is refused too. A search error is a give-up. The hybrid feature also gives tree-sitter's regex the lazy DFA, in a release build and in tests alike, so its #match? predicates run on one engine.
alternatives: The meta engine of the regex crate: rejected because it falls back to the PikeVM, whose cost per byte follows the pattern, so only a per-pattern estimate bounds a call

Keep a Unicode word boundary on the PikeVM, charged by weighed NFA states: rejected because the weights are an estimate a constructed pattern outruns, and they overstate every ordinary pattern a thousandfold
Clear the cache when full, as the engine does by default: rejected because each clearing builds the states again, so the construction of one search has no bound
ASCII word boundaries alone: rejected because a word would split at its first letter outside ASCII
origin: quality findings: a work limit in state-bytes, paged with from

choice: Release profile: fat LTO, one codegen unit, stripped symbols, overflow checks, and panic=unwind so serve survives a panic
reason: Cargo.toml [profile.release] sets lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1, strip = true, overflow-checks = true and panic = "unwind": the binary is distributed, so size and speed are worth the compile time, and overflow checks stay on for safety. Unwind is what lets the MCP server answer a request that panics with -32603 and serve the next one; with abort, one bug in one tool call ended the session and every call after it, and the client saw a dead server instead of an error. The lints still deny every panicking path outside tests, so the unwinding machinery is only reached by a bug. The dev profile builds dependencies at opt-level 2 to keep debug builds fast.
alternatives: panic = "abort": rejected, a panic in one tool call kills the MCP session; the lints make panics rare, not impossible
Default release profile: rejected, the binary is distributed and its size and speed matter

choice: repair_anchors takes listed repairs, all or none, or a map from stale anchor to repair, of which the store leaves a repair the bar refuses or cannot judge; the store reads no code
reason: The store imports no code index and runs no project git, so which anchor repairs which is the caller's. A listed repair is held to what every op is held to: the decision exists, it holds from, from and to are anchors by the anchor rules, and to differs from from, each refusal naming repairs[j] and the part at fault; an empty list is no_repair. A map is applied where the op runs to every decision ever accepted that holds a key, so a planned anchor is never moved, and a key no decision holds is passed over. A repair to an anchor the decision holds already drops the stale one rather than refusing. A repair never grows a decision's list, so the limits on the whole list are not judged. Each anchor a repair brings is held to the patterns alone, as the op runs, over the caches and the bytes of the batch. A listed repair the bar refuses refuses the batch, naming that decision as the op's node and the repair that brought the anchor.
