A repair of the map the bar refuses, or a pattern cannot judge, is undone and left in Applied::left with its rule, and the others are written: the caller wrote none of them. A change of anchors leaves the status alone. Applied::repaired lists each anchor replaced.
alternatives: Refuse a repair to an anchor the decision holds already: rejected because every repair the tree shows would then fail on a decision that held both
Judge a repaired decision on its whole list: rejected because one decision already past anchors_max, or one holding an anchor a pattern refuses, would block every repair of the tree
Let the store compute the repairs: rejected because store imports only error, console and git for its own repository
Refuse the batch on a repair of the map the bar refuses: rejected because the caller wrote none of them, and an earlier op filling a cache would turn a repair into the batch's refusal

choice: A file's index holds its scopes and definitions for every kind, and Rust's module files and invoked names apart in RustFacts, empty for every other kind
reason: The forward walk of module files and the hint on a name only an invocation spells read facts only a Rust file states, and a language the general resolver reads has none of them; held beside the scopes and definitions as fields of every index, they would read as facts of every language. Grouped in RustFacts, they are Rust's by their type, the role walk and the resolution read index.rust, and another language's index leaves them empty, which costs two zero counts in its cache entry. A per-language fact type would be an abstraction with one implementation, since no other language has a second step over its files but its test places, which are data in its row.
alternatives: Option of RustFacts: rejected because every reader would unwrap an option whose None and empty mean the same
A trait or enum of per-language facts: rejected because Rust is the one language with such facts, and an abstraction with one implementation is none

choice: serve starts with no store or an old one; every tool call finds the store from the server's directory and is refused naming trurlic init or trurlic migrate
reason: serve refused to start without a .trurlic/ or with one in another format, so a client showed a failed server with no reason, and an install that registers serve for every project could not serve a directory with no graph. The server now keeps the directory it was started in, and each tool call runs discovery::discover from it: no store is the no_project refusal, whose message names trurlic init, and a store in another format the unsupported_format refusal naming trurlic migrate (or an upgrade). initialize and tools/list answer either way. Finding the store per call costs a walk of stat calls where the tree holds its graph, and two git processes in a linked worktree of a shared graph, and keeps the server free of state: the call after an init or a migrate is served without a restart.
alternatives: Refuse to start: rejected, the client shows a failed server with no reason, and the fix is not named
Find the store once at start: rejected, an init or a migrate while the server runs would need a restart

choice: One Error enum with thiserror and a crate-wide Result alias; install returns its own InstallError, and a tool's CLI twin the tool's ToolError
reason: Every module and every command except install uses the one Error enum (src/error.rs) with #[derive(thiserror::Error)] and a type alias Result<T> = std::result::Result<T, Error>; there is no separate store error. Every variant has a descriptive #[error("...")] message. A failure that comes from a file names it: Error::Io { path, source } and Error::Toml { path, source } print the path first, and there is no From impl for std::io::Error or the toml errors, so a ? cannot drop the path. Error::io(path) and Error::toml(path) are the map_err adapters. An I/O call with no file behind it (a standard stream, the working directory, the path of the running binary) is Error::System { what, source }, naming the call. Cases callers branch on are data, not sentences: VersionMismatch, NoMigration and BadFormatVersion, which MCP reports as unsupported_format; NodeTooLarge { path, max }; InvalidPath { path, fault } with the AnchorFault; CheckFailed with the issue count; PlacementUnknown with its PlacementDoubt and ConstrainsCycle with the cycle's members, the two refusals of migrate. A git invocation that cannot run is GitMissing or GitSpawn, and one that fails is GitFailed with its directory, arguments, exit status and stderr. The error module imports types from store alone. A batch apply refuses is Error::Refused with the store's typed Refusal. trurlic install, which never opens a store, returns commands::install's InstallError, which wraps Error for its I/O; the CLI twins of the tools return the tool's own ToolError, so a command refuses as the call does, and Error has a variant for neither.
alternatives: Per-module error types with conversions: rejected because the crate is a single binary and the added indirection provides no benefit
Use anyhow for ad-hoc errors: rejected because typed errors enable match-based handling and better compile-time guarantees
A GitError type of the git module that Error wraps: rejected because Error would then name a module that is not store, and a public Error variant cannot hold a crate-private type

choice: The tools/list result is built once in a LazyLock, spec-built tools first, and returned by reference
reason: The tool catalogue never changes while the server runs: TOOL_DEFINITIONS builds it on first access from every spec-built tool's definition (its input schema walked from its Args) followed by the hand-written schemas of the tools that predate specs, and every tools/list answer serializes it by reference. is_listed reads the same value, so a call is refused as an unknown tool exactly when tools/list does not list it. The initialize answer is built per request, since it carries the protocol revision negotiated with that client.
alternatives: Rebuild tool definitions on each request: rejected because the data never changes at runtime
Embed tool schemas as compiled-in byte slices: rejected because they are harder to maintain, with no advantage over JSON built once in a LazyLock

choice: status computes its anchors section, with counts.anchors by kind, only when section asks for it, judged in the calling tree alone; origin narrows it to the decisions recorded under it
reason: The anchor findings read every source file of the tree, while the rest of status reads the graph's files: on the seeded corpus of 2000 decisions and its generated tree the findings take about three times a whole default status call warm and nine times cold, and status is called often. So the default report leaves the section out, and section: anchors gives it the whole budget, its items unresolved first, each with decision, anchor, kind and cause, and its counts by kind in counts.anchors; more names trurlic check, which prints every finding. status asks the project's git nothing, so the section holds what the calling tree alone shows: unresolved, malformed, ambiguous, unverified and weak. On a terminal the count line is printed even with no finding, so a clean tree is told from one not asked. origin narrows which decisions are judged, never the verdict on an anchor.
alternatives: Every report holds the section: rejected because each status call would read the whole tree for findings most calls do not use
A separate tool for the findings: rejected because status already carries sections fitted to the budget, and the surface is six tools

choice: status lint shows each rule of the bar a stored decision breaks, warn patterns too, judged by the store's Bar::audit_limits and Bar::audit_pattern; never an error, never a refusal
reason: A write holds an op to the bar only in the fields it changes, so a graph below its bar loads, passes check and stays revisable; the section makes that graph visible. The rules keep one home: Bar::audit_limits and Bar::audit_pattern in store::quality judge a whole stored decision and return every fault where a write stops at the first. Each fault carries the field, the element, the level and the typed QualityFault a refusal carries, so lint restates no rule or limit. A pattern that reads origin judges the stored origin on its own, as judge_origin judges a batch's, and the other fields it reads as judge_patterns does. So one pattern can give a finding in a field and one in the origin, as a write gives two; a test holds the audit to the write over the seeded corpus. The text rules of store::text are validation issues already, reported under issues and failed by check, so the audit leaves them out. require_origin binds a batch that records, and a stored decision without an origin predates it or was written by hand, so the audit does not apply it. A warn pattern is a finding marked with its level, since a graph below its own bar shows here first.
alternatives: Report the first fault per decision, as a write does: rejected because a decision fixed in one field would show its next fault only on the next call
Restate the limits in lint: rejected because two homes of a rule drift apart
Apply require_origin to stored decisions: rejected because every decision older than the key would be a finding nothing can fix but a rewrite
Read the origin after the fields, one match per pattern: rejected because a write judges a batch's origin apart from its ops, and a match in the origin would hide behind one in a field

choice: status has a lint section whose items are a LintItem enum tagged by kind: a duplicate names its two decisions, first by name, and its score; a page's pairs best first, then by names
reason: Findings of other kinds will join the section, the code index's anchor findings and the quality checks over the graph, each with fields of its own. So an item is an enum whose kind tag names the variant and whose fields are declared once in its Output, a new kind being one more variant. The decision field is common to every kind; a duplicate adds other and score, a string of six decimals so every machine prints the same text. Pairs come a page at a time, best first then by their names within the page, so the ones most worth reading lead it. The budget cuts a page's pairs while they are listed by probe, so the page ends at a probe and the next page lists the rest. The quality and file-anchor findings are further variants.
alternatives: An item of kind and message, as issues have: rejected because a caller merging a pair would parse names out of prose
The score as a JSON number: rejected because a float's text is the printer's, and six fixed decimals are the same bytes everywhere

choice: status reports what the graph's files and a shared graph's own history hold; whether git contradicts the placement, which needs the project's git, is check's alone
reason: status is a read an agent calls often, and the placement facts cost several git processes in the project's repository (toplevel, ls-files, check-ignore, worktree list) on every call; the history findings run git only in a shared graph's own repository, which the store runs already. One rule: status reads the store, check also runs the project's git. Its sections: the validation issues, the history findings, each component's decision counts, the likely duplicate pairs, the quality findings and the decisions with only file anchors under lint; beside the counts, how many limits and refusing and warning patterns [quality] sets. origin narrows the counts, the component rows and the lint findings to the decisions recorded under it.
alternatives: Placement issues in status: rejected because every status call would spawn git in the project's repository for a fact that changes only with git operations

choice: stdout and stderr are written only through console (out!, diag!) and the MCP transport, enforced by lint
reason: Under `serve`, stdout carries JSON-RPC, so one stray print corrupts the stream, and println! panics when stdout is closed (`trurlic status | head -0` died with SIGABRT while release builds aborted on a panic). The console module owns the streams: out! returns a failed write as Error::System ("cannot write to stdout: Broken pipe") so the command fails with status 1, and diag! drops a failed diagnostic since stderr is where it would be reported; no command prompts. Cargo.toml denies print_stdout and print_stderr, and clippy.toml's disallowed-methods refuses std::io::stdout and stderr; console's two accessors and the transport's stdout lock in mcp::run_server are the only #[expect] sites. Under cfg(test) the console writers print through println!/eprintln!, which the test harness captures per test.
alternatives: Keep println!/eprintln! and only lint stray prints: the panic on a closed pipe stays, and every command keeps its own copy of the output path
Pass a writer into every command: tests could assert on output, but it threads a parameter through every command signature for one destination
A logging crate (log/tracing): a dependency for what two functions do, and stdout must stay protocol-only anyway

choice: store::text is what every graph file holds, an issue check reports; the quality bar binds only writes, so a graph below it loads, passes check and stays revisable
reason: A text rule guards what a reader sees: a hidden, reordering or control character or tool-call markup in any text. It also guards each field's shape: a choice on one line within 200 bytes, a blank alternative or tag, a tag or an origin on two lines. A hand edit that breaks one must fail check, so validation reports it. The bar measures how good a decision is: at least one alternative and one anchor, and the limits and patterns of the project's [quality]. A migrated graph holds decisions without alternatives or anchors, and a project may tighten its bar at any time; as validation issues, the bar would fail check on every such graph at once. So the bar refuses a write alone, and the breaches a graph already holds are a section of status, never an issue of check. A write holds each op to the text rules, the limits and the patterns as it runs, in one order (Bar::judge).
alternatives: Make the bar validation issues: rejected because every migrated graph and every tightened [quality] would fail check at once
Move the text rules into the bar: rejected because a hand edit holding a bidi control or a leaked tool call would then pass check

choice: A file the general resolver reads is test code whole in a test place its language's row lists, Python's tests/ and test_*.py and C's tests/ and *_test.* among them
reason: A file's bytes do not say whether pytest reads it as a test module, so the place is a rule of the second step over the tree, and the places are data in the language's row, as its query is, not a branch of code per language. A fixture in conftest.py, a helper module under tests/ and a module pytest collects by its name are test code though no test function stands in them. A place is a directory name anywhere above the file, or a file name in which one * stands for any run of characters. The rows list Python's tests/, test_*.py, *_test.py and conftest.py; TypeScript's __tests__/ and the *.test and *.spec names over .ts, .mts and .cts, and over .tsx, .js, .jsx, .mjs and .cjs for TSX; C's and C++'s tests/, test/, and the *_test and *_unittest names over each extension of the language. Rust's places stay Rust's own rule, its crate's tests directory and the forward walk of module declarations, since they need its crates.
alternatives: The bytes alone: rejected because a helper in conftest.py would be counted as code
Places written as code per language in roles.rs: rejected because a language is data, and a new one would need code
Read pytest's configuration for testpaths and python_files: rejected because the index keeps no INI or TOML values, and the defaults cover the conventional layout

choice: Test code is under an attribute whose path ends in test, or bench, or a cfg that holds only under test; a file is test code under its crate's tests/, or when only test code declares it
reason: A diff review leaves tests out of the share of code no decision covers, and a decision's proof must be a test, so each definition says whether it is test code. #[test], #[tokio::test] and every attribute path ending in test mark a test function, and #[bench] a benchmark. A cfg predicate marks test code only when it holds under test alone: test, an all() that holds test, an any() whose every member does. Outer and inner attributes mark the item and everything under it, a plain comment between attribute and item included. The file rule reads the tree in the second step: from each crate's targets as cargo finds them without a manifest table (src/lib.rs, src/main.rs, build.rs, and the files of src/bin, tests, benches and examples) it follows each file's recorded mod name; declarations forward, to name.rs or name/mod.rs in the module's directory, which takes a segment for each inline mod around the declaration and none for a function or other item, or to the file a relative #[path] names; an absolute #[path] names no file of the tree. A file is test code when it is under its crate's tests/ or only test code reaches it, and one no target reaches keeps what its bytes say. A crate of its own under tests/ is code by this rule.
alternatives: Mark test code by file name or a tests segment anywhere in the path: rejected because a module named tests under src is not always test code, and the declaration says which
Treat any cfg that mentions test as test code: rejected because cfg(any(test, feature)) builds into a release with the feature
Guess the declaring file backward from a file's path: rejected because lib.rs beside main.rs, a module declared twice and #[path] all defeat the guess
Read the manifest's target tables: rejected because the index keeps no TOML values, and the conventional layout covers this repository and the production project

choice: The 0.3 write tools, the CLI add, rename, remove, decide and gc, and the 0.3 workflow reads are deleted; apply is the one write that replaces them
reason: The write tools wrote the 0.4 shapes (attribution, code_refs, history, patterns, graph.toml), and porting them to the new store would be code written to be deleted when the single write tool replaces them. Deleted with them: record_decision, update_decision, remove_decision, record_pattern, remove_pattern, add_component and add_connection, and the reads check_pattern, get_decision_history, get_architecture and verify_against_decisions, which served the deleted workflow or a deleted node kind; apply, on MCP and as trurlic apply, is the one write that replaces them, its ops covering what they did (record, revise, rename, merge, remove, the component ops), with the cascades and checks in the store; tools/list holds apply and status, then get_context and get_decisions_for_file until brief replaces them. A hand edit stays legal: every load validates it, and trurlic fmt and check hold it to the same rules.
alternatives: Port the 0.3 write tools onto the new store: rejected because the single write tool replaces them soon after
Keep the CLI write commands meanwhile: rejected because each would need cascade and validation logic that a hand edit gets from the load
Keep verify_against_decisions: rejected because it listed the decisions on each changed file without judging the change, which get_decisions_for_file already answers

choice: The CLI keeps a required --ide whose one value is claude-code; project commands, tool twins and install are three groups, each reported alike
reason: --ide stays required with a one-variant ValueEnum (InstallIde::ClaudeCode): help lists the one accepted value, any other value is refused by clap with exit status 2, and main destructures the variant in its pattern, so a second target fails to compile until it is handled. cli::Command holds the flattened ProjectCommand (init, query, serve, check, fmt, migrate, which return Error), the flattened ToolCommand (the twins apply and status, which return the tool's ToolError) and Install, which needs no working directory and returns InstallError. main sends each to report, generic over Display, so every command fails the same way: error and its message on stderr and exit status 1.
alternatives: Drop --ide or make it optional with a default: rejected, the first breaks `trurlic install --ide claude-code` as typed and the second adds a bare `trurlic install` form that the rewrite would have to keep or break
Accept --ide as a string checked against "claude-code" and discard it: rejected, an untyped value the code never reads, with no compile error when a target is added
A cli-level enum over Error and InstallError returned by run: rejected, a third error type whose only job is Display, and every arm of run would convert into it
Box<dyn std::error::Error> from run: rejected, it erases two concrete types to print them

choice: A C or C++ definition is at the path its source writes: members under their type, X::f out of class a function at X::f, a friend under its class, a constructor only in the class it names
reason: An anchor names a definition as a reader of the file finds it. An enumerator is under its enum (color::RED), a nested type under its outer one, a member of an anonymous struct or union under the outer type, and a struct no tag names under the typedef that names it; a template's arguments are no part of a name, so a specialization shares its template's path, and an anonymous namespace adds no segment. A definition out of its class (void a::Foo::f() {}) is a function at a::Foo::f, since no syntax says whether a::Foo is a class. A friend is a function under the class that declares it. A declaration with no type is a constructor only in the class it names, a template one and one of a class defined by a qualified name (struct A::B {) among them; elsewhere it is a macro's call (BIT(flag);) and defines nothing. A function that returns a function pointer and one whose name stands in parentheses (int (max)(int, int)) are functions. A lambda a namespace binds is a function, any other a scope of its own. A concept is an interface, a named set of requirements a type meets by its shape. Each name a structured binding at a namespace's top binds is a variable. A body no definition captures, a misparse's, is a scope whose locals define nothing, so a class a macro hides yields no variables at the top.
alternatives: Enumerators and nested types at the file's top, as the language scopes them: rejected because a symbol is a suffix and the nesting as written costs nothing
A method's kind for X::f when the file defines a class X: rejected because it guesses
Specializations named with their arguments: rejected because a symbol could then not name the template and its specializations together
A concept as a type alias: rejected because it names no type, only a requirement on one
A misparsed body's locals at the top: rejected because the members of a class a macro hides then read as variables of the file
origin: c and c++ review: macro scope, shapes and visibility

choice: The duplicate score is integer arithmetic: idf in Q32 from a fixed-point ln, exact weights and dot products, the threshold tested exactly in 256 bits, a score printed to six decimals
reason: What a call returns must be a function of the files, byte for byte, and a float's ln comes from the platform's libm, which need not round it the same on two machines. sqrt is correctly rounded by IEEE 754, but the score has no use for a float once ln is an integer. So fixed::ln computes ln in Q64 by k ln 2 plus an atanh series, within 90 units of 2^-64, pinned against 100-digit values; the inverse frequency is rounded to Q32; weights, their squares and dot products are exact integers whose sums saturate and cannot overflow for a 1 MiB text; the test (2 dot)^2 >= |a|^2 |b|^2 is exact in 256 bits, so a pair whose cosine over the weights is exactly 1/2 is listed; the score divides by integer square roots and is within 2^-29 of the real-valued cosine, printed rounded half up to six decimals.
alternatives: f64 with the platform's ln: rejected because two machines can differ in the last bits, and a pair at the threshold or a printed digit can flip
f64 rounded to six decimals before comparing: rejected because rounding moves the boundary without removing it
A big-number or decimal crate: rejected because a 256-bit product and a series of twenty terms are a few dozen lines

choice: A page of the duplicates pass keeps its probes' pairs by a bounded selection over a total order, probe first, and ends before a probe whose pairs pass what a result holds
reason: A graph whose decisions share one text has a pair for every two of them, half a million at a thousand decisions, while a status result holds a few hundred. So each probe offers its pairs to a bounded selection, a heap that keeps one more than the limit of the smallest keys of the order probe, score descending, other decision, and counts each probe's pairs. The kept pairs are then those of the earliest probes: the page ends before the probe of the first pair past the limit, but for a first probe whose own pairs pass it, of which it keeps the best and moves on. The key order is total, so the kept pairs are the same whichever order the pairs come in, which lets the probes run on the thread pool, each task with its own selection, merged after; a walk at one thread and eight gives the same pages. status asks for the budget over the smallest duplicate finding, apply's nearest for three.
alternatives: Collect every pair, then fit: rejected because memory and time grow with the pairs, not with the result
A fixed count of pairs: rejected because the count a result holds follows from the budget and the size of a finding

choice: The example [quality] ships as examples/quality.toml, a generic bar for decisions agents follow, which a test loads through the real reader and holds to its own bar
reason: A config kept in the README alone rots: a renamed key or a pattern that no longer compiles goes unseen. A file a test loads is read as every project.toml is, compiled, shown to let a decision at its bar through and to refuse one below it, and written back canonical. Its rules translate a length and style bar for decisions into keys and patterns; a rule that needs judgment, such as no measurement in a reason, is a warn. It names no project. The apply bench runs under it.
alternatives: A block in the README: rejected because no test reads it
This repository's own table as the example: rejected because it holds this repository's rules, such as ASCII prose, not a general bar

choice: The format after 0.4.0 is 0.4.1, the version key rename, so the restructure that follows keeps the name 0.5.0
reason: Each format change takes its own version and one migration step, because a store must state exactly the shape it holds: the 0.4.0 to 0.4.1 step renamed one key and kept the 0.4 node shapes, so stamping it 0.5.0 would have claimed a layout it did not have. The restructure into node files only is its own step, from 0.4.1 to 0.5.0. The numbers only order formats; the registry decides which ones exist, and a version no chain leads from is refused.
alternatives: Number formats with one integer counter - rejected: the plan, the CHANGELOG and the docs name formats 0.4 and 0.5, and every historical store states a three-part version
Fold the key rename into the 0.5.0 restructure - rejected: a store would state 0.5.0 while it holds 0.4 shapes, and one step would carry two changes

choice: The general resolver walks each node once with a frame per ancestor, starts the query at each named node at depth 0, and refuses a hit match limit or predicates past budget
reason: A query cursor run once over a whole tree walks invisible ancestors at every node, which goes quadratic on the deep error trees of hostile input; started at each named node with a start depth of 0, it matches each pattern only where the pattern is rooted, in linear work and with the same matches on real code. Node::parent and prev_sibling descend from the root, so each costs the node's depth: the walk keeps a frame per ancestor instead, built from its parent's (its kind and span, whether a test mark holds it, the innermost visibility mark, how far each span growth and wrap reaches from it, and where the run of each preceding set's siblings right before it starts). A capture names a node at or below its match's root, which the preorder walk reaches then or later, so what it captures waits by node id until then. A match limit that is hit drops matches without a sign, so it refuses the file; the text predicates read goes through a provider that charges it to SCAN_WORK_PER_BYTE, so a predicate over a large node at every level of a deep tree is refused, never quadratic.
alternatives: One cursor over the whole tree with a progress callback: rejected because the ancestor walks it goes quadratic on are work its counter does not see
Node::parent in span growth: rejected because each call descends from the root, quadratic on a deep tree
Keep the matches found before the limit: rejected because the index would be partial with no fault to report

choice: git is a leaf module that runs the git CLI as a child process, with a typed function per question and -z output, and the graph's own repository in git::graph; no libgit2
reason: The plan calls the git CLI rather than libgit2, a C library with its own configuration and repository discovery. Discovery, init and check ask it for the top of a work tree, the common dir, the worktree list and the files the index tracks or an ignore rule matches, and under shared placement the store's writer protocol commits through it to the graph's own repository (git::graph), so the runner must be one every module can use: a top-level module like budget and console, importing nothing but error, so no arrow points from it to another module. Each question is a function with typed arguments and a typed answer (tracked returns the paths ls-files -z lists, toplevel None outside a work tree), running git -C <dir> with stdin closed; -z output is split on NUL and read as raw bytes into paths, so no name is quoted or cut at a newline. A missing binary is Error::GitMissing, a spawn failure Error::GitSpawn, and a nonzero exit Error::GitFailed with the directory, the arguments, the status and stderr. The module holds only the functions a caller needs.
alternatives: libgit2 through the git2 crate: rejected because the plan calls the CLI, and a C dependency brings its own discovery and configuration rules
git inside store: rejected because a writer protocol and a command both need it, and process spawning would sit in the module that holds the graph
git inside commands: rejected because the store's history commits will need it, and store may not import commands

choice: git in the graph's repository names it outright, reads no system or user configuration, overrides with -c each local key that runs code or changes bytes, and stages bytes unconverted
reason: Nothing from the caller's or the user's configuration may break or redirect a history commit. --git-dir and --work-tree name the repository, so git discovers nothing, a missing .git is git's error and never the project's repository answering, core.worktree is beaten, and the ownership check of discovery does not apply. GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM and GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL (the empty file) shut out the system's and the user's files whole: their keys are open-ended (include, init.templateDir, user.useConfigOnly, core.compression and more), and no list of overrides could name them all. The repository's own configuration, which no variable shuts out, is overridden with -c where a key runs code or changes bytes: core.hooksPath to the empty file (no hook runs, .git/hooks/ included, since --no-verify skips only two), core.fsmonitor, core.excludesFile and core.attributesFile (read from $XDG_CONFIG_HOME when unset), core.autocrlf, core.fileMode (an exec bit is no change; every graph file is 100644), commit.gpgSign. The identity is set in the environment, which beats every key, and GIT_AUTHOR_DATE and GIT_COMMITTER_DATE are removed, so the dates are git's clock. git init runs with --template= and --initial-branch=main. A file is staged as its bytes by one update-index -z --add --remove --stdin over every path of the commit, which runs the conversions the attributes ask for; the repository's info/attributes, which beats every .gitattributes and core.attributesFile, unsets each converting attribute (text, and with it eol, filter, ident, working-tree-encoding), is written at creation and is checked, and written again when it holds anything else, before every staging, and git commit and git status read through it too. A symlinked node file alone is staged through hash-object -w --no-filters, as the bytes a load reads through it. The commit is git commit --cleanup=verbatim, so a comment character cannot strip a trailer. core.fsync=committed puts objects and refs on disk before the journal that would make the commit again is deleted, and core.fsyncMethod=batch (git 2.37) flushes the loose objects of one object transaction, update-index's and git commit's trees, with one hardware flush before any of them gets its name; a git before 2.37 warns, ignores the value and flushes each object on its own; the index, replaced by a rename, is rebuilt from the last commit if a power loss tears it. tests/integration/history.rs sets a user configuration, an environment and a repository configuration against every one of these, and finds each commit the fixed identity with git's dates on main, holding the bytes on disk, with nothing run.
alternatives: Override the user's configuration key by key: rejected because its keys are open-ended, and one missed key breaks or redirects a commit
Run git with an empty environment: rejected because git needs PATH and HOME, and the locale of its messages is the user's

Stage with hash-object -w --no-filters and update-index --index-info: rejected because hash-object opens no object transaction, so every object is a hardware flush of its own, 18 to 21 s for the first commit of a 2000-decision seeded graph against 0.6 s
Stage with git add: rejected because it passes over ignored paths, which a hand edit's commit must hold, and its porcelain defaults change between releases
Commit with commit-tree and update-ref: rejected because it is four processes where git commit is one, and the repository's attributes make git commit read bytes unconverted
Pass safe.directory: rejected because an outright --git-dir skips the ownership check that reads it

choice: Each file's index is cached in .state/symbols/ in a compact encoding under the hash of its kind, grammar, versions and bytes; a read writes its misses when the exclusive lock is free
reason: Parsing every Rust file of a large tree on each status call costs more than reading cached indexes, and the gap grows with the tree. The key is by content, with the file's kind, the identity of the kind's tree-sitter grammar, the span hash scheme, INDEX_FORMAT and every bound the index is built within (BOUNDS), the sizes of its values and each kind's room among them. So an entry is never read under other rules or bounds, and the trees of one shared graph share entries. A fingerprint test of the fixture corpus, a case per rule and per bound, makes a change to how a file is indexed raise INDEX_FORMAT. An entry is a sum, its key and a binary encoding, within the room of its file (an-entry-s-room-is-its-file-times-what-its-kind-s-densest-definitions-cost). A read charges an entry as the write did before it allocates, within the room of the file it is read for, a fault's alone past the kind's size. So every entry a write makes reads back, and a forged one and its decode take no more memory than that room. A read takes no lock to read entries, which are renamed over their names. After its own work a read tries the exclusive lock without waiting and skips the write when it is busy: the cache is never authoritative. A torn, swapped or unreadable entry is a miss, and one entry that fails to write stops no other. The directory is bounded without a clock: past twice the call's live set and 256, every entry outside the set goes.
alternatives: No cache: rejected because each status call would parse the whole tree, which grows with the project
Key by path and modification time: rejected because a checkout can keep a time, and the trees of a shared graph would not share
Wait for the lock to write: rejected because a read would then stall behind a writer for an optional speedup
One read cap for every entry: rejected because a forged entry near a cap sized for the largest file cost every call seconds and gigabytes, whatever file it named
Prune by age: rejected because it needs a clock, which a read has no business reading

choice: The lint section lists duplicates, then quality findings, then file-anchor-only decisions, each kind fitted to the budget on its own and counted in counts.lint
reason: Duplicate pairs grow with the square of the decisions and quality findings with the decisions times the rules, so in one list cut by its prefix the first kind would crowd out the others. Each kind is a part of the level search on its own, so a short kind stays whole and the long ones share the rest; the section is their kept items in kind order, its total and omitted their sums. Each kind is gathered to lint_limit of its kind, the budget over its own smallest finding, and counted in counts.lint. A lint call alone reads a page of the decisions from from on by name for the pairs' probes and the patterns alike: each kind ends at its own bound or room, the page at the earlier of the two, and counts.lint.pairs and counts.lint.patterns name it in next, so a walk from next to next lists each pair and each finding once. Another call reads the first page of pairs and judges the limits alone. The decisions with only file anchors left out follow the last listed by name. origin narrows the findings to the decisions recorded under it, a pair when either decision is.
alternatives: One list cut by its prefix: rejected because thousands of pairs would hide every quality finding
A section per kind: rejected because the section argument would grow a value per kind, and the kinds share one budget anyway

choice: The lint section judges the [quality] patterns by decision name while their bytes fit MAX_REPORT_PATTERN_BYTES, their caches the page's total, and the page has room; next names where it ended
reason: On the lazy DFA alone a pattern's time is the bytes it reads and the states its caches build, so a page bounds both: Bar::pattern_bytes charges each pattern the texts it reads, one byte more per text, as a write charges them, and the caches of a page grow within MAX_PATTERN_CACHE_TOTAL_BYTES, as a write's do. The section holds no lock. The patterns read the decisions in name order, one decision at a time, while the sum stays within the bound, the first whatever its bytes, so a walk advances. Each pattern keeps one cache for the page. A cache that gives up on a decision, or caches that pass the total over it, end the page before it, so the next page judges it first over fresh caches. When fresh caches fail on the first decision of a page, that is a finding of the decision at refuse, pattern_gave_up or pattern_cache_total, as a write of it is refused, and the page ends after it. The patterns stop at the decision whose findings reach what a page keeps. A page lists whole the quality findings of the decisions before next, the limits' included; next is the first decision the bytes, a cache or the result's room left. A call with from set to next reads on, so a walk from next to next lists every finding once. A decision whose findings alone pass a page lists those that fit, counts the rest and the page moves on. Over one decision the patterns run one task per pattern, so a cache belongs to one thread, and the parts merge by decision and rule.
alternatives: A wall-clock deadline: rejected because the answer would depend on the machine and its load, and lint reads no clock
Charge bytes times weighed NFA states: rejected because on the lazy DFA alone the cost per byte belongs to the engine, so the weights only overstate an ordinary table
Two cursors, one for the bytes and one for the listing: rejected because a walk following one skips the findings the other left out

Reset a cache that gave up and retry the decision a few times a page, naming in a list apart the decisions a fresh cache gives up on: rejected because ending the page bounds it with less, and a give-up is a finding like any other
Every pattern over every decision on the whole pool: rejected because each thread keeps its own cache of each pattern, so memory grows with the threads

choice: git::toplevel answers None outside a work tree: with no .git at or above it runs no git, and --is-inside-work-tree false is None; any other failure is git's error
reason: Git exits with status 128 for "not a git repository" as for every fatal error (dubious ownership, a broken .git file), and its message is translated, so neither the status nor stderr tells the case apart. Its discovery looks for a .git at each directory upward, so the runner does too (git::dot_git, symlinks followed): none means no work tree holds the directory, answered without a process. With one, --show-toplevel answers; when it fails, --is-inside-work-tree prints false inside a git directory or a bare repository, which is None too, and otherwise the first failure stands with git's stderr, as for a linked worktree whose main worktree was deleted. migrate's placement, init and check branch on the None, and the migration names it as PlacementDoubt::NoWorkTree.
alternatives: Parse stderr for not a git repository: rejected because the message is translated and other fatal errors share the status
Treat any status 128 as no work tree: rejected because a broken or untrusted repository would pass for no repository, and a tracked graph in it for one outside git

choice: The step to 0.5 moves each edge of graph.toml into its source file, writes A constrains B as B depends_on A, and refuses one that closes a depends_on cycle
reason: graph.toml goes, so its edges must land where format 0.5 holds them: connects_to in the component that connects, depends_on in the decision that depends, and a constrains edge in the decision it constrains, as the dependency it states from the other end. A belongs_to edge restates the decision's component and goes without a word. A turned constrains edge can close a cycle no 0.4.1 write could make, a depends_on edge one way and a constrains edge the other way along one pair: the step finds the cycles of the depends_on edges with and without the turned edges, and a cycle the turned edges add is Error::ConstrainsCycle naming its sorted members, refused before anything is written, so the owner removes one edge from graph.toml and migrates again. A cycle of depends_on edges alone, which only a hand edit made, is migrated as it is, and check reports it. An edge whose ends are not nodes of its kinds, or of a kind 0.5 has no place for, is a reported loss. Each turned edge is listed in the report.
alternatives: Drop constrains edges: rejected because each states a dependency the graph would lose
Keep a constrains field in 0.5: rejected because it states depends_on from the other end, and every walk and the cycle check would handle two kinds for one relation
Migrate a cycle and leave it to check: rejected because the migration would write a graph with an error that its own step made

choice: The step to 0.5 maps agent to proposed and user or none to accepted, drops history with its count, and moves patterns and component tags out of the graph into the report
reason: An agent's decision is one the owner has not accepted, so it is proposed; a user's, and one with no attribution, which 0.4.1 read as the user's, is accepted, with no accepted_via, since no acceptance was recorded. An attribution 0.4.1 refused to read is a loss and the decision proposed: no acceptance is known. History goes, and the report counts its entries per decision; under tracked placement git keeps the revisions. A pattern leaves the graph whole: the report holds its stem, its name and description fields, the decisions of its member_of edges, the components of its applies_to edges and its tags, as a TOML table the owner can read or turn into a decision. A component's tags, and the project's, leave with it; a decision keeps its tags. project.toml's [project] fields move to the top level, and every node file loses its name field: the stem is the name, and a name that differed from the stem is listed.
alternatives: Map every migrated decision to accepted: rejected because an agent's decision would claim an acceptance the owner never gave
Keep patterns as project-wide decisions: rejected because a pattern names decisions and components, which is no choice, and the owner decides which of them states a rule
Drop pattern and component tags without a record: rejected because they exist nowhere else after the migration

choice: The store judges placement from PlacementFacts that check gathers from git, as the migration takes git's listing; the store asks git nothing about the project's repository
reason: The judgement is pure: ProjectState::placement_issues takes the graph directory and PlacementFacts (no work tree, or the tracked and ignored paths and the main worktree: bare, this graph with the other graphs of the linked worktrees, or elsewhere with its shared graph if any) and returns sorted issues, so each rule is a unit test with no repository. commands/placement.rs gathers the facts in the directory that holds the graph, never inside it: git::toplevel, tracked, ignored and worktrees, then discovery::worktree_graph for each worktree's .trurlic and the placement the main worktree's graph states. The migration's placement is read the same way, through commands/placement.rs tracked and PlacementSource. These are not issues of ProjectState::validate, which every read and every write runs without git. The store runs git only in a shared graph's own repository, through git::graph, for its history.
alternatives: Ask the project's git from the store: rejected because the command can hand the store the answer, and the store's one use of git is the graph's own repository
Judge in commands: rejected because the counting rule is shared with the migration, which lives in the store
Make them validation issues: rejected because validate runs on every read and every write, which would all need git

choice: Before a C or C++ parse, the macros the tree defines only as attributes, specifiers or namespace openings, and the comments inside a continued #define, are blanked; no list of macros is configured
reason: The index runs no preprocessor, and a macro tree-sitter cannot read wrecks what follows it: class LEVELDB_EXPORT DB { reads as a function, FMT_BEGIN_NAMESPACE swallows its namespace, and a comment inside a continued #define ends the directive for tree-sitter-c. A name is blanked when every #define of it is empty, specifiers, attribute forms or other such names, a function-like one with one body not empty, or only namespace openings or closings and an opening is defined. Blanking is spaces in place of the bytes outside directives, comments and literals, so offsets hold, and the parse and the hash read the blanked text. On the corpora measured the tree's own #defines recovered most of the definitions such macros damaged and halved the parse errors, where a list in project.toml recovered next to none past them. What stays unseen is stated where a user reads it: what a function-like macro writes, a macro defined outside the tree, and the segments of a namespace a macro opens. Which #defines reach a file, and how its set is cached, is a-header-s-defines-reach-every-c-or-c-plus-plus-file-and-a-source-file-s-only-itself.
alternatives: A list of macros in project.toml: rejected because it recovered next to nothing past the tree's own
Nothing, tree-sitter's recovery and patterns per damage shape: rejected because a C++ project then loses a third of its definitions

choice: The verdict follows the cause: a missing file or symbol is stale, pending, planned or unresolved; a malformed symbol is an error and an unreadable file a warning, whatever the status
reason: A reader mends each finding differently, so lint::anchors gives each (decision, anchor) one kind and keeps the cause. A missing file or symbol means the code moved, went or is not written yet: on a decision never accepted it is planned and asked of no other worktree; on a decision ever accepted, an accepted one or a proposed revision of one, it is pending with the branch of the first worktree in git's order whose facts resolve it, when the caller asked git, else stale, which check fails on. Only the project's git tells pending from stale, so status judges such an anchor unresolved and gives a planned one no finding. A symbol out of the grammar or on a directory can never resolve as written, so it is malformed, an error whatever the status. A symbol on a kind of file no resolver reads, or on a file that cannot be read or indexed, may name real code trurlic cannot see, so it is unverified, a warning. A symbol that names definitions of several paths is ambiguous, an error, since no reader can tell which one the decision means. check's findings and status's are two types, Finding<Checked> and Finding<Unasked>. Findings sort by kind, the errors first, then by decision and anchor; each distinct anchor is resolved once per call.
alternatives: One stale for every cause: rejected because a file of a kind no resolver reads would fail check although its code exists, and a malformed symbol on a proposed decision would pass as planned though it can never resolve
Name the anchor stale in status too: rejected because status asks the project's git nothing, so it cannot know that no other worktree holds the code
One kind type for status and check: rejected because status would then carry stale, pending and planned kinds it never yields, and check an unresolved one
List planned anchors in status: rejected because the section reports what this tree shows to be wrong, and a planned anchor is not

choice: The walk takes every source file of a language and every Cargo.toml, passing over dot entries, node_modules, __pycache__, __pypackages__, directories a marker names, and symlinks
reason: A count of the tree's definitions needs every source file, and a Rust file's role needs its crate's manifest and the module declarations that reach it, so the facts hold every source file of a language and every manifest; a data or prose file is read when an anchor names it, since none counts as code and a tree's JSON and Markdown can run to megabytes. An anchor's own path is looked at wherever it is, a dot directory or an ignored file included. The rule says what the tree's sources are without asking git, each part a fact a tool states: a dot entry is tool or editor state, the graph, .git and .venv among them; node_modules, __pycache__ and __pypackages__ are the fixed names npm, CPython and PDM install and compile into; a directory holding .git is the top of another work tree, whose definitions would count twice; CACHEDIR.TAG marks a cache, which cargo writes into its target directories; pyvenv.cfg marks a Python virtual environment and conda-meta a conda environment, whatever their names; a symlink is never followed, so a loop cannot hold the walk. A directory named build or target holds source in some trees, so neither name is passed over: setuptools' build copies cost counted definitions twice, never a wrong anchor, since an anchor names its path. status is called often and spawns no process on a tree that holds its graph.
alternatives: git ls-files with --others --exclude-standard: rejected because it spawns a process on every call, and a tree with no git would need a second rule
Parse .gitignore files: rejected because git's ignore rules have many layers (global, info/exclude, negation) that a partial copy would get wrong
Pass over target, build and dist by name: rejected because a module or package of those names holds source, and the tools that fill them mark them or are marked otherwise
Walk the data and prose files too: rejected because they are no code a count of definitions measures, and a lockfile of megabytes would be read on every call

choice: Timestamps are a std-only Timestamp type in the store, written as RFC 3339 UTC strings byte for byte as chrono wrote them
reason: chrono, which typed every stamp, is flagged unmaintained for all versions (RUSTSEC-2026-0543), so cargo deny fails on it. The crate needs one UTC instant that parses, prints, orders and adds a duration, so store::time::Timestamp replaces it on std alone. It holds i64 seconds and u32 nanoseconds since the Unix epoch, within 0000-01-01T00:00:00Z to 9999-12-31T23:59:59.999999999Z: the derived order is time order and a value means the same on every platform. A decision's created stamp is part of its canonical form, and a stamp an older release wrote must read back canonical so that fmt and a migration leave it as it is, so Display writes exactly what chrono 0.4's serde wrote (write_rfc3339 with SecondsFormat::AutoSi and Z): YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS, then the fewest of 0, 3, 6 or 9 fraction digits that hold the nanoseconds, then Z. Before chrono was removed a differential test matched it on 2 million random instants, on every stamp in this repo's graph and on every mutated string the new parser accepts, and the seeded corpus kept its bytes. Parsing is RFC 3339's date-time and nothing else: T or t; 1 to 9 fraction digits; Z, z or a +HH:MM / -HH:MM offset folded into UTC. It refuses a space for T, UTC for Z, signed years, more than 9 fraction digits, the leap second :60, impossible dates and instants outside the range with a TimestampError, which a node file's TOML error reports with the file's path. Civil dates convert with Howard Hinnant's days_from_civil and civil_from_days. Timestamp::now is the crate's one clock read, enforced by a disallowed-methods lint on SystemTime::now, and fails with Error::Clock when the clock reads outside the range.
alternatives: A maintained datetime crate such as jiff or time - rejected: a new dependency and its tree for one instant type that only needs to parse, print, order and add a duration
Keep chrono and ignore the advisory in deny.toml - rejected: an unmaintained crate stays in the build and the ignore entry stops cargo deny from guarding it
SystemTime as the representation - rejected: its range and resolution are per platform (100 ns on Windows), so a 9-digit fraction would not round-trip byte for byte

choice: TOML and JSON define every key path from the document root; an array's elements define their keys under the array's path with no index, so a key two elements hold is one path of two definitions
reason: A configuration anchor names a key, workspace::lints or stages::order, and a suffix names it as a suffix names a Rust item. A TOML key's span runs from its key, or its table's header, to the end of its value and of everything below it, so a table holds its sub-tables wherever their headers are and an implicit table is defined once; its text is hashed whitespace-normalized. An array of tables, or of inline tables, or a JSON array of objects, is one definition of its key over every element, and each element defines its keys under the array's path: an index in the path would change with every insertion, so the key the elements share is one path, which a symbol resolves to with each element's span, and a change to any element moves its hash. A JSON key written twice in one object is the same. TOML is read with the toml crate's spans, whose parser refuses a nesting past its recursion limit; JSON with a scanner of its own that keeps spans, holds its containers on a stack of its own and refuses a nesting past MAX_NESTING and anything that is not JSON at the byte it fails.
alternatives: Index array elements (bin::0::name): rejected because an inserted element would move every later anchor
Merge a key of all elements into one span: rejected because it would span the unrelated keys between them, whose edits would move its hash
serde_json for JSON: rejected because it keeps no spans

choice: TOML is the one format of the graph, one file per node: project.toml, components/<name>.toml and decisions/<name>.toml
reason: Each node is a TOML file whose top-level keys are its fields, with no wrapper table and no name key: the file stem names the node. TOML was chosen for human readability and git-friendly diffs, and one file per node lets two branches that add different nodes touch different files. project.toml's format_version (FORMAT_VERSION) names the format; a change of shape appends a migration step. Every file is written in the canonical form, which leaves out an empty set or list, so a file holds only what it says.
alternatives: One JSON file for the whole graph: rejected because every change conflicts with every other, and it is hard to read
SQLite: rejected because a binary file is opaque in git diffs and adds a C library dependency for a store of a few thousand nodes
YAML: rejected because its implicit typing (the Norway problem) makes values change meaning silently

choice: Rust definitions come from tree-sitter and tree-sitter-rust; TOML, JSON, Makefiles and Markdown are read by lexical resolvers of trurlic's own, with no grammar crate
reason: An anchor names a definition, and a definition is a node of a syntax tree, not a word that a regular expression finds in the text: a name in a string, a comment or a call is no definition. tree-sitter parses any bytes into a tree and recovers from syntax errors, so a file mid-edit still yields the items that parse, and its leaf tokens give the span hash its comment-free normalization. Its grammars are C compiled by the crates' build scripts, so no system library is needed. The crate is used without default features: std adds only debug-graph output and the regex crate's literal optimizations. The serde_json its build script reads with pulls foldhash, under the Zlib license, which deny.toml allows as a permissive OSI license. The data formats need no grammar: the toml crate already gives key spans, and JSON keys, Makefile targets and Markdown headings are a few lines of scanning each, so their grammar crates would add C code and build time for nothing the scanners lack.
alternatives: Regular expressions over Rust text: rejected because a name in a string, comment or call reads as a definition, and spans are guesses
syn: rejected because it refuses a file that does not compile, so a file mid-edit has no index, and it is Rust alone
rust-analyzer as a library: rejected because it is a large, unstable dependency for a question a parse tree answers
tree-sitter grammars for TOML, JSON, Make and Markdown: rejected because each adds C code and a crate for what a short scanner does

choice: trurlic init requires --placement tracked or shared and writes it to project.toml, where placement is a required key
reason: Placement says whether the project's git versions .trurlic/ (tracked) or the graph stays out of it (shared), and how the graph is found and versioned follows from it, so the owner states it once at init instead of inheriting a default that is silently wrong for one of the two. Project.placement has no default, so a project.toml without it is refused at load, and status prints it. This repository is tracked.
alternatives: Default to tracked: rejected because it would choose how the graph is versioned without asking
Detect it from git at init: rejected because a new store has no files whose tracking could tell
Keep placement out of project.toml and ask git on every call: rejected because the answer would change with the state of the working tree

choice: trurlic install has one target, Claude Code, until the installer is rewritten; the other ten config writers are deleted
reason: Users reach Trurlic through their coding agent over MCP, and the installer's only job is to register `trurlic serve` with that agent. Ten of the eleven targets (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Cline, Windsurf, Copilot, Codex, OpenCode, OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Antigravity) did nothing but merge one `trurlic` entry into a JSON, TOML or YAML file at a per-OS path guessed from each client's conventions, with no test against any real client; an entry the user can paste from the README does the same. They carried about 800 lines of writers, path logic, error variants and tests, and the serde_yaml_ng dependency with the unmaintained unsafe-libyaml under it, for one target. Claude Code, the client the owner and the quick start use, stays, so `trurlic install --ide claude-code` works as typed until the installer is rewritten. With the targets gone, tempfile, which only the config writers used outside tests, leaves the release build.
alternatives: Keep all eleven targets: rejected, each is an untested guess at a client's config path and format, kept up to date by nobody, and one of them pulls in a YAML parser built on an unmaintained unsafe C translation
Keep the JSON-file targets and drop only YAML and TOML: rejected, it removes the dependency but keeps the untested per-client path logic and a shared writer for clients the owner does not use
Delete trurlic install altogether: rejected, registering with Claude Code is the second command of the quick start and the rewrite of the installer replaces it, not a gap

choice: Typed ToolEnvelope serialized directly into the JSON-RPC response; its text and its structuredContent come from one fitted value
reason: A tool result is the typed ToolEnvelope (one TextBlock, an optional structuredContent, an optional isError). truncate::fit_value fits a payload once: one that fits is serialized into a buffer that stops at MAX_TOOL_RESULT_BYTES and kept as it is, one that does not is cut and the cut value serialized. structured_result sends that value as structuredContent and its serialization as the text, so the two cannot differ, cut or not, and no text is parsed back, which also failed for a value nested deeper than a JSON reader reads. The envelope goes into the response through Body, an untagged enum beside initialize's and tools/list's values, so protocol::write_success serializes the whole response in one pass into the line it writes.
alternatives: Serialize the text, then parse it back for structuredContent: rejected because it parses every result twice, and a parse that fails sent the uncut payload beside a cut text
Serialize everything through a serde_json::Value intermediate: rejected because to_value then to_writer doubles the allocations on the hot path

choice: A .ts, .mts or .cts file is read by tree-sitter-typescript's typescript grammar, a .tsx file and every JavaScript file by its tsx grammar, each with TypeScript's query
reason: tree-sitter-typescript holds two grammars. The typescript one reads <T>x as a cast, which the tsx one reads as an element, so a .ts file needs it; the tsx one reads JSX, so a .tsx file needs it. JavaScript is a subset of TSX as a grammar sees it: the tsx grammar reads plain, CommonJS and JSX JavaScript with fewer error nodes than tree-sitter-javascript and the same definitions, so a JavaScript file is read by it with TypeScript's query, and no third grammar crate is compiled into the binary. It reads two forms of valid JavaScript differently, stated limits: a comparison chain that reads as a generic call (a < b > (c)), which changes no definition, and a class field named abstract or accessor on a line of its own before another member, which it reads as that member's TypeScript modifier, so the field and the member after it are lost. Flow is no JavaScript and is not read. A file kind is a grammar and its query, so TypeScript and TSX are two kinds, and a .js file shares the tsx kind with a .tsx file, since the same bytes index alike. The query is one file for both grammars, and TSX adds what only its grammar has (JSX text) in a second file read after it.
alternatives: tree-sitter-javascript for JavaScript: rejected because it is a third grammar in the binary and reads JSX with more error nodes
The tsx grammar for .ts too: rejected because it reads a <T>x cast as an element
A file kind per extension: rejected because a .js and a .tsx file of one content would be indexed twice under one rule

choice: Uncommitted covers the graph files, project.toml, components/*.toml and decisions/*.toml one level deep, modified, deleted, new or ignored; never .state/, never another file
reason: The graph is what a load reads, so the history holds exactly that: graph_files are :(glob) pathspecs of the three kinds, one level deep as list_toml_stems reads them. git status runs with --porcelain=v2 --untracked-files=all --ignored --no-renames, so modified, deleted, untracked and ignored graph files all count: no ignore rule can keep a graph file out of the history. .state/ (lock, journal, temp files) is never matched, whatever the ignore rules say, so a lost info/exclude cannot commit the journal. A file that is no graph file, such as notes the owner keeps in .trurlic/, is the owner's: no commit takes it and no finding names it, and the owner may version it by hand.
alternatives: git add -A over the work tree: rejected because it commits .state/ the moment an ignore rule is lost, and every file the owner keeps there
Every .toml at any depth: rejected because a load reads one level, so a deeper file is no part of the graph
Report files that are no graph file too: rejected because the history is the graph's, and the owner's own files are no finding

choice: Validation holds every text a node file holds to store::text, so a hand edit that breaks a text rule in any field is an issue check reports, naming the file and the key
reason: What a reader sees must be what an agent is held to, and a text is read wherever it is: in a choice, a reason, an alternative, a tag, an origin, the accepted text a revision keeps, a component's description. Each field broken by a hand edit is an issue of its own kind (InvalidChoice, InvalidReason, InvalidAlternative, InvalidTag, InvalidOrigin, InvalidDescription), naming the file, the key such as alternatives[1] or accepted_text.choice, the fault and its byte offset, so every surface and every hand edit meet one rule set with one message. A broken text is an issue, not a load failure, so status and the reads still answer and check names every fault in one run. An anchor's file and symbol meet the same character rule as part of their type, whose faults a load refuses with every other anchor fault.
alternatives: Check the choice and the reason alone: rejected because a hidden or reordering character in an alternative, a tag or an origin misleads a reader as much
Fail the load on a text fault: rejected because one character in one file would stop status, check and every read
Normalize instead of reporting: rejected because it silently changes what the author wrote and keeps a leaked tool-call fragment as content

choice: Validation issues carry an IssueKind and a subject, and ProjectState::validate returns them sorted once at its exit
reason: An issue's identity is (kind, subject): the subject is a node name, an edge as `from -> to (field)`, or a cycle's sorted members. The message names the file at fault and what is wrong; it is for people and may change while the issue stays the same, so nothing matches on it. Every issue is an error; a file that is only not in canonical form is no issue but an entry of ProjectState::non_canonical. validate() sorts by kind, subject and message, so the order of the checks never reaches check output or the no-new-issues comparison, and one sort at the single exit holds for a check added later. A repeated tag, anchor or edge reads as one element of its set, and its file is listed as non-canonical until fmt rewrites it, so there is no duplicate-edge check.
alternatives: Iterate every check in BTree order: rejected because every site must stay sorted by convention, and a new check that iterates differently reintroduces nondeterminism silently
Identify issues by message: rejected because counts and file names in a message make the same issue compare unequal across validations
A severity per issue: rejected because a second field beside the kind can disagree with it; what is only a matter of form is a list of its own

choice: A C or C++ prototype is a definition of its function's kind, function or method; a macro is a definition of kind macro where its #define stands; an inline namespace adds its own segment
reason: A kind states what a thing is, not whether it has a body: no reader asks whether a function is defined in the file, and a symbol names every definition of its path, so a prototype in a header and its definition in a source file, two overloads or two arms of #if resolve as one set of one kind. A macro, object-like or function-like, is a definition of the file, and a reader finds it where its #define stands, under the namespace or class that holds the directive; each #define of one name under #if is a member of one set. An inline namespace is written as a namespace, so its name is a segment of what it holds, as any namespace's is. Where every other definition stands, and what defines nothing, is the-definitions-of-a-c-or-c-plus-plus-file-are-at-the-path-their-source-writes.
alternatives: A prototype of its own kind: rejected because no reader asks whether a function has a body, and the set already resolves both
Macros at the file's top, as the preprocessor scopes them: rejected because a reader finds a #define where it is written
An inline namespace as no segment: rejected because its name is written as any namespace's

choice: A C or C++ span hash takes a literal as one token and a macro's body one unit a token of the C lexer; a line continuation is blank between two tokens and spliced inside one
reason: A hash must move with the code and stay under a reformat. A string or character literal, a raw string and an include's path are one token each, their spaces kept, since they are values. tree-sitter keeps a #define's body as one leaf, so the body is hashed by the tokens the blank pass's lexer reads in it, comments left out: a formatter's spacing of an operator, a re-wrap over continued lines and a comment move nothing, and ((a)+1) hashes as ((a) + 1). A backslash before a line break is blank between two tokens, in a body and between nodes; inside a token it is spliced as the preprocessor splices it, so a, a continuation and b are the one token ab, never the two that a b is. The comments of a continued #define are blanked before the parse, which keeps tree-sitter from ending the directive at them. Concatenated strings and digraphs are hashed as written.
alternatives: A macro's body verbatim: rejected because a re-wrap would read as a change
A body hashed one unit a run between blanks: rejected because a formatter's spacing of an operator moved its hash

choice: A Python def is a function, a method directly in a class; a class a class; a name a module or class binds by assignment a variable; type a type alias; an import, a local and self.x define nothing
reason: An anchor names what a reader looks for in a Python file: its functions, its classes and the names its modules and classes bind. A def in a class body, under an if or a try included, is a method; one in a function is a function under that function's path. Each target of an assignment at module or class level is one variable spanning the statement, annotated or not, each of a = b = 1 and of a, (b, [c, *d]) = ... included. A name a function binds is a local, and self.x is an attribute of an instance the class never states, so neither is a definition; an import names what another file defines, which its anchor names there. A type alias, generic or not (type Pair[T] = ...), is a type alias. A .py, .pyi or .pyw file is read. A name is matched as spelled: Python folds an identifier to NFKC, so two spellings that fold alike are one Python name and two here. Definitions of one path, an overload's signatures and its implementation, a property and its setter, the two arms of if TYPE_CHECKING, resolve together. A test_ function, a Test class and a unittest TestCase subclass, TestCase[int] included, with all they hold, are test code, as pytest and unittest collect them.
alternatives: Instance attributes from self.x in __init__: rejected because which assignments a class's instances get is a runtime question no statement of the class answers
Imports as definitions: rejected because the name is defined in another file, which an anchor names instead
Every test prefix pytest collects (test, not test_): rejected because a helper named testing_support would be counted as a test

choice: A Python span hash groups statements and blocks, hashes delimiters, numbers and escapes by meaning, and leaves out docstrings, a ; between statements, and commas and parentheses of no meaning
reason: Python's NEWLINE, INDENT and DEDENT are tokens of no width in no node, so the query marks each statement of a module or a block and each block a group: a statement moved into or out of a block, or split, moves the hash; a re-indented block or two statements joined by ; do not. A string's text is one token with its spaces, cut at each escape. A delimiter, a number and an escape hash by what they mean in Python 3: prefix letters in any case or order and u none, either quote, letters in any case, 1. as 1.0. A line continuation is whitespace wherever it stands. A trailing comma is left out in arguments, parameters, an import list, a parenthesized with, a list, set or dictionary and their patterns, and a tuple of two or more; a one-element tuple and a subscript keep it. Parentheses are left out around a primary, a power under a unary operator, the whole expression of an assignment, return, del, for or condition, a tuple or target there, an assert's message and its condition but a yield, and a class's empty (). Elsewhere they bind an operator, or a comma may follow that a yield inside takes in. Each rule is exact: no two programs of different meaning hash alike. So black and ruff format move a hash only by what no exact rule states: a quote escape added or dropped, strings joined, parentheses elsewhere. An = interpolation's text up to its format specifier is its output, kept as written but its comments; a format specifier is its text, its nested fields hashed as code. A docstring, a class's or function's first statement whose one child is a plain string, is left out.
alternatives: Hash the leaves alone, as for Rust: rejected because a statement moved out of its block would leave the hash as it was
Hash docstrings: rejected because a documentation edit would read as a change to the code
Leave out every comma before a closing bracket and every parenthesis: rejected because (a,) and (a), x[a,] and x[a], f((yield a), b) and f((yield a, b)) would hash alike
Hash a string by its decoded value, joined strings as one: rejected because decoding needs Unicode's name table for an escape such as \N{...}, for the few strings a formatter changes so
State that a reformat moves the hash: rejected because every black or ruff run would then touch a third of a tree's definitions in a diff review

choice: A Rust file defines its items, fields, enum variants and their fields, trait members, what an impl holds and pub use leaves; a container gives what it holds a segment
reason: Every item with a name is a definition: fn, struct, union, enum, trait, type, const, static, mod (inline or declared), macro_rules!, an associated type or const, a trait's method signature, an extern block's items. A struct's or union's named fields, an enum's variants and a struct variant's fields are definitions under their type. A container gives what it holds a segment, a function included, so an item in a body is outer::inner and a test helper is tests::helper; a tuple field has no name and defines nothing. An inherent impl gives its items the type's segment, its generics, path and references dropped, and is no definition itself, so impls spread over a file add to one type and Table names the struct; a trait impl is the definition Type::<Trait>. A pub use leaf, an alias, or a self in a list, is a definition under the module, once per module and name however often the uses repeat it, unless the file defines that path itself (pub(crate) use name after macro_rules! name); a use without a visibility, a glob and an alias _ define nothing. A macro invocation defines nothing (a-macro-invocation-defines-nothing). An item's span takes in its attributes and outer doc comments.
alternatives: Make an inherent impl a definition of the type: rejected because the type's anchor would then span its impl blocks too, and its hash would move with every method
Leave functions out of the container path: rejected because a nested item and a module-level one of the same name would collide
Count every use as a definition: rejected because importing a name is no definition of it

choice: A TypeScript or JavaScript declaration, a class's members, a function or class bound to a name and a name a module binds are definitions; an import and a local define nothing
reason: An anchor names what a reader looks for in a TypeScript or JavaScript file. A function, a generator, an overload's or an ambient declaration's signature, and an arrow function, function expression or class expression a const, let or var binds are functions or classes at any depth, as a nested def is in Python; so is a named class expression an assignment binds (module.exports = class A {}, X ??= class A {}). A class, interface, type alias, enum and namespace are definitions; namespace A.B is two segments and declare module "x" is named x. A class's methods, accessors and constructor are methods and its properties fields, of a class alone: an unnamed class's members (return class { m() {} }) are no one's. An interface's members are fields and methods, an enum's variants. Any other name a const, let or var binds, each of a destructuring's names included, is a variable at a module's or a namespace's top, whatever its keyword, and a function's locals are no definitions. A file a wrapper holds whole (an IIFE, a UMD or AMD factory) is read as its module, and an unnamed module.exports function or class is default, as export default is. An import names what another file defines. Definitions of one path resolve together: overloads with their implementation, a getter and its setter, merged interfaces. A constructor's parameter property, an exports.x or X.prototype.y assignment define nothing.
alternatives: Constant for a const at a module's top: rejected because a const binds any runtime value, and let and var would then name the same thing two ways
A kind of their own for getters, setters and constructors: rejected because each is a method the class holds, as a Python property is
Variables at any depth: rejected because a function's locals are no part of what a module offers
An unnamed class's members under the function around it: rejected because outer::m names a path the source does not have

choice: A TypeScript span hash takes a string or regex as one token, walks a template string, groups each statement and member, drops a ; or , ending one and an empty JSX expression
reason: Automatic semicolon insertion makes a line break carry syntax that no token holds: return then x on the next line is two statements, return x one. The query marks each statement of a program, a block or a switch case, and each member of a class, an interface or a type literal, a group whose marks enter the hash, so the two hash apart; with groups in place the ; that ends a statement and the ; or , that separates two members carry nothing and are left out, so a file with and without semicolons hashes alike. A string and a regular expression are one token with their spaces, quotes as written: prettier's change of quotes, of a trailing comma and of the parentheses around an arrow function's one parameter moves the hash. A template string is walked: its text runs are tokens with their spaces, while a space or a comment inside its ${} moves nothing, and a definition inside one is found. A JSX comment is written {/* c */}, whose braces are tokens: a JSX expression that holds no expression, a comment or nothing, is left out whole. JSX text is hashed as JSX renders it, a token a character and an empty one a run of whitespace, a run at an end of the text that holds a line break dropped, so a reformat moves nothing, Hi there hashes apart from Hithere, and a{/* c */}b hashes as ab.
alternatives: Hash the leaves alone: rejected because a statement split by a line break would leave the hash as it was
A template string as one token: rejected because a space or a comment inside its ${} would move the hash
JSX text verbatim: rejected because a formatter that rewraps it would read as a change to the code

choice: git::worktrees reads worktree list --porcelain -z into typed entries: path, Head (bare, branch or detached) and prunable; unknown attributes are skipped
reason: Discovery takes the main worktree from the first entry, init refuses a shared graph in a bare repository's worktree, and check walks the linked worktrees for second graphs, skipping prunable ones and naming each by its branch. --porcelain -z ends each attribute with NUL and each record with an empty one, so a path is read as raw bytes, a line break in it included; a branch drops refs/heads/ and is read lossily, since it is only shown. HEAD, locked and any attribute a newer git adds are skipped, and a record that does not start with its worktree line, or no record, is Error::GitOutput. The common dir (git::common_dir, joined to the directory when git prints it relative) names the info/exclude a shared graph is kept out of git by.
alternatives: Parse the line-based porcelain output: rejected because a path holding a line break would split a record
Refuse an unknown attribute: rejected because every newer git that adds one would break discovery
